Snopes has debunked similar pieces of media before, including the story that musician Eric Clapton once brought a deaf teenager onstage.

On Sept. 29, 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump's administration launched America.gov, an artificial intelligence chatbot intended to answer questions related to the government. Shortly after, a rumor circulated online that the chatbot said former President Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential vote, contradicting a longstanding claim by Trump that Democrats "stole" the 2020 election.
Trump made the claim that he won the 2020 election as recently as Sept. 9, 2026, saying, "We won the presidency three times," referring to the 2016 and 2024 elections that he won as well as the 2020 election that Biden won.
"Trump just launched an AI government website called America.gov, and it immediately told everyone he lost the 2020 election," one popular Facebook post read (archived).
The claim was true — the America.gov chatbot said Biden won the 2020 election, not Trump. "Joseph R. Biden won the 2020 U.S. presidential election," the chatbot stated.
When the rumor first spread on Sept. 29, screenshots showed similar responses by the chatbot. When we first attempted to verify the claim on Sept. 30, the chatbot deflected, claiming that it "did not provide political commentary."
After several attempts using varied wording, the chatbot then explicitly confirmed Trump was incorrect, as follows (our question in bold):
It then linked to the National Archives and Federal Election Commission results as evidence of Biden's victory.
(America.gov)
Trump announced the chatbot's launch in an event alongside AI tech leaders including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Tesla.
The Associated Press reported that the site was modifying its answers "as Trump was speaking" at the Sept. 29 launch event, changing its response to say it couldn't answer "political questions." According to the AP, it also said that "official federal sources do not show that widespread fraud changed the 2020 presidential election outcome. Isolated election crimes did occur and have been prosecuted."
Snopes did not received the same response when we asked the same question later. As of this writing, it's unclear what the Trump administration's process is for modifying results related to specific topics of inquiry.
We reached out to the White House seeking further information and will update this story if we receive a response.

Tech executives have long touted the potential for their AI models to accelerate the pace of biology discoveries. Last week, they announced one. In a September 23 announcement, Anthropic claimed that its large language model Claude had identified an enzyme system with properties “reminiscent of Crispr,” the Nobel Prize-winning gene-editing tool.
According to Anthropic, about 950 Claude agents running simultaneously found the interesting genetic sequences in 21.5 hours. “I sincerely compliment Anthropic for telling the world about their discovery,” says Fyodor Urnov, a gene-editing expert at the University of California, Berkeley and director for therapeutic R&D at its Innovative Genomics Institute. (IGI is collaborating with Anthropic, but was not involved with the new discovery.)
Other scientists are less enthusiastic about the finding, which is the first to come out of a research group formed by Anthropic earlier this year. “The experiments are still in the queue. The PR is already live,” says Le Cong, a professor at Stanford University focused on integrating AI into genome engineering research.
Anthropic, which has set up a wet lab for drug discovery, has been clear that the finding isn’t the end of its work. (“We don’t yet understand what this system does,” the company said in an X post, “but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA.”) One physical experiment was included in a technical report, which has not been peer-reviewed. However, a lot more needs to be done to determine the significance of this discovery. It remains unknown whether this enzyme system can be used as a gene-editing tool and, if so, whether it’s a useful gene-editing tool.
“Let's say we are on Santa Monica Beach and trying to scan through all the sand to find a diamond,” Cong says. “AI found this thing that looks very shiny, and then you have to go back to the lab to know—is it glass? Is it a diamond?”
Claude found this shiny object after researchers at Anthropic prompted it to search through huge genomic databases for “interesting new examples” of reverse transcriptases, proteins that copy RNA into DNA. This is the opposite of the normal process in our cells, in which DNA is transcribed into RNA, but is used by other organisms in a variety of biological functions, including inserting segments of DNA.
Claude agents initially identified more than 200,000 possible reverse transcriptases, according to Anthropic, and, after picking out several thousand that appeared to be new, narrowed the scope even further, eventually finding an “unusual” reverse transcriptase family containing a long region of repeat DNA sequences that resemble Crispr. Anthropic is calling this system ART, short for array-associated reverse transcriptases. The system is found in jumbo phages, large viruses that infect bacteria.
“I can see by eye a tandem repeat array … that's a Crispr-like … repeat array?!” an AI agent wrote. The agent also acknowledged that this system could be a retron, as noted in the technical report. Crispr and retrons are both bacterial immune systems, and while retrons have some utility in gene editing, they’re not the same multi-tool Crispr is. It’s therefore not too surprising Anthropic’s blog post played up the Crispr comparison.
Seth Shipman, associate investigator at the Gladstone Institutes, doesn’t think what Anthropic found is a new Crispr system, but says the discovery is still interesting. “The novel thing is how they found it, not what it is,” he says. His lab has used retrons to make gene-editing systems, so it is possible to use retrons in this way.
Identifying new reverse transcriptases can take months of mining genome databases manually, so Shipman says the fact that Anthropic was able to do this in a day is impressive. But he cautions against attributing the discovery entirely to an AI model. “I think we have to be careful about saying that Claude autonomously discovered something, because there are scientists involved in the study,” he says.
In fact, this same reverse transcriptase was previously identified by Jason Gill, a microbiologist at Texas A&M University, and his colleagues in a 2021 paper on jumbo phages. What’s perhaps new is that Claude identified repeats around it that hinted the enzyme might be part of a Crispr-like system.
“These models are good at finding patterns, better than a person staring at it with their eyeballs can,” Gill says. “A person could do all this but you have to already have a hypothesis in mind.” He adds that ART appears to have no “obvious relationship” to any known Crispr system, and it’s on Anthropic to prove that it actually has gene-editing activity.
Cong credits the scientists for finding the perfect kind of problem for Claude to tackle, given its pattern-seeking abilities. It’s possible the model could be used for similar large-data projects, but that doesn’t mean Claude will suddenly be accelerating all sorts of discoveries in the life sciences.
What kinds of information this model was trained on is also not something the scientific community can evaluate, which makes these findings unusually opaque in an era where major journals require scientists to freely publish their code in the name of reproducibility. This has also led a researcher who had been studying these exact enzymes to become suspicious that the model was trained on his work, since he’d shared yet unpublished findings with the public version of Claude. (“Claude was,” Anthropic told the New York Times, “not trained on any user transcripts, and our molecular biology team has no such access, either.”)
Even if Claude did identify the next big thing in gene editing, it would still take human scientists testing out that hypothesis in the lab to prove it. In a post on X about the discovery, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei mused, “Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment.” Even if this does prove possible, it will be in a fairly distant future. (The idea, of course, raises many questions about safety and oversight, and Amodei quickly followed up this thought by mentioning that Anthropic’s labs are at the lowest biosafety levels, and thus don’t contain anything greatly harmful to humans.)
Answers in this area don’t come quickly. It took 25 years from the initial discovery of Crispr sequences in bacteria in 1987 until Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier demonstrated it could be a programmable tool to cut DNA in 2012. And while Crispr is now ubiquitous in labs and is being tested in dozens of clinical trials to treat cardiovascular conditions, cancers, autoimmune diseases, and rare disorders, there is only one drug on the market so far that uses the technology, approved in late 2023. It’s a testament to the long arc of scientific progress—and the difficulties of translating promising basic science findings into medicines.
The limits of Anthropic’s finding also point to a more fundamental issue. What made Crispr revolutionary was that scientists identified a biological system that was previously unknown. It remains to be seen whether any AI model is capable of finding something useful without knowing exactly what it’s looking for.
“If you have an AI that only trained on knowledge from before people ever discovered Crispr, and then that AI actually discovered Crispr, that seems to be a better setup to test an AI scientist,” Cong says.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

Recently, I may have saved a woman’s life on the road. Somehow, this was something I had expected to happen.
On that day, I saw a truck leave a construction site with a tangled wire trailing behind. I frantically looked to see what the wire was attached to and spotted the scaffolding a few meters ahead. I shrieked and grabbed the hand of the woman walking in front of me just as the metal pipes came crashing down. We hugged for a brief second, and then walked our separate ways.
Mumbai (pictured top) is a city that is being made every day, and so much of the Bandra-Khar area that I inhabit is never not under construction. Since I moved here from Seoul earlier this year, I have learned to be hypervigilant every time I walk the streets.
I was reminded of that moment last week as news broke about the collapse of a five-storey building in Delhi, which killed seven people. Authorities had flagged safety concerns in the neighbourhood months earlier, the Hindustan Times reported, after 23 people died in a fire at another building.
As the world’s most populous country, India can feel like a place where life can be startlingly cheap, and people die every day in tragedies that could have been prevented. According to analysis of government data by the Times of India, between 2020 and 2004 nearly 33,000 deaths occurred due to building collapses, fires or people falling into pits and maintenance holes.
The collapse in Delhi has prompted questions, once again, about the state of urban infrastructure in India’s biggest cities. At a time when the country is undertaking a rapid infrastructure boom – new airports, high-speed expressways, luxury residential towers– daily life in cities like Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru appears to be deteriorating.
Indian cities are not walkable, they rank among the worst for air quality, construction is poorly regulated, seasonal flooding is common and waste management remains under pressure. These challenges are only going to increase; the World Bank expects India’s urban population to double, going up to 951 million, by 2050. More than half of the urban infrastructure the country will need by then has yet to be built, it said.
So, what would it take to make our cities better and safer? The experts I spoke to broadly agreed that Indian cities don’t lack rules as much as the political will and institutional machinery to enforce them.
For infrastructure veteran Vinayak Chatterjee, one solution lies in giving urban local bodies more power. He points to a constitutional amendment from 1992 that was meant to strengthen municipalities and give them greater responsibility over urban planning. “But it remains largely unimplemented – in spirit and will. It is a serious matter that affects the very fabric of our urban existence,” said Chatterjee, founder of the Infravision Foundation.
Rahul Goel, an expert on transportation safety and a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, believes the problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking. “People are using public space for personal use. Everything becomes better when you remove on-street parking,” he said, arguing that freeing up roads would make pedestrians and cyclists safer, reduce traffic jams and make walking easier.
In other cities in the global south, from Bangkok to Manila to Cape Town, one cannot just park their car on the road to run errands, Goel said. He described it as a governance failure, saying there is a need to create more parking spaces and perhaps have civil defense personnel or municipal workers enforce fines.
“Our streets are self-run,” Goel said. “That’s why they are in complete disarray.” He pointed to the Delhi Metro as an example of a space where people follow rules and things are orderly. “When rules are enforced, people follow them.”
The same gap between rules and enforcement is evident at construction sites.
India has detailed guidelines for construction approvals, including how traffic must be managed, what signage must be put up, and creating paths for pedestrians. But compliance remains a significant problem, says Geetam Tiwari, emeritus professor at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. In an audit of construction sites on highways, including bridges, Tiwari and her colleagues found widespread violations. Contractors had a financial incentive to complete projects quickly with payments being tied to the pace of construction, she said, adding that penalties for violations were low enough that it was cheaper to simply pay the fine than make fixes.
For unsafe buildings and unauthorised renovations, Tiwari said, the solution also requires bringing stakeholders together: resident associations, landlords, lessees and local authorities to conduct audits, raise awareness and penalise contractors who violate safety requirements. Actions, she said, that should not wait for the next tragedy.
In the aftermath of the Delhi case, the high court has directed authorities to inspect student accommodations for safety. Building owners have been arrested and several municipal officials in charge of the area have been suspended.
A similar governance deficit shows up when it comes to air pollution, another long-time challenge for Indian cities. Ronak Sutaria, founder and CEO of Respirer Living Sciences, has been working on one aspect of this issue: by developing affordable air-quality monitors for construction sites. Respirer’s air-quality monitors are now installed in 5,000 locations across 10 cities in India, helping authorities identify pollution hotspots. (Some cities, including Mumbai, require construction sites to monitor pollution levels.)
“A number of sites are getting alerts [from authorities] and are taking dust-suppression measures, for instance, to bring down [pollution] levels. So, the entire loop is sort of working,” Sutaria said.
Indian cities continue to grow, but the question is whether governance can keep pace. On that afternoon in Bandra, I recall thinking how lucky the woman and I were not to be grievously injured. But we shouldn’t have to rely on luck to survive.

Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
This week, writer and professor Amitava Kumar (@amitavawriter), whose latest book, The Social Life of Trains, explores how railways helped shape India’s national identity, suggests the work of a poet he discovered on Instagram:
“Can I begin with a confession? I have been a professor of literature for more than three decades, but I don’t often understand poems. How lovely it is, then, to discover a poet whose lines are as clear and beautiful as the dawn! Recently, I came across the poems of a young Hindi poet named Parag Pawan. They spoke to me and, more importantly, they spoke to our moment. I immediately sat down to translate them into English.
A series of his poems could be translated as Poems for the Unemployed. One of the poems, sharp and precise, begins with the funny, acerbic lines: ‘On the topic of our unemployment / the prime minister gives speeches / but he doesn’t give us jobs. / He works for eighteen hours / while we believe that asking anyone to work / for more than eight hours / is exploitation.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing
2,192
That’s the number of days Umar Khalid has spent in jail since his arrest on 13 September 2020 – without trial. Last week, the student activist wrote a searing account describing the daily drudgery of life in prison, published in The Quint. Earlier this year, in his first interview since being jailed, Khalid told the Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Peterson: “Humanity is a privilege that is not granted to people like me.”
Vibe check
As more people read news online, watching Ayan Shaikh (@paperboy_ayan) delivering newspapers with serious swag gave me great joy and some hope. The 22-year-old from Ahmedabad posts videos of it on Instagram, and it’s a feat to watch. Watch his papers swerve, reach gravity-defying heights and land with pinpoint accuracy and tell me his deliveries don’t rival Jasprit Bumrah.
Delivering papers was Shaikh’s first job after he dropped out of school. He spent four years mastering the techniques that would allow him to make faster deliveries to earn more money. The first video, filmed by his friend, had 20m views and a recent one has crossed 128m, more views than many Bollywood stars might command. He starts his day at 4:30am, making 300 deliveries in two hours, before he begins a second shift as a gig worker for quick commerce apps.
“I think people love [the videos] because I do it passionately … from my heart,” he said. “If you do things dedicatedly, anything is possible. It won’t work out once, twice, thrice, but it might on the fourth attempt.”

For a few years now, the PS5 hacking community has been chipping away at various exploits that let users fully jailbreak their locked-down console. For the most part, though, those exploits have only worked with years-old versions of the PS5’s frequently updated firmware, making them less than useful for many everyday users.
That changed Tuesday with the release of the new Relapse exploit, which works with any PS5 up to firmware version 13.6 (released in July). That means jailbreaking is now possible on any PS5 that was last updated before the mid-September release of firmware version 14.00.00.
The so-called Relapse exploit makes use of a long-known WebKit vulnerability in the PS5’s hard-to-access web browser, escalating from there to gain write access to the PS5 kernel and install an ELF loader to streamline the running of arbitrary code. The new method is also a lot more efficient than previous PS5 jailbreak exploits, which could hang the system for 50 minutes per attempt.

Six years into this mostly virtual world, I now know we were not meant to look at ourselves 24/7.
Save for a glimpse before leaving the car, and then another full-body and ass scan in the bathroom mirror before heading into in-person meetings. Yet there was something comforting about seeing, in real time, how I show up for others.
Then I began questioning, "Does my hair always puff out to the side?" "Does my head always shake or only when stressed?" Or "Which nervous habits am I mimicking?"
Watching me watch others watch me, with the barrage of reels from strangers, while simultaneously responding to emails and chats and sharing screens, left my brain overloaded. Something had to give.
My need to change set off a chain reaction toward intentionality.
I deleted all Meta apps
My first action was to turn off phone notifications and create distance with social apps throughout the day. As a caregiver to my mom with Alzheimer's, turning on "Do Not Disturb" didn't feel safe, but flipping the phone over and having it out of reach was a reasonable approach when working.
I checked messages less often but found I was still "tapping" into Facebook and Instagram on quick breaks between calls, like a woodpecker excavating its next home. My youngest suggested deleting all Meta apps from my phone, which immediately freed my mind for healthier activities such as stretching, having a snack, or actually going to the bathroom.
I scheduled conversations the old-fashioned way
In addition to work, I was frequently on FaceTime after recently moving out of state and away from family and friends. Thinking back decades ago, twirling the spiral telephone cord while yammering with girlfriends, I swapped virtual face-to-face for audio-only calls with several people, never feeling like something was missing. In fact, not having to get dressed or pay any attention to my own face seemed to make me more present.
Avigail Lev, director of Bay Area CBT Center, said that "Self-monitoring takes us out of the moment, meaning, you are no longer in the interaction." Adding, "You are seeing yourself as the object rather than your own subjective experience." Lev explained how this affects one's self-esteem, confidence, and psyche. I never thought of myself as self-critical, yet it's likely impossible not to consider appearance and mannerisms when constantly in observe-mode.
One of the benefits of the 21st century is not being tethered to a wall phone jack, so as Minnesota's seasons changed to spring and summer with nearby lakes and trails, I combined personal and professional walks and talks, sans camera, which, as Lev noted, took me right out of the equation. No surprise, exercise and fresh air work well in fighting camera fatigue.
Another bonus in separating myself from my device has been actually forgetting it at times when heading out for an evening stroll. It's hard to believe that walks even happen without an app counting steps, but I learned to calculate miles manually after ditching my smartwatch years ago.
I made my virtual meetings shorter
While some research indicates Zoom meetings are not as exhausting as in-person meetings (perhaps because they've become the norm), there is evidence that the length of time (more than 44 minutes) one spends in online meetings is. I now schedule meetings for 30-45 minutes, allowing my colleagues and me to have at least a 15-minute break between calls.
I know many people love working from home, and I love that people can. But it drives me a little crazy to be in one place all day, so I've created distinct spaces where I can meet virtually with others, and when possible, I stand and work at my kitchen island. Moving around seamlessly offers a little less monotony and a needed change of scenery. On days when I have to strategize and prepare for working sessions, I visit my local library, taking advantage of study rooms, free printing, and just the right level of white noise that makes me feel like I'm back in an office. Doing these things helps minimize distractions and support my state of mind.
It's been easy to blame my nervous system on technology, yet as a coach, I recognized the need to assess my own mindset and confidence levels. In the end, it doesn't matter how many chins show up on screen — it's not for me to see or worry about. I've been invited to conversations with coworkers, family, and friends for the value I bring to these relationships.
So, with an understanding of the impact tech was having and enjoying being more present for others, I glance in a mirror (once again) before joining a call and add "hide self-view" to my routine. The results have been meaningful: more patience, improved memory, and not feeling so drained at the end of the day. Turns out, with intentionality comes more presence. And that's something worth looking at.

Respect and laughs as Fury and Joshua face off
- Published
After more than a decade of public feuding and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua exchanged pleasantries, traded jokes and even discussed going for a pint at a news conference in London.
The British heavyweight rivals will fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.
But for all the history between them, the launch felt more like two veterans in the closing stages of long, turbulent careers taking stock of how far they had both come.
"He's been a role model and poster boy for British boxing for years," Fury, 38, said of Joshua. "I mostly find myself defending my arch rival to fans in the street."
On Monday, there was still uncertainty over whether the fight would happen because of contractual disagreements surrounding the promotion.
There had been plenty of reason to expect fireworks on Wednesday. Instead, Joshua, 36, spoke about the magnitude of the event.
"It's breathtaking and I'm not saying that lightly," he said.
"I'm really grateful for this opportunity and bringing it to Great Britain because I know people in pubs have had proper fights about who will win and family members have fallen out."
The mood was perhaps best summed up at the face-off, when Joshua smiled and pretended to tickle Fury's stomach.
Common ground, catchphrases & old sparring stories
There was something almost surreal about seeing Fury and Joshua finally sitting side by side after so many years in which their rivalry had existed mostly through interviews, social media and failed negotiations.
Both had arrived hours earlier for one-to-one interviews. When the news conference began, master of ceremonies Michael Buffer introduced the pair as fireworks shot up from the front of the stage.
They entered from opposite sides at the same time - Joshua relaxed and composed in a grey tracksuit and sunglasses, Fury in more flamboyant fashion in a vivid emerald-green suit covered in crown motifs over a white shirt.
Alongside the world's media, a few hundred fans filled the balcony above and quickly made their allegiance known as "Oh Anthony Joshua" rang around the British Airways ARC.
Joshua has been credited with pushing to keep the fight in Britain and, if Wednesday was any indication, can expect strong backing in Cardiff - even with the main event potentially starting about 02:00 GMT to suit American audiences.
For two men whose names have been linked for so long, Fury and Joshua have spent remarkably little time together. But their famous sparring session in 2010, when Joshua was still an amateur, soon became the topic of conversation.
Fury suggested he had got the better of it, prompting one fan to shout: "Liar." Joshua smiled and said he could not remember.
For those who believe the fight has come years too late, Fury had a simple response. "It's the icing on the cake of two great careers," he said. Moments later, he glanced back at the word "Finally" on the giant screen behind them.
There were several moments of common ground. Fury nodded along as Joshua spoke about his Christian faith and, even when the pair traded insults, they rarely felt venomous.
"This man here is carved in stone and every time he gets cracked on the jaw, he falls over," Fury said.
"When I crack him on the jaw with a big right hand, he's going down."
Joshua laughed and shouted back Fury's own catchphrase: "Get up."
White absent after week of uncertainty
The fight has been reported as being for the vacant WBA 'super' heavyweight title, although current WBA heavyweight champion Murat Gassiev's team has lodged a formal objection over the proposed title arrangement.
For a moment, it appeared the mood could turn when Joshua revealed he had received a call asking whether Fury's name could appear first in the promotion.
"You've been crying behind the scenes to get out of this fight. I've checkmated you. You have to fight," Fury replied.
"I've actually never won a world title here. Now it's on the line, we can become a three-time."
That exchange came after several chaotic days in which the role of UFC and Zuffa Boxing chief Dana White had threatened to overshadow the fight.
Netflix had presented White as part of the promotion alongside Turki Alalshikh's The Ring, despite Joshua promoter Eddie Hearn insisting his fighter's contract prevented White from having a promotional role.
But White did not attend Wednesday's launch. And when Alalshikh thanked the American from the stage, his name was met with jeers from sections of the crowd.
Fury did momentarily take aim at Hearn, calling him a "sausage" - but even that did not last long.
Within minutes, Fury was offering to go for a pint with the Matchroom boss - and extended the invitation to Joshua.
"I hope after this fight we can have a pint of Guinness together," Fury said. "Win, lose or draw, let's bury the hatchet."
"I don't know if I can trust you," Joshua replied, drawing laughter.
The overriding mood was one of relief between two veterans, who were seemingly happy to let the fight settle what years of talk could not.

A video has gone viral on social media platforms, showing two women slapping a man wearing a saffron scarf. Users claim that it shows a Muslim man masquerading as Hindu by wearing a saffron scarf, and that he was allegedly caught stalking college girls in an attempt to snatch their phones.
Right-wing handle @MeghUpdates posted the clip, which garnered more than 116,000 views, and has been shared around 2,000 times at the time of this article being written. (Archive)
A “Peaceful” in a saffron scarf was allegedly STALKING college girls and ATTEMPTING to snatch their phones before the Hindu girls CAUGHT him RED-HANDED and BEAT him up. 👏 https://t.co/EK2q3vkgN1
— Megh Updates 🚨™ (@MeghUpdates) September 25, 2026
In Right-wing social-media discourse, the term ‘peaceful’ is used as a a code word for Muslims as a negative stereotype, while avoiding saying ‘Muslim’ directly.
An X user with the handle @Hinduspirit0 had also posted the viral clip on September 24 with the same claim that a Muslim boy pretending to be Hindu while wearing a saffron scarf had been “caught red-handed and beaten up badly”.
Other users who shared this clip with the same claim included the user ‘Boiled Anda’ (@AmitLeliSlayer), Vishal Deep Singh (@VishalDeep5151), Amitabh Chaudhary (@MithilaWaaala), and (@singh31919). Archives: 1, 2, 3, 4
The readers should note that many of this handles, like ‘Boiled Anda’, Amitabh Chaudhary, and MeghUpdates, have been found sharing misinformation and communal propaganda several times in the past.
Fact Check
To verify the veracity of the claims, we broke down the viral video into several keyframes. A reverse image search on one such keyframe led us to a news report by Aaj Tak, published on August 10.
According to the report, the viral clip is from Gwalior in Madhya Pradesh. On August 8, twin sisters Harshita and Rashita Agarwal, while on their way to college on a scooter, had one of their phones snatched by a miscreant trailing them on another scooter.
A chase ensued, after which the sisters were able to apprehend the man at an intersection and proceeded to thrash him, visuals of which began to circulate on social media soon after. The report identifies the culprit as a resident of Jalandhar, Punjab, named Manpreet. We found another news report published by The Free Press Journal, on August 9, which corroborated this finding.
On using relevant keywords, we also came across a video uploaded by ANI Bharat, in which Gwalior SSP Dharamveer Singh lauded the bravery of the twin sisters in nabbing the motorcycle-borne mobile snatcher.
So, to sum up, the viral claims suggesting that the man being slapped in the clip is Muslim, is false. The man in the viral video was identified as Manpreet.

Last UK and US troops leave Iraq as anti-Islamic State mission ends
- Published
The last British and American troops have left Iraq after a military presence of more than a decade in the country.
The exit of the remaining UK military personnel - around 100 - from Irbil, in the northern Kurdistan region, was co-ordinated over recent weeks with US forces, who also departed on Wednesday.
It follows an agreement between the US and the Iraqi government, signed two years ago, to withdraw foreign troops by the end of this month.
British and US forces have been present in Iraq since 2014, as part of the international coalition to help defeat the extremist Islamic State (IS) group. Their departure brings the mission, known as Operation Inherent Resolve, to an end.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the end of the coalition's mission marked "Iraq's transition to a phase in which it assumes full responsibility for its security and stability".
Iraq is set to hold four "Sovereignty Days" as a national holiday to mark the withdrawal.
"Following more than a decade of operations, training and capacity building, Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) and the Kurdish Peshmerga have secured the enduring territorial defeat of Daesh in Iraq and are now well placed to take primary responsibility for the country's security," the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in a statement, referring to IS by an Arabic acronym.
"With these objectives achieved, Iraq and its international partners can begin a new chapter focused on enduring security co-operation under Iraqi leadership."
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the coalition's departure from Irbil marked "the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated [IS] in Iraq".
He added: "The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including [IS] remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the government of Iraq."
The Iraqi government declared the military defeat of IS in 2017, but coalition forces remained to help prevent the group's resurgence.
A recent UN report estimated that sustained counter-terrorism pressure by Iraqi security forces had left IS with several hundred fighters who were "able to carry out unsophisticated operations only".
The Iraqi government also faces the challenge of Iranian-backed militias in the country.
Zaidi, who took office in May, has vowed to disarm them and bring all weapons under state control following the coalition's exit.
But several powerful factions have resisted his plans and could now see their influence grow without the US presence.
Since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran earlier this year, militias have been targeting the remaining US and UK forces stationed at Irbil air base.
Hundreds of Nato troops stationed in Baghdad left the country in March as tensions rose.
A BBC team visited the coalition base in Irbil in April this year, during a fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran.
They were forced to circle the base in an RAF transport aircraft while drones were being launched nearby.
At the height of the US bombing campaign against Iran, the coalition base was being targeted by up to 28 drones and missiles a day.
RAF Regiment Gunners, who were among the last British military personnel stationed there, had shot down more than 100 drones in the first six weeks of the war. Many of the attack drones were being launched by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.
On Wednesday, signalling the end of the mission, the MoD paid tribute to UK personnel who had contributed to the counter-IS mission.
It said they had provided "valuable support, training and assistance" to more than 111,000 members of the Iraqi Security Forces, including more than 21,000 Peshmerga forces in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region.
It also said the RAF had conducted thousands of sorties, striking more than 2,300 IS targets. The RAF is expected to continue flying missions over neighbouring Syria, to prevent the remnants of IS from gaining a foothold.
The Pentagon said the US would continue to provide "targeted training and intelligence support" to its Iraqi partners.
US Central Command said the coalition's joint taskforce remained operational and was now based in Jordan.
US forces will also continue their mission against IS in Syria, where the UN estimates that the group has up to 3,000 fighters.
This is the third time US and UK forces have withdrawn from Iraq.
Tens of thousands of US and British troops were deployed to the country in 1991 following Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait.
They returned to Iraq in 2003, when US President George W Bush ordered Operation Iraqi Freedom to remove the dictator from power and eliminate weapons of mass destruction that turned out not to exist.
The fierce sectarian insurgency that engulfed Iraq following the invasion cost tens of thousands of lives, including those of nearly 4,500 US military personnel and 179 British military personnel.
US and UK forces left Iraq in 2011, only to return three years later, when IS threatened to take control of the country.

Rallying-Ford to make full factory return to WRC in 2028
LONDON, Oct 1 : Ford will return to the World Rally Championship (WRC) as a full factory team from 2028 with long-standing partner M-Sport, it announced on Thursday.
The U.S. marque is the fourth constructor to commit to building a Rally1 car for 2029 under the governing FIA's new WRC27 regulations which are aimed at reducing the cost of competing at the top level.
It will be Ford's first full works programme since 2012 in the WRC, which is planning to expand its presence in the US and Britain.
"Today’s announcement represents another significant moment for the FIA World Rally Championship," said FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem in a statement.
"With a new promoter in place, three constructors already committed to the new technical regulations, and now Ford confirming its return as a full works manufacturer, there is real momentum behind the championship’s next era."
M-Sport currently competes with Ford Puma cars and has received technical support from Ford since 2012. Before that, it ran the works team.
Ford is already involved in Formula One with Red Bull, is set to compete in the World Endurance Championship from 2027 and is present in the World Rally-Raid Championship that includes the annual Dakar Rally in January.
Ford cars have won 94 WRC rallies and the previous works team took three manufacturer titles.
The manufacturer is trying to revive its fortunes in Europe where Chinese automakers are expanding fast.
The company said in May that it will launch seven new models in Europe by 2029.
“Rallying is where Ford’s character faces its toughest test, and where generations of fans come to share the thrill of seeing a car take on the impossible," said Ford Europe president Jim Baumbick on Thursday.
"We want our next generation of European vehicles to carry that same unapologetic spirit."

While the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, was being decorated in Quito by Ecuador’s president for “helping to promote peace in the region”, 10 Ecuadorian fishers whose boat had been blown up by US forces were adrift in the eastern Pacific.
On 8 September, a day before Rubio arrived, a US patrol vessel intercepted the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters near Ecuador.
“The gringos were all armed as if they were going to war,” said the boat’s captain, Mero Calderón, 50. “I tried to show them our catch to prove that we were there working, but they wouldn’t listen,” he added.
“They brought two huge bombs aboard, took us to their ship, handcuffed and blindfolded us, and blew our boat to pieces,” said Calderón, who along with five other fishers, was handed over to local authorities.
But another 10 crew members were fishing farther out to sea in a smaller boat that was not equipped to make it back to shore. The Ecuadorian navy only rescued them on 10 September, when Rubio was already in Peru preparing to return to the US.
US Southern Command posted an edited 14-second video of the operation and said “intelligence confirmed” that the vessel was being used by a gang as a “floating refuelling station” for speedboats allegedly carrying drugs – which the fishers deny.
It was one of eight operations involving Ecuadorian boats in just more than two weeks – the latest on 16 September – to follow the same pattern. Unlike the nearly 70 US airstrikes in the Pacific and Caribbean that have killed 234 people since last year, crews were removed before the vessels were sunk.
Also, rather than unilateral US attacks, the new wave of operations has the open support of Ecuador’s far-right president, Daniel Noboa, who is calling them “joint operations”.
Donald Trump has compared the drug trafficking operations to the campaign against the Islamic state. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing,” Trump said on Tuesday.
Some analysts see the shift as an indication that the US’s military strategy against drug trafficking in Latin America has entered a new phase.
“Noboa has offered Ecuador as a ‘laboratory’ for the implementation of this new phase,” said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations.
Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, over the past decade it has become a major trafficking hub because of its access to the Pacific, including the area where the attacks on boats have been taking place.
Noboa has responded with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, issuing repeated states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces.
This crackdown however has done little to reduce violence, and instead has eroded human rights. The most notable example of human rights abuse came last year in the case of the “Guayaquil Four”, the forced disappearance of four Afro-Ecuadorian boys between the age of 11 and 15. All four boys were found dead, there bodies charred and dismembered.
Despite pushback from voters, Noboa signed an agreement with the White House authorising joint operations and granting US military personnel involved in counter-narcotics operations immunity from criminal prosecution. The operations have also extended to land, with US troops taking part in raids last Thursday.
“Noboa is interested in the optics of a very lethal crackdown and in making Ecuador a place where the Trump administration can refine those methods and show them off,” said Freeman, who has also reported on the boat attacks in Ecuador for the New Yorker magazine.
Trump has pressured Latin American presidents to join an anti-drug cartel coalition he created called Shield of the Americas. With Peru and Colombia recently joining, the group now includes all but the few countries still governed by the left, such as Mexico and Brazil – where a far-right senator is a serious contender in October’s election.
So far, the coalition’s primary goal appears to have been increasing joint operations against alleged drug traffickers.
Adam Isacson, director for defence oversight at the Washington Office on Latin America, expects joint operations to expand across the region.
Isacson stressed that though more people are being turned over to local authorities instead of killed, the US is “still doing the bad old stuff”. On 19 September, four people were killed in the Caribbean. As with the other airstrikes, the US has not disclosed their identities or any of the alleged evidence linking them to criminal activity.
During his trip to Ecuador, Rubio said the decision on what approach to take was “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depended on the threat and location of the boat, but that the US would “still blow up ships if need be”.
Human rights organisations have described the airstrikes as extrajudicial killings, and a special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that they constitute “crimes against humanity”.
Despite Trump’s claims, available data show they have had no impact on the volume of cocaine entering the country.
Journalists and human rights groups have managed to identify some of the victims, who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, poor people at the bottom of trafficking networks.
In Ecuador, the local NGO Permanent Committee for the Defence of Human Rights estimates that more than 220 fishers have been subjected to “violent boardings, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, torture and the destruction of vessels” in this year’s US operations.
None of the fishers remains in custody and, while some are still facing prosecution, many have already been acquitted for lack of evidence.
“Fishers are losing their livelihoods when the US destroys the boats. Besides, if the US says the vessels were being used to refuel drug boats, why destroy the evidence?” said the committee’s lawyer, Fernando Bastías.
A US Southern Command spokesperson said it conducts operations “in compliance with US and international law” and that leaving boats “intact could permit their reuse by criminal networks”.
Although the US and Ecuador have celebrated the recent operations on social media, three cases from earlier this year remain unclaimed.
The first was on 20 January, when the fishing vessel Fiorella disappeared with eight crew members on board; days earlier, some of them had told relatives they were being monitored by drones and by a vessel on which they said they had seen a US flag.
Human rights organisations and journalists identified two more cases with similar patterns in late March, although the fishers survived. The Washington Post reported that the three cases were part of a covert CIA programme, and the agency declined to comment.
A US Southern Command spokesperson said it had no knowledge of, nor were its forces “involved in the incidents described in reports involving the Fiorella”.
Both the husband and brother of María Mero, 43, were aboard the Fiorella: Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado, 44, and Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva, 25. “Where did they take them? Do they have them in the US, in a prison somewhere? We don’t want any trouble; we just want them to send them back to us,” she told the Guardian.
The families say they have spent months trying to get answers from the Ecuadorian government, so far without success.
“They were fishers, not criminals. Let the great president come here to my house and see whether I have luxuries, anything that would show I’m a drug trafficker. No, because all of us here are poor, and we just want our loved ones back,” added Mero.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

The zardozi embroidery on a Dior dress, the T-strap leather sandals at a Prada show, the mirror-work technique used on a Fendi bag – for decades, the skill of Indian artisans has been an invisible force behind some of the world’s most coveted fashion.
Now, that work is beginning to claim its own place in the spotlight, and the Mumbai-based textile and embroidery atelier Chanakya International is at the forefront.
Chanakya marked its 40th anniversary this month, celebrating with three exhibitions that trace its journey from an embroidery powerhouse to a present-day craft and cultural institution. The person steering it is 49-year-old Karishma Swali, whose father set up the group’s operations in the 1980s.
“What we have as a country is unique,” she tells me of India’s rich textile and craft heritage. “It’s unparalleled in many ways, and it’s the only place where we continue to practise it.” During the Renaissance, she says, France and Italy had established and varied traditions. “But what we have in India today is [what] other parts of the world have lost.”
Chanakya has a network of 1,400 artisans, and says that some are 13th-generation craftspeople, skilled in hundreds of embroidery traditions and supplying almost every luxury label you can imagine. Among the techniques they have revived is the Mughal-era silver filigree lace, or chaand jaal, reintroduced in a lighter form that has since become a regular feature in couture collections.
In 2023, Dior held a show at Mumbai’s Gateway of India, showcasing its partnership with Chanakya, in a high-profile acknowledgment of Indian craftsmanship. The runway saw sari-inspired skirts, vibrant madras-checks sets and Nehru-collar jackets.
These collaborations are supported by expert craft knowledge passed down and refined over generations, and they need institutional support to survive. The Kalhath Institute, a craft-preservation centre in Lucknow, runs residencies that pair artists from across the world with local artisans.
Kalhath’s co-founder Mohammed Amine Dadda tells me that Indian craftsmanship’s defining quality is “intelligence of the hand” – a sensitive, slow and cumulative process underpinned by patience and dexterity. “Without this technical mastery, and the considerable time required to create the most demanding pieces, haute couture and contemporary luxury simply could not bring their most ambitious creative visions to life.”
This mastery is not limited to textiles. When it comes to jewellery, global luxury brands have long sought Jaipur-based the Gem Palace, established in 1852 by the Kasliwal family, who still run it today. Samarth Kasliwal, 33, says part of the appeal lies in the visual language of Indian artistry itself. “There is something about Indian artistry that is inspired by nature,” he tells me, pointing to the recurring use of floral patterns and animals across Indian art and design. These motifs are universal, and travel across the lines of culture and language.
One recent collaboration Kasliwal is particularly proud of is a collection for Dior featuring green onyx and rock crystals, with engravings of birds, animals and flowers. The combination, he says, is reminiscent of traditional Indian jewellery, while drawing on techniques that remain central to the atelier’s work today.
With increased visibility, the question of credit and appropriation has become harder to ignore. Last week, a Ralph Lauren gown from the designer’s spring 2027 collection attracted criticism after many Indians pointed out that the embroidery the brand described as “embellishments” looked a lot like Indian zardozi, but without any accompanying credit. (Ralph Lauren did not respond to my request for comment.)
Then, Fendi came under fire when people noticed that a baguette bag from its autumn/winter collection featured mirrorwork often seen in Gujarati crafts. In April, Fendi credited Chanakya artisans in a social media video showcasing the same embroidery. But the product description on its site failed to mention any Indian inspiration, and its final label read “Made in Italy”.
After I asked Fendi about the discrepancy, the brand cited its “creative partnership” with Chanakya of more than three decades, saying it “remains committed to supporting and recognizing India’s rich craft heritage”. The website descriptor now reads: “Made in Italy and India with Chanakya”.
A recent Financial Times report noted that under EU rules, garments embroidered in India can still end up with a European label – so long as the final construction and finishing take place in Europe.
Last year, Prada was accused of appropriating Indian culture with Kolhapuri-inspired sandals, a controversy that showed us these debates around recognition can sometimes produce a more structural response. “We acknowledge the sandals … are inspired by traditional Indian handcrafted footwear, with a centuries-old heritage,” Lorenzo Bertelli, the corporate social responsibility chief at the Italian fashion house, had written in a letter to the Maharashtra chamber of commerce at the time.
Prada subsequently partnered with state-backed organisations in Maharashtra and Karnataka to produce a limited-edition collection, Made in India, and committed to a three-year training programme for artisans specialising in the craft.
Might these collaborations, controversies and corrections represent a shift in India’s place in the fashion industry? Anthropologist Phyllida Jay, author of Inspired by India: How India Transformed Global Design, appears to think so, placing the debate in a longer arc. “The stories of the ateliers producing highly skilled Indian craft in the elevated realm of European luxury and high fashion is part of a broader paradigm shift,” she writes, “where over 70 years after the end of colonial rule, India is being looked at in a different way on the world stage.” It is, in a way, a reversal, moving from a colonial history of extraction toward one in which Indians themselves get a voice in how their craft is represented.
Swali is ensuring this visibility also lives on through the Chanakya School of Craft, which she set up in 2016. Its 18-month programme provides free embroidery training and a travel honorarium to dozens of women, some of whom have gone on to work at the main atelier. Others have set up their own independent studios.
I had a chance to visit the space – inside a high-rise in Lower Parel, where those as young as 18 learn intricate needlework alongside grandmothers in their 60s. “Craft in India has never been institutionalised,” Swali says of the ethos behind the initiative. “It’s intergenerational,” she says, adding that women have often been excluded.
India’s culture of craft has always been precious. Growing up, I loved having the choice to affordably create any type of clothing. At one point, I had a small army of tailors, each with a different specialisation, whom I’d go to for different needs. I’d buy ajrakh and mashru silks from Dastkar or Nalli, and hand it to the right Masterji to stitch, embroider and tweak to my size. So, to me, Indian craftsmanship is not just a part of luxury, but a luxury itself.
What else we’re reading about
Travel | Time Out just confirmed what everyone in Mumbai’s Bandra West knows: that it’s one of the coolest neighbourhoods in the world. The other Indian spot to make the cut is Delhi’s food and fashion centre, Humayunpur. The top spot went to Jongno 3-ga in Seoul – my second home!
Business | India will levy a 0.4% charge on merchants for UPI payments above Rs 2,000, starting on 15 October. The charges will not be applicable when the payment is made from one person to another. Ashneer Grover, co-founder and former CEO of fintech firm BharatPe slammed the move, describing it as “tax collection”.
Immigration | An investigation by Scroll’s Rokibuz Zaman has revealed a troubling pattern in West Bengal: since June, at least nine Muslim men and two children have been picked up by the police from their homes over allegations that they are Bangladeshi nationals – without being given a chance to prove their citizenship. Most were picked up and detained in midnight raids, the report said, and family members accused the police of not producing warrants.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Fashion designer Payal Khandwala, whose spring-summer ’26 collection featured handwoven silks, cottons and brocades, recommends the perfect saree weave: “The delicate poetry of a Jamdani saree is definitely my favourite. A 2,000-year-old craft, typically woven in fine muslin and of Bengali origin, it’s somewhat an unsung hero. The weaving process itself is exceptionally intricate. Using a supplementary weft technique, thousands of markings are meticulously mapped on to the warp to recreate the pattern, interlaced by hand with a wooden shuttle and metallic needle to guide the motifs in silver and gold yarn, on fine mulberry silk and organza.”

Vibe check
The true measure of my love for my friends is in the number of memes I send them. One of the accounts I rely on is Bahaish Kapoor’s. The screenwriter-turned-meme evangelist pairs black-and-white Bollywood stills with contemporary gen Z sass, and lets incongruity do the rest. What makes an image meme-worthy? “I always look for people who are in a deep philosophical, romantic, dramatic action moment which I can repurpose to bring in a whole new meaning,” he tells me. “I try to mix and match and see what’s working.” His 340,000-plus followers include Sharon Stone and Hrithik Roshan.
“I just want to make people feel a little better,” says Kapoor, adding that he receives a lot of DMs from people about how his page helped them through a bad day. “People confessing that they are lighter because of this experience is all that I can hope for. I mean, that’s the endgame.”

The intricate web Man City spun to con the Premier League
- Published
"To cheat, trick, deceive, delude with false pretences; to impose upon, take in, hoax."
That is the Oxford English definition of the word "sham".
And that word appears eight times in the independent commission's ruling published on Tuesday, which found Manchester City guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of financial rules, and all but one in relation to a failure to co-operate with the investigation.
The 40-page document makes fascinating reading.
It catalogues how the club's owners, Abu Dhabi United Group, knew from the 2009-10 season that there would be major overspends if the club was to reach the level they wanted to get to.
So, the ruling says, City found a way to boost sponsorship income. Season, after season, after season.
For nine seasons, in fact.
The report shows how the club's owners were topping up the value of the deals.
The so-called Disguised Funding Scheme is the central plank in a series of charges that Manchester City have been found guilty of by the Premier League.
This scheme managed to hide more than £830m of sponsorship funding, while other devices hid £90m in expenses.
We break down the key findings from the document.
The problem became apparent very quickly for the new owners
Manchester City were bought by Abu Dhabi investors in 2008 but, the document says, their predicament had become clear from the start of the 2009-10 season.
These were ambitious new owners who did not just want the club to be competitive. They wanted to have the best players and be winners.
That was not going to be possible without spending more money. And lots of it.
Total losses for the 2009-10 campaign were going to exceed what was, at that time, the record single-season financial loss by a Premier League member club. That was Chelsea FC in 2006, of £140m.
According to the ruling, that was a record that the City owners were adamant the club should not break
And not only that.
The club knew they would likely continue to suffer large losses for at least the following five seasons.
This was when both Uefa and the Premier League were about to bring in financial fair play rules.
This was clearly going to be a problem.
To address this the only option was to significantly increase commercial revenue - and reduce the reliance on their owners.
Sham contracts and the disguised funding scheme
In early 2010, Manchester City took the first steps to get the additional funding into the club.
City would enter into sponsorship agreements which were record amounts and were significantly above fair market value.
It is referred to as the 'disguised funding scheme'.
This is how it worked, according to the ruling.
The sponsorship deals were split into two parts: a base fee, and a tagged sum.
The sponsors would pay the base fee.
And the club's owners would pay the tagged sum.
Ergo, the sponsors would not have to pay the full value of the contract. The club's owners would pay the vast majority, which enabled them to invest in players.
This, the document states, "gave the misleading impression to third parties (including regulators and its auditors) in its financial statements and any required FFP returns that its commercial revenues from sponsorship agreements were far, far greater than was in fact the case".
But the club also knew they had to be nimble.
From time to time the disguised funding scheme would be tweaked to "assist with continued concealment" and "reduce the likelihood of difficult questions being asked".
What did this all mean in reality?
Commercial income from sponsors totalled £949.94m in the seasons from 2009-10 to 2017-18.
The ruling says only £119.25 million represented base fees.
A total of £830.69 million represented tagged sums - the amount paid by the club's owners.
Man City have denied the claims and say the Premier League had misunderstood the sponsorship agreements.
However, the panel said it "rejected that explanation as untrue".
It said it was "concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the disguised funding scheme".
An example given of the disguised funding scheme in action: plugging an unexpected shortfall in May 2013.
Less than a week before the end of that 2012-13 financial year the club knew they were £9.9m short of complying with Uefa's financial rules.
In a matter of days, without sponsors even being approached, a number of modified sponsor agreements were generated which increased recorded sponsorship fees to pay bonuses for events that had already taken place and to pay for a US tour.
The feared Uefa FFP shortfall was thus "plugged".
Project Longbow
In 2012, City launched what it called Project Longbow.
The ruling does say many of the strands of Project Longbow were genuine, and legitimate attempts to achieve the aims of boostings revenues and reducing operating losses.
One strand was not genuine, according to the ruling: the Fordham Arrangement.
This was an agreement between City and a third party called Fordham which was, according to the ruling, "little more than a front".
Funds from the club's owners "would be used (and were used) to enable Fordham to acquire from the club (at a sizeable, artificially-inflated price) the club's entitlement to benefit financially from its players' image rights".
It was a "further device by which funds could be paid into the club in a manner that concealed their true origin".
And this "enabled the club to pretend that such funds represented operating income".
In the financial statements wrongly recorded as operating income was the sum of £24.5m, and £49.414m was wrongly excluded from operating expenses.
The ruling says said the Fordham Arrangement was "operated with the knowledge and approval" of a number of individuals whose names were redacted.
Contracts paid by other means
Another way the club attempted to pass the financial rules was to move expensive contracts for players and managers off the books.
This was done by paying remuneration, or wages, through third parties. In reality this was being paid by the owners.
This was "instead recorded in a consultancy agreement" and "concealed the true extent of the club's liabilities".
There are three separate cases attributed to this, with all names redacted from the document. These may be published when the full written reasons are released.
City used this method for payments of £8.866m, £7.4m and £0.5m.
City's witnesses 'lied knowingly' during inquiry
"By its conduct the club clearly intended to circumvent the Premier League rules.
"The club made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League investigation".
This is another damning section, which brings into question the integrity of undisclosed people associated with City.
City served witness statements or documentary evidence from 24 individuals, most of whom who gave evidence at the hearing.
This could be problematic at a later date, as the new Independent Football Regulator is able to look at the honesty of integrity of directors and owners.
At present, no one has been named so we do not know the position of the people the ruling referred to.
It said that the evidence given by a number of important factual witnesses "was false in a number of key respects".
It added that certain factual witnesses provided evidence "that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest".
The ruling also said that City knew that the annual accounts "did not provide a true and fair view of the financial position" and that the club "was reckless as to whether those annual accounts provided a true and fair view".
All in this, it was said, showed that City failed to act "with utmost good faith" and "breached duties of co-operation that it owed to the Premier League".
How the ruling breaks down
This is how the club's financial statements for the seasons between 2009-10 and 2017-18 did not show a true and fair view of the financial position:
Sponsorship
- Income from overstated by over £830m
Contracts and image rights
- Wrongly excluded expenses by £8.866m
- Wrongly excluded expenses by £7.4m
- Wrongly excluded expenses by £0.5m
Fordham Arrangement:
- Wrongly recorded as operating income £24.5m
- Wrongly excluded expenses totalling £49.414m
Total: £920.68m

A gaggle of investors. A shimmering “Science City.” And a surefire confidence that drug development in China is faster, cheaper, and more efficient than anywhere else in the world — including the United States.
STAT’s Jason Mast flew to Shanghai to witness a two-day biotech summit that featured a frenzy of dealmaking as everyone tried to cash in on Chinese-designed drugs, which now make about a third of the world’s pipeline and draw more than half of all licensing or collaboration deals.
