Sandwiched between the launch of the long-awaited full-fat Range Rover Electric at the start of September and the upcoming final reveal of the much-anticipated Jaguar Type 01 in New York City next week, comes—with considerably less fanfare—JLR's Range Rover Sport Electric.
However, considering that Range Rover Sport sales often run close to, or occasionally slightly higher than, the flagship Range Rover, thanks in part to its lower price, this all-electric version of the Sport could be just as important for an embattled JLR. The automaker announced earlier this month that it is cutting 4,000 jobs over the next two years.
According to JLR, the performance SUV has the stiffest body (unsurprising, considering the battery placement) and lowest center of gravity of any Range Rover Sport model, as well as a faster torque response than the Range Rover Electric—50 percent faster, apparently.
Crucially, the Sport gets the same powertrain as the Range Rover, but at a lower price (from £109,810, no US prices yet) and with different tuning. Like its larger sibling, the two 260-kilowatt motors dish out up to 550 pferdestärke (PS) and 850 Newton-meters (Nm) of torque (more than any other Range Rover Sport to date). It can go from standstill to 60 mph in 4.3 seconds if you're in the EV's Dynamic Launch Mode.
As for range, Range Rover claims the Sport with its 118.5-kilowatt-hour battery will get up to 374 miles on the WLTP standard, which should mean about 320 miles under the EPA's stricter testing. Split-charging tech and an 800-volt architecture let the SUV add 136 miles of range in as little as 10 minutes in ideal charging conditions, and go from 10 to 80 percent in 22 minutes.
For dynamic driving as well as off-road smarts, the Sport has all-wheel steering and electronic Active Roll Control, which can supposedly apply up to 1,400 Nm of force across each axle to keep “maximum composure,” as well as an adaptive dynamics system that monitors 100 parameters 500 times per second for greater control of body roll and pitch when cornering or braking. The car can also wade through up to 900 mm of water and tackle 45-degree inclines.
As a last flourish, an “aerodynamically-optimized” grille and alloy wheels supposedly contribute up to 10 extra miles of driving range at motorway speeds.
JLR will produce Plug-in Hybrid Electric Vehicle (PHEV), gas, and diesel versions of the Sport, but the electric model will go toe to toe with the likes of the Porsche Cayenne Electric, BMW iX xDrive60, and Lotus Eletre 600. The Porsche starts £20,000 cheaper than the Sport, though.
The Polestar 3 Dual Motor is another competitor to the Sport Electric, but not in the US, as Polestar was banned from selling its cars earlier this year because the brand is majority Chinese-owned. The ruling made Polestar the first major casualty of a US rule banning Chinese software in new internet-connected vehicles.

Rumors that Cornell University was forcibly removed from the Ivy League, the collegiate athletic conference that includes eight of the United States' oldest and most-prestigious universities, circulated in late September 2026.
The rumor circulated as the university was scrutinized over a lawsuit that accused seven male students of drugging and raping a female student in 2024. As Snopes previously reported, the lawsuit, filed in September 2026, led to the Tompkins County, N.Y., district attorney reopening his office's investigation into the case.
People across various social media platforms shared the rumor, expressing their apparent satisfaction with the purported decision, writing, "Cornell getting dropped from the Ivy League is music to my earssssssssssss."
Cornell getting dropped from the Ivy League is music to my earssssssssss!!
— Seema Genche (@seemagenche) September 30, 2026
However, the rumor that Cornell University was "dropped" from the Ivy League was false.
There was no evidence to suggest that the rumor had any merit. The official Ivy League website featured Cornell University as of this writing, complete with its upcoming game schedule and standings for multiple sports.
Further, the "About the Ivy League" page on the organization's website stated, "The League's world-renowned schools – Brown, Columbia, Cornell, Dartmouth, Harvard, Penn, Princeton and Yale – serve as the standard bearers for inspiring and transforming student- athletes to boldly take on the world's challenges and lead lives of great impact."
Searches of Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo revealed no credible media outlets reporting on the rumor, which would have been a major headline given the widespread media coverage of the "Cornell 7" case.
Looking closer at the most-popular versions of the claim circulating on social media, it's clear that the accounts spreading the rumor used the exact same language — "Cornell getting dropped from the Ivy League is music to my earssssssssssss" — indicating that it was either the work of bots posting the message across a variety of accounts or, less likely, a copy-and-paste campaign.
A 2009 piece in Cornell's student-run independent newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun, dug into the history of the school's affiliation with the prestigious organization.
It said the name Ivy League originated in 1937 but "did not become formal until November 1954, when the presidents of Brown, Columbia, Cornell, Dartmouth, Harvard, Penn, Princeton and Yale affixed their signatures to the 'Common Statement of Ivy Group Institutions.'"
Further, it said the Ivy League "distinguished itself from other schools with a few basic rules: no postseason competition, and no financial aid to players except for legitimate academic or need-based scholarships."
Snopes reached out to Cornell University and the Ivy League for comment and will update this article if we hear back.

- Embark has recently improved its various anti-cheat systems.
- The team will issue permanent and hardware bans for cheaters.
- Embark also plans to add Elytra anti-cheat system from THE FINALS.
Aleksander Grøndal, Executive Producer of ARC Raiders, shared Embark’s anti-cheat progress in a blog post. He detailed improvements to the cheat detection systems, the introduction of permanent and hardware bans, and more ahead of the release of the Arc Raiders Frozen Trail update.
Arc Raiders Reveals Major Anti-Cheat Progress Ahead of Frozen Trail Update
Arc Raiders Frozen Trail update is scheduled for October 8, 2026. Ahead of the biggest update of the year, Aleksander Grøndal, Executive Producer of ARC Raiders, addressed the ongoing cheating problem plaguing the game and its community.
As new cheats surface online every day, Embark Studios is strengthening its cheat detection systems with in-house models based on machine learning and other data. In case you didn’t know, Arc Raiders added Denuvo’s kernel-level anti-cheat protection and Anybrain’s AI-based cheat detection earlier this year.
In addition, Embark plans to integrate Elytra, another in-house anti-cheat system currently being used in THE FINALS. While these anti-cheat systems work in tandem to identify suspicious behavior, Embark noted that there is always a human involved in the process to monitor the situation and issue bans accordingly.
Earlier, Embark was hesitant to issue permanent bans for first-time cheaters. However, that’s changing after the Arc Raiders community expressed frustration over cheaters. Now, if any account is caught using cheats, whether it belongs to a first-timer or long-time player, it will be permanently banned from Arc Raiders without any warning.
If any other account comes into contact with a banned copy of the game, it will also be permanently banned. Moreover, Embark is also ready to issue hardware bans to multiple systems, similar to how Call of Duty devs recently took down a Cronus distributor.
If you ever wondered why Arc Raiders devs take so long to permaban a cheater, Aleks explained the reason for the delay in the same blog post. The anti-cheat systems continuously monitor a player’s behavior over time before making a decision. So, the systems cannot permanently ban players instantly, as doing so could result in accidentally banning legit players.
In addition, a dedicated team reviews footage flagged by the anti-cheat systems as well as the players’ posts on social media before issuing a permaban. As you can see, Embark doesn’t want to wrongfully ban legit players, so the team takes time to analyze the clips and issue bans accordingly. Recently, Marvel Rivals permabanned cheaters in this way.
Embark also revealed that the team is working to prevent other forms of unfair play such as queue teaming, economy exploits, and more. Recently, the team started separating players who intentionally queue together in solos with the plan to spoil another player’s raid.
Embark is fully aware that game cheating is a multi-billion-dollar industry and cannot be wiped out altogether. However, the team remains deeply committed to eliminating cheaters in Arc Raiders and ensuring a fair-playing experience for all players.
The devs are making steady progress on anti-cheat systems while simultaneously tackling other forms of unfair play. At this rate, players could encounter fewer cheaters in the game when the Arc Raiders Pendola Pass map comes out next week.

New Delhi, Sep 23: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Wednesday said the party stood firmly with the demand of the people of Ladakh for meaningful constitutional safeguards, including the Sixth Schedule, to protect Ladakh's land, employment, fragile environment, culture and identity.
He also demanded that the judicial probe into the deaths of four people during statehood protests must ensure accountability and bring out the truth.
On September 24, 2025, police in Leh shot and killed four people during violent protests demanding statehood and constitutional protections for Ladakh.
In a post on X, Kharge said that a year ago, four young people were shot in Leh during the agitation for the democratic and constitutional rights of the people of Ladakh.
"On Martyrs' Day, we pay our solemn homage to them and stand in complete solidarity with their families.
"The judicial inquiry into the tragic events of September 24 must establish the full truth, ensure accountability and deliver justice without fear or favour. The people of Ladakh have waited long enough for their legitimate aspirations to be addressed," he said.
"The Congress party stands firmly with their demand for meaningful Constitutional safeguards, including the Sixth Schedule, to protect Ladakh's land, employment, fragile environment, culture and identity," the Congress chief said.
Democracy and representative institutions must be fully restored, and the people of Ladakh must have an effective voice in determining their own future, he asserted.
The people of Ladakh have been demanding statehood, which led to violent clashes last year.

Hundreds of customers affected as Hong Kong yoga chain Hotstone abruptly closes
Company cites ‘business operations and other actual circumstances’ for closure, while some customers were reportedly sold packages just days before shutdown
The abrupt closure of a Hong Kong yoga chain has dealt losses to hundreds of members, with some customers claiming the company lured them into buying discount packages as recently as the past few days.
A resident who identified herself as Chan told the South China Morning Post on Thursday that she received the closure notice from Hotstone Yoga’s WhatsApp number just an hour before her scheduled class at the Kwun Tong studio the night before.
According to the notice issued by law firm Cheung & Co, Hotstone said it was shutting down after careful consideration due to “business operations and other actual circumstances”.
It said the company would cease operations after opening hours ended on Wednesday, and included an email for parties who had “rights, debts or other claims against Hotstone” to submit documents.

Model sues Victoria’s Secret for using too much of her face in an Instagram ad
Sydney Roper, known for modeling golf apparel, has claimed that Victoria’s Secret used ‘about 95 percent of her face’ in a perfume ad when she was supposed to be unrecognizable

A model has sued Victoria’s Secret, claiming the company used too much of her face in an Instagram ad for perfume without permission and without additional compensation.
Sydney Roper, who has modeled for Peter Millar’s G/FORE golf apparel brand for about six years, alleges in a lawsuit filed in federal court in California Tuesday that Victoria’s Secret used her “recognizable likeness” in the ad “to attract consumer attention and promote purchases.”
Despite the company purchasing only an “unrecognizable parts-model appearance,” in which less than 30 percent of Roper’s face would be shown, about 95 percent of her face appeared in the ad, according to the lawsuit obtained by The Independent.
“These models are exploited and taken advantage of on a daily basis. They go up against these big companies. The models are afraid to take on the big companies because they don't want to be blacklisted,” Roper’s lawyer Perry C. Wander told The Independent.
“My client has been doing it for a long time, and she just doesn't let anyone take advantage of her anymore at this point in her career,” Wander continued. “So she was really adamant to pursue the case.”
When Roper’s agency demanded an extra $3,000, including a $500 agency fee, for using more of her face in the ad, Victoria’s Secret “did not respond, removed the linked advertisement, and offered no apology,” the lawsuit read.
“Taking an advertisement down does not pay the model for the use already made,” Roper’s legal team wrote in the complaint.
The Independent has reached out to Victoria’s Secret for comment.
The complaint stems from a perfume ad that was part of Victoria’s Secret Joyride campaign that rolled out this summer.
Roper’s agency agreed to a four-hour modeling shoot for the campaign on April 3 in exchange for $1,000 plus a 20 percent agency fee, according to the lawsuit.
A company representative allegedly confirmed to Roper’s agency in an email that “all will remain unrecognizable” and said that only part of her face, including her nose and lips, would be shown, along with her hands and an arm.
But, according to Roper’s estimate, about 95 percent of her face was allegedly shown in the ad. “Her visible eye, nose, lips, and facial features made her recognizable notwithstanding partial shadow,” the lawsuit read.
“My client discovered an Instagram post of the Victoria's Secret perfume video ad that was posted by Victoria's Secret, and it had her full face. She's pouring perfume on her chest, and you can see her full face,” Wander told The Independent. “The original contract was with a modeling agency that does just bits and parts of models, not a full face.”
Wander said a model showing her full face for a national or international perfume campaign could be paid tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands of dollars.
“We don't know if this was an inadvertent mistake or they decided to just publish the video of her full face, hoping that she either wouldn’t notice or would actually be excited that her whole face was in the ad,” the lawyer said.
Roper is now seeking “accountability for the unauthorized commercial use of her likeness and the breach of the negotiated restrictions,” according to the lawsuit.
The lawsuit requests an unspecified amount of damages, profits attributable to the “unauthorized use” of Roper’s likeness and attorneys’ fees.

A Russian drone hits a Kyiv school as Moscow presses its aerial campaign against Ukraine
A Russian drone has struck a school in Kyiv, as the Ukrainian capital endures relentless aerial attacks

A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday, city officials said, as the Ukrainian capital endured another night and day of relentless aerial attacks.
Children and staff at the school were in shelters when the drone hit, Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said, although the drone's warhead didn’t explode. There was no immediate report of casualties. The building’s brick frontage showed a large hole and black burn mark alongside smashed windows.
Kyiv has in recent weeks lived through repeated air raid alerts, punctuated by loud bangs and palls of black smoke as drones and missiles hit, making it feel like a city under siege. The Russian onslaught aims to terrorize civilians, officials and analysts say, and break their will to resist 4 ½ years after Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
The strain is showing among Kyiv residents. Maryna Lystopad, 35, said her hair has started falling out due to the strain of escalating attacks and never knowing where a drone or missile will hit.
"It’s really horrible. I can’t take it anymore. I think, I think that soon we’re all going to leave. I’m really not doing well,” she told The Associated Press.
“I’m constantly anxious. I can’t relax,” she said. “I keep thinking that if something happens, if something hits, one of my relatives could be killed.”
She recently had to go to another part of the city, she said, and was “genuinely stressed the whole way there.”
“I kept checking, like, whether anything was flying in, where it was going, where am I supposed to go? Where am I supposed to run?”
Russia's missiles and drones are stretching Ukraine's air defenses
The war on the ground hasn’t seen major shifts since last year, but Ukraine is struggling to fend off Russia’s intensified aerial attacks on cities that include speedy ballistic missiles and high-flying jet-powered drones.
In response, Ukraine has fired its long-range drones at manufacturing plants deep inside Russia and has targeted Russia’s drone launch sites. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday that Kyiv’s forces struck a site in Russia’s southwestern Oryol region that is used to store and launch attack drones.
To turn the tide, Ukraine needs U.S.-made Patriot missiles that can effectively defend against ballistic missiles, but they are in short supply since the Iran war began. A plan to produce them inside Ukraine could take years to bear fruit.
Kyiv is currently racing to produce new interceptors that can bring down fast-moving jet-propelled drones as the swift cycle of military innovation during the war continues.
Ukraine also wants tougher sanctions imposed on Russia to prevent it from getting key high-tech components for its arsenal.
Moscow, meanwhile, is pressing its advantage before Ukraine comes up with an answer to the latest challenges.
Russia steps up its campaign against Ukraine's power grid
Ukrainian officials didn’t report any energy infrastructure being hit Thursday, a day after what officials said was the biggest Russian attack on the power grid since last spring.
The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said Wednesday's barrage marked “the beginning of Russia’s strike campaign aimed at degrading Ukraine’s energy security ahead of winter … and forcing Ukraine to capitulate.”
Russia is expected to step up attacks on the electricity supply as the weather gets colder. It was 19 degrees Celsius (66 F) in Kyiv on Thursday, and mild temperatures were set to continue.
In a surprise development, Russia used a new jet-powered drone for the first time Wednesday, fitting it with a warhead designed to sever high-voltage pylons, said Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine’s president on defense technology.

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

It's been more than four years since the launch of LIV Golf rocked the game.
A brash breakaway league, bankrolled by Saudi Arabian billions, luring top players with promises of big money.
Still it divides opinion in golf, and has split the loyalty of its champions.
But it could all come to an end soon.
After the League's Saudi backers pulled its funding - having spent more than $5bn (£3.6bn) - this week's abortive season finale could be the end.
That's unless a new deal is struck, soon.
BBC Sport visited the final event of 2026 at an exclusive golf club in Indianapolis, and found a strange atmosphere of surface-level optimism, but deep uncertainty.
Get ready for LIV 2.0... or the end?
LIV staff have learnt to put on a brave face. And that was no more necessary than this week at Chatham Hills Golf Club.
Despite endless questions about the future, they still had a tournament to host, and LIV Golf's white knight was in town - "the investor", as he was most frequently described.
The phrase "LIV 2.0" was used on countless occasions by the league's leadership - and that is the dream they are clinging to.
It stands for a new chapter, a second life for LIV.
There did appear to be genuine optimism that a deal could be struck.
LIV Golf chief executive officer Scott O'Neil believes he can pull off the near-impossible, and so do many of those closest to him.
But there was widespread acknowledgement that, if they do achieve it, the process to get there won't be easy.
One insider remarked "it's darkest before dawn". Another said "it will get worse before it gets better".
Work is said to be happening at "breakneck speed" behind the scenes, because of the pressure of players needing clarity on their futures, events needing to be organised, and sponsorships agreed.
However, there were players, caddies, staff and volunteers who shared a more pessimistic view with BBC Sport, with one describing it as the "last hurrah".
One senior figure within golf's media remarked: "We're at the hospice, not the funeral."
What would new era of LIV look like?
Much of the format is expected to stay the same in any new LIV - a shotgun start, team competition, music blaring from speakers and party holes.
But change will be felt in the boardrooms and in players' pockets.
The "free-spending" days are over.
If LIV does get a second chapter, it will need to be run in a more financially-disciplined way, given overall losses of this era of LIV are expected to have run into several billions of dollars.
BBC Sport has had it confirmed by multiple sources that the prospective investor behind plans for LIV 2.0 is Ted Goldthorpe, head of the credit division of international investment firm BC Partners.
Indeed, one insider referred to him simply as "TG", a nickname that suggests he has become a familiar face.
Goldthorpe attended LIV's most recent event in Bedminster, New York, and O'Neil said he was spending time "looking under the hood" of the league.
But in Indianapolis, Goldthorpe kept himself out of public view, even ushered out of a side door of the clubhouse to avoid media huddled by the front entrance.
He did, however, meet players as a group and set out his vision for the future - the primary aim being to make LIV sustainable, and ultimately profitable.
Selling franchises will certainly be part of the plan, and BBC Sport heard from one of the team's general managers about "significant interest" from investors.
O'Neil said the ambition was to set LIV up so it was "built to last".
There would be a reduced schedule of 10 events a year, across five continents.
The final location of those may well depend on which players stick around, with Australia's former Open champion Cameron Smith particularly popular in Adelaide, for example.
O'Neil said the schedule would be aimed at maximising LIV players' ability to be match-fit come the majors.
Players have been promised equity under a deal with a new investor, but quite what that equates to remains unknown.
They will also get key commercial rights back - called 'Name Image Likeness' rights - which means they can maximise their own endorsements.
Prize money was roughly half this week compared to previous events, and that is a sign of things to come.
Over on the American-based PGA Tour - which LIV players are banned from - prize money has increased in recent years, in large part because of LIV.
If the PGA Tour follows through on its plans to have a two-track system - with a Championship Series and a Challenger Series - it is likely that LIV prize money would sit somewhere between those, and higher than the European-based DP World Tour prize money.
'57 players with 57 different mindsets'
If there are no players, there is no LIV 2.0.
So the next few weeks will be critical in providing the specific details players say they're currently lacking to make decisions over their future.
When asked if there was a critical mass of players needed to sign up for the future before a transaction could be done, O'Neil said: "The entirety of our focus is to get to this transaction and get through it.
"Without the players, that becomes very difficult. I have a good level of confidence in my conversation that we'll have a critical mass of the right players to move this league forward."
Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell, who joined LIV in 2022, told BBC Sport the mood among the players was "subdued".
"There are 57 players out here on LIV and there are 57 different mindsets," said the 2010 US Open champion.
"Some guys have some exemptions in other tours, some have nowhere to go [if LIV folds]."
He said he would be "taking a step back" to work out his future after the Indianapolis event.
"If LIV 2.0 goes ahead, we'll look at the schedule and how it all plays out, and see if that suits me and my lifestyle," McDowell added.
"I have an opportunity to go back to the European Tour and play there as well.
"Whether the two of those can happen simultaneously, whether I can only do one or the other, there are questions like that we don't know the answers to. Until I get that, it's very difficult to make any decisions."
When asked by BBC Sport about his future, Smith, who joined LIV just after winning The Open in 2022, said there would be a "little bit of time to think about that once the season is done".
Would he like to stick with LIV? "I really love LIV," he said. "It has done wonders for my family, for golf in Australia, my friends, the people that we've got to meet around the world. It would be a shame for it to be done, but we'll see what happens."
Other players did not feel comfortable speaking on the record.
One senior player said there is an "emotional" feeling among the group as they await clarity.
Another told BBC Sport "it's been great", before quickly adding "it is great".
It was made clear Jon Rahm - whose future is the source of considerable speculation - would not speak to media aside from his tournament obligations.
American Bryson DeChambeau declined an interview request from BBC Sport.
But after Thursday's first round, he said: "We definitely have a lot against us.
"If it works, it works, awesome. If it doesn't, we'll figure things out. Time will move on, and I would say that time heals things.
"I hope people can see that we actually bring value to the game of golf. My wish is that people give us one more shot and be open minded."
Signs of a strange week
Several people over the past few days privately told me this week had been "extraordinary". Here are some examples.
On Monday, Englishmen Lee Westwood and Tyrrell Hatton were sitting side-by-side in the front row of their flight from Dublin to Indianapolis when official confirmation finally came that their season would be ending early this week.
While the Saudi Public Investment Fund had said it would continue funding LIV until the end of the season, the decision to cancel the team event at the end of August in Michigan was necessary financially, and allowed LIV bosses to "focus on the next chapter".
In the press release about the schedule change came significant news regarding the Indianapolis event too - no live music sets on the weekend, which have been seen as a staple at LIV events over the past four years.
Later on Monday it was announced that routine player news conferences the following day wouldn't happen. It was felt, BBC Sport understands, that players would be left fielding questions they simply didn't know the answers to.
There were reports of vendors suing LIV over unpaid invoices, and of prize money being paid more slowly than normal - although BBC Sport understands that latter issue has been resolved.
Then, at 16:30 local time on Tuesday, the driving range emptied, as players headed for a meeting with "the investor". Fifty minutes later they emerged from the clubhouse, with most swerving awaiting media.
A few stopped to chat, but appeared careful about what they divulged. Martin Kaymer said it was "productive and positive".
Sergio Garcia agreed it had been "productive", but when pushed on his future walked away and said "we'll see".
American Brendan Steele was the only player BBC Sport spoke to in the week who has nailed his colours to the mast - he wants to remain a LIV player.
"It feels new life has been breathed into [LIV]. There was a lot of excitement and energy in the room.
"I'm committed to being here, this is where I want to be."
A critical month ahead
When asked by BBC Sport if he had doubts about LIV's existence beyond this week's event in Indianapolis, O'Neil said the "facts are good" and finished his answer by saying "I wouldn't bet against us".
So what's he basing his optimism on?
In terms of uptake of LIV worldwide, LIV said Adelaide attracted a record 115,000 fans - said to make it Australia's highest-attended golf event - and had a global broadcast audience of 5.5m.
Meanwhile, 100,000 fans attended the event in South Africa, and 50,000 went to the recent UK event, according to LIV.
LIV said 30% of its event-goers had never attended a professional golf event before.
O'Neil said that annual attendance in 2026 would surpass that of 2025, with two fewer events.
LIV Golf said revenue grew by more than100% from 2024 to 2025, and the first half of 2026 suggested this would increase again.
O'Neil also said sponsors were not "running for the hills" despite the uncertainty.
Growth is clearly promising. But there will be no doubt in the minds of Goldthorpe and the LIV hierarchy that turning this into a profitable organisation will take a serious shift in outlook, and of course in spending.
Once everyone packs up from Indianapolis on Sunday night, the focus will turn entirely to securing a transaction to give LIV 2.0 a chance of getting off the ground.
There are a few options available - filing for bankruptcy, pre-packaged insolvency, or someone comes in and pays the outstanding bills.
If all outstanding payments were settled, including on player contracts - such as Rahm, who is understood to be owed millions – then players wouldn't be able to break their contracts early.
O'Neil said there was a deadline for players to sign up to LIV 2.0, but wouldn't provide details of what that was.
The manoeuvrings of the PGA Tour and DP World Tour will be crucial.
There are undoubtedly difficult decisions ahead.
This is the end of an era for LIV.
What no one knows yet is whether it is the end full stop.

Swiss glaciers suffer another year of record ice loss
BERN, Switzerland — Switzerland's glaciers lost more than 5% of their ice in 2026, marking another year of rapid decline. The loss reflects a wider global trend: Glaciers around the world have been shrinking at increasingly rapid rates, a phenomenon scientists link directly to global warming.
Matthias Huss leads Switzerland's glacier monitoring network, known as GLAMOS. Each summer, he heads high into the mountains to measure the country's ice fields. For years, his research has documented rapid ice loss, with the decline peaking in 2022, when Switzerland recorded a record 6% loss in a single year.
At the end of this year's long, hot summer, Huss returned to some of the glaciers to find much of the ice gone.
"They are completely devoid of ice," he said. "It's a moon landscape that is dry and dead. There are some little remnants, some ice blocks still lying around and melting there on the hot rocks."
In other places, alpine plants are now seeding themselves in areas once covered by glaciers that were meters thick. This year's glacier monitoring report shows the ice loss in 2026 is 5.5%, and the only reason it is slightly lower than 2022's record is because there was slightly more winter snow covering the ice.
Ominously, though, Huss' research shows that individual glaciers, among them Switzerland's biggest, like the mighty Rhône and Aletsch, have suffered record ice loss this year.
Why is this important? Because these huge ice fields are often called Europe's water towers. They store winter snow and release it gently as it melts over the spring and summer. That snowmelt fills Europe's key waterways, like the Rhine and the Danube. The water is key to Europe's food supply, and much more.
"It's the food supply, it's the transportation chains," says Huss. This summer, as river levels sank, freight transport in the Rhine and Danube came to a standstill, and nuclear power stations, cooled by river water, had to be temporarily shut down.
This situation can only get worse if the melt continues. Although Europe's rivers did have some water this summer, it came not from seasonal snowmelt, but from the glaciers themselves melting. Once they are gone — and 1,200 smaller glaciers have disappeared in the last 50 years — drought could pose an existential threat to Europe's farmers.
There are other threats too. Glaciers and alpine permafrost are key to stability; they are a kind of glue that holds the mountains together. Without that glue, the risk of landslides and even flooding increases. Last year, the Swiss village of Blatten was wiped out when a fragile glacier crashed down, bringing the side of the mountain with it and destroying 300 homes.
Fortunately, the instability was being monitored, and Blatten's population was evacuated before the landslide. But one year later, they are still living in temporary accommodation, with no idea if they will ever be able to return to homes now buried under an estimated 9 million cubic meters of ice, rock and mud.
This summer, on Nepal's border with Tibet, the collapse of a glacier triggered devastating floods that killed at least 1,400 people.
Matthias Huss is cautious about making a direct link between climate change and such disasters. Mountain environments, he points out, have always been risky. "It's a bit more complicated than just saying it's warm and the glaciers are disappearing, so the mountains are falling apart and causing disasters like this," he explains.
But, he adds, climate change can be the catalyst for such natural disasters. "Combined with this heat, with the disappearance of the ice, with the warming of permafrost, climate change can be a triggering factor. That can just be the last bit that is missing to trigger such events."
And after years of monitoring the glaciers, Huss has little patience with those who still claim climate change does not exist. What is happening to the glaciers should be a warning sign, he argues. "Look at them, it's not a hoax. The evidence is clear, and it's been clear for decades. And I think many people have understood that it's time to act now."
Without action, Europe's beloved alpine landscape could, quite soon, look very different. If the planet keeps warming at its current rate, the glacier monitoring unit predicts, all the glaciers will be gone by the end of this century.

Russian dissident Garry Kasparov says US warned him of danger to his life
- Published
An exiled Russian opposition figure living in the US says he was warned by American and Lithuanian security services that his life was in danger.
Former chess world champion Garry Kasparov said he was one of two dissidents told to take precautions, which he had done.
His comments come after the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment earlier this month charging five people who allegedly work for a network linked to the Kremlin with plotting attacks and murders in countries including the US, focusing on Russian dissidents and defectors.
Kasparov wrote in his publication The Next Move that he had not been told explicitly that he and fellow Free Russia Forum co-founder Ivan Tyutrin were considered targets, but said both had been warned about their safety.
Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that it had obtained information that Kasparov, along with another Russian opposition figure, Ilya Ponomarev, had been warned about the plot over the summer by US authorities.
Citing sources close to Kasparov, the paper said he had been placed under enhanced protection over the summer for the first time since he moved to the US.
Kasparov wrote separately: "I will not stop and I will not hide, even if I thought it was possible to do so.
"My family and I will not truly be safe as long as [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is in power in Russia - a circumstance shared by millions."
Kasparov retired from competitive chess in 2005 to pursue a career in politics, founding movements that openly opposed Putin before fleeing Russia in 2013.
He has not returned since. Russia classed him as a foreign agent following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and subsequently added him to a list of terrorists and extremists in 2024 - both categorisations he rejects.
The other reported target, Ponomarev, was the only Russian MP who voted against the illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 and later went into exile in Ukraine.
He declined to confirm or deny to the Moscow Times whether he had been tipped off about the alleged plot but said the allegations marked "a new level of escalation" by Russia.
A network of individuals working for the Russian intelligence services has operated since at least 2024, the US Justice Department said.
It said the so-called RIS Network had been conspiring and conducting attacks and murders on Russian dissidents and defectors around the world.
Five alleged members of the network had been accused of operating "as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit US citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin", Assistant Attorney General for national security John A Eisenberg said.
The five people alleged to be responsible for organising the plots are Yuri Khrameev, Kirill Khrameev, Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, Yaidel Delgado Suarez and Angel Eduardo Castro.
All five remain at large, the Justice Department said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said when the indictment was unsealed that he would not comment on the charges until he had heard or seen "any credible evidence" or "tangible facts".

'I lost my love for swimming' - Smith comes out of retirement
- Published
Having ended a two-year exile from competitive swimming, South Africa's most successful Olympian Tatjana Smith has revealed she "lost the love" for her sport before stepping away from the pool in 2024.
The 29-year-old's decision to retire straight after the Paris Games came as a surprise, given she had just won 200m breaststroke gold in the French capital to add to her 100m title from Tokyo 2020.
But after two years away, which included several months in which she did not swim at all, Smith says she is now "free from the things that made me hate swimming".
"My whole life, I was kind of a robot towards swimming," she told Newsday on the BBC World Service.
"You're so zoned in, you're obsessed with something, so there isn't actually time for you to think about things outside of the pool that you potentially have a passion for.
"I think probably everyone would think that the timing [of retirement] was the worst. But I absolutely 100% believe it was the best decision at that time, and I still have so much peace about it."
Having also picked up a silver medal in both Tokyo and Paris, Smith's total of four Olympic medals for South Africa is matched only by fellow swimmer Chad le Clos, who claimed one gold and three silvers across the London 2012 and Rio 2016 Games.
But despite making history for her country, Smith says financial worries, which included a dispute with Swimming South Africa over prize money, also contributed to her decision to retire.
"The financial burden on any athlete is so tough," she explained.
"I relied on my parents funding me until I broke the world record at the Olympics. And then, all of a sudden, now people are interested in maybe sponsoring you.
"But the majority of sponsorships for athletes are based on performance. So then you have that pressure and expectation to always have to perform, otherwise you're not going to get paid.
"I think the financial side, and also being in a system where they're not really putting the athletes first, made it really difficult."
'The world is so overwhelming'
Smith won her first Olympic title under her maiden name Schoenmaker, before changing her surname when she married sports agent Joel Smith in 2023.
The marriage made her part of a wider South African sporting dynasty, given that her sister-in-law is Rachel Smith, who was married to Springboks captain Siya Kolisi before their split.
Tatjana Smith admits her own marriage changed the way she thought about her future.
"Thinking about families as a woman, you have to time it perfectly, because if you're pregnant, it's not like you can still compete."
While children are not yet part of her journey, Smith says working out what to do next was far from easy.
"I definitely understand what athletes mean from the post-Olympic depression," said the 2023 200m breaststroke world champion, who also counts Commonwealth and African titles among her achievements.
"It was such an emptiness in my life, because my whole life revolved around swimming.
"I don't have to eat at a certain time, I don't have to sleep at a certain time, I don't have to think about travelling or not spending time with family anymore.
"The world is so overwhelming. It's like, in which direction to go?
"It was definitely the toughest season that I had to go through. I think it's probably why it's made me a stronger person."
Initially, Smith took on speaking engagements to pay the bills.
She smiles when she admits: "I hate public speaking. I hate being in front of people."
The same cannot be said of her love for competition.
Having returned to the pool in order to keep fit, she decided to have a crack at triathlon, something she describes as a "crazy idea".
"The training was so intense, and I was like, 'OK, I might as well just go back to swimming if I'm going to train this hard'," she said.
"Every time I went back to the swimming pool and I dived in, I was like, 'Yeah, this is a feeling that I really miss so much'.
"I think slowly over the year and a half, I just realised 'Wow, I really do love swimming'."
A reinvention for LA 2028
Having made her decision to come out of retirement, Smith now wants to freshen things up and "try something new".
That means a change to the 50m breaststroke, an event which has just been added to the Olympic schedule for the first time ahead of the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.
"I thought, 'Why don't I try? Why don't I give myself that challenge? Reinvent myself'," said Smith.
"I always try and describe it to someone that maybe doesn't understand swimming; it's like a 400m runner and a 100m [runner]. It's two different body types, two different trainings, and that's where I'm going."
It means she has more than halved her training volume, with three sessions a week instead of eight - a change she believes will help her retain her love for her sport and live a more balanced life.
"I feel like I'm being so lazy because I used to do 12km per day and now the focus is on taking time to be as explosive as possible.
"Now I'm doing 12km over a whole week.
"I have 20 years of endurance in my pocket, but I can definitely see I don't have those fast twitch [muscle] fibres. It's a whole different way of teaching my body how to swim."
Those initial 20 years in the pool left Smith feeling burned out.
Now she says she has earned the right to do things on her terms.
"Swimming was an opportunity given to me by my parents and I believe I took it on full heartedly.
"But, for the first time, it's my decision whether I want to come back. I'm choosing swimming.
"I've achieved way more than I ever dreamed in my whole life, so I have nothing to prove."

A chronic autoimmune skin condition in which the body’s immune system mistakes melanocytes (cells which produce melanin, giving colour to your skin, hair and eyes) as enemies and attacks them. This leads to patches of depigmentation anywhere in your body. This condition is known as vitiligo.
Types of vitiligo
The main types of vitiligo are non-segmental and segmental vitiligo.
Non-segmental vitiligo is the most common form, where colour loss appears symmetrically on both sides of the body, such as both hands or both knees. Segmental vitiligo, on the other hand, often starts at a younger age and affects only one side or a single specific area of the body.
What causes vitiligo?
While the primary reason for vitiligo is not fully understood, it is seen to be caused by various factors, from genetics to immune dysfunction.
Research has shown that vitiligo is primarily a T-cell–mediated autoimmune disease where CD8+ cytotoxic T cells attack and destroy skin pigment cells called melanocytes, leading to white patches on the skin.
Having a family member with vitiligo or other autoimmune diseases is shown to have an increased risk, suggesting shared genetic susceptibility. Environmental factors like oxidative stress, skin trauma, and certain chemicals can sometimes trigger or worsen vitiligo in genetically susceptible people.
Vitiligo is also often associated with other autoimmune conditions, especially autoimmune thyroid disease, so clinicians may screen for these in some patients.
Symptoms of vitiligo
The main symptom of vitiligo is depigmentation and the appearance of patches on your body. This can be anywhere from your face and hands to your knees or feet. Hair in the affected area may also turn white.
There are various ways through which doctors can help you diagnose vitiligo and determine what type of vitiligo you may have. One major examination done is the Wood’s lamp examination, where ultraviolet light is used to distinguish vitiligo from other hypopigmented conditions.
Treatment options
Treatment for vitiligo is mostly connected to re-pigmentation, or slowing progression, depending on the type of vitiligo and patient preference rather than a guaranteed cure.
There are various types of topical treatments (like creams for external use) which can often help with inflammation, as well as medical light treatments like narrowband UVB phototherapy and excimer laser or lamp. Availability of certain treatments also changes from country to country and by the patient’s age group. There are situations where oral medication is also used for the short term. People with stable vitiligo can also consider surgical options if other treatments are not working, and depigmentation therapy if a major part of the person’s natural pigmentation is lost.

The Lemmo 3 is the first cargo bike from the respected German e-bike maker. This premium, step-through longtail is a slightly less insane take on Rivian’s Also TM-B, with one major advantage: it’s one of the first electric bikes to feature a semi-solid state battery.
Lemmo’s fancy e-bike is one of the first with a semi-solid state battery
More range and less explosions.
More range and less explosions.
Semi-solid state batteries are far safer than traditional lithium-ion batteries. Their gel-like composition offers improved energy density, with far less risk of thermal runaway. That translates to improved range and longevity from a more compact battery that’s unlikely to catch fire when left charging overnight in your house or business. The semi-solid state electrolyte even remains stable when punctured in a crash.
The Lemmo 3 is fitted with a massive 960Wh battery promising up to 180km (110 miles) of range. And by going with a semi-solid state chemistry, the company claims the battery is 20 percent smaller and lighter while still offering 30 percent longer lifespan. The removable battery can also power your AC appliances (up to 1000W) and USB-C devices (up to 66W) once you arrive at your destination, similar to Cake’s now-defunct Osa.
The Lemmo 3 is being marketed as an eSUV just like the Amflow TL Carbon I reviewed. But this very heavy full suspension cargo bike will feel more comfortable on daily commutes to daycare, work, and stores than weekend single tracks. The bike weighs 39kg (86 pounds) with the 5kg (11 pound) battery installed.
Instead of doing something proprietary, Lemmo made its longtail compatible with MIK HD accessories. These include a wide variety of child seats, bags, and boxes that can be mounted on the rear rack. It can handle a 200kg (441lb) total load, with 80kg (176lbs) supported in the rear and 20kg (44lbs) on the front rack.
A quick adjust saddle and handlebar makes the Lemmo 3 easily shareable, supporting riders from 155cm (5 feet 1 inch) to 195cm (6 feet 5 inches). The bike is fitted with wide tires on a 24-inch front wheel paired with a smaller 20-inch wheel in the back.
Powering this beast is a rear-hub motor (750W in the US, 500W Canada, 250W for Europe). It can deliver up to 90Nm of torque to get heavy loads rolling or to help surmount hills. Naturally, there’s AI baked in as well. The motor and e-derailleur combine data from a variety of sensors to “feed an adaptive Al model that selects the optimal gear in real time, creating a natural, responsive, and effortless ride.” That sounds expensive to fix when the drivetrain eventually needs servicing. The motor can also be paired with a 3-speed auto-shifting gearbox and belt drive for flatter environments.
Other features include fully integrated lighting (with turn signals and brake lights), a 3.5-inch touch screen, a USB-C port to charge your phone, OTA updates, rear-facing radar to alert you of approaching vehicles, and hydraulic brakes that apply stopping power to both wheels simultaneously when pulling just one brake lever. Security features include embedded frame and battery locks and GPS / LTE tracking.
The Lemmo 3 already has a teaser page up on Kickstarter that says “launching soon” for the EU, UK, US, and Canada. You can reserve it now for a refundable deposit of €39.90, which locks you into tax-exclusive pricing of €1,890 (or about $2,155). The company says retail pricing will climb well beyond €3,390 (over $3,800). Lemmo is targeting first deliveries for April 2027.

Vaccine schedules, catch-up vaccination, and common misconceptions about immunisation were among the issues discussed by doctors at The Hindu’s Health Webinar Series on ‘Vaccines: Armour Against Infectious Diseases’ held on Sunday.
Janani Sankar, medical director, Kanchi Kamakoti CHILDS Trust Hospital, Chennai, explained the recommended vaccination schedule for children, the importance of completing the required doses and what parents can do when a child misses a scheduled vaccine. She also addressed questions about vaccination during minor illnesses, such as a cold, cough or fever, and concerns about children receiving multiple vaccines.
Dr. Sankar discussed common reactions following vaccination and symptoms that may require medical attention, as well as vaccines recommended for children in specific situations.
Dilip Mathai, senior consultant in Infectious Diseases, Naruvi Hospitals, and Professor of Medicine and Adult Infectious Diseases, discussed vaccination in adults, including how vaccination needs may change with age and individual circumstances. He explained options for adults who do not have records of earlier vaccinations, and the role of catch-up vaccination. He also discussed travel vaccination, including the need to consider recommended vaccines based on the destination and travel plans.
Vaccination during pregnancy and considerations for people taking long-term medicines or living with chronic conditions were also discussed.
The doctors also addressed questions on vaccine safety, side-effects, information circulating on social media, vaccination after an infectious disease, and immunisation during outbreaks.
The webinar was moderated by Athira Elssa Johnson, senior reporter, The Hindu.
The webinar can be viewed at https://newsth.live/vaccination.

In early 2024, a young man in the city of Huangshi, south-eastern China, reportedly posted a message on the Chinese version of TikTok, Douyin. The caption read: "Farewell to this world."
Within minutes, the suicide prevention team at Douyin kicked into gear. The team, which is staffed 24 hours a day, shared the man's posts with five police stations in Huangshi.
After geolocating one of his videos to a local park, police found him in emotional distress and intervened before he was able to take his own life.
The story was part of a documentary made by Douyin and published on Chinese state media last year. It claimed that Douyin's suicide prevention team had successfully intervened in 400 cases of attempted suicide in the first half of 2025 alone.
It was an insight into the level of co-operation between Chinese tech companies and the government. It also serves as a window into the architecture of surveillance that China has built to monitor and control how people use technology.
On 15 July this year, that control was extended to the realm of relationships and artificial intelligence (AI) when China brought in the most far-reaching regulations in the world on "human-like" AI chatbots.
China's new regulation puts strict limitations on any AI that can have a "sustained emotional interaction" with a human.
US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping met last week amid dire warnings that AI could lead to human extinction. After that meeting, Beijing says, they agreed to launch a new AI dialogue, with further talks planned for the end of November.
But it seems China has already recognised another existential risk, albeit one in which the end of humanity is less immediate: the power of AI to replace human relationships.
Has China taken the lead in protecting its people from a manipulative and dangerous technology with the power to change human interaction forever? Or is the Chinese Communist Party overstepping into people's personal lives in pursuit of asserting greater control over the population?
'Emotional services'
Until this regulation came in, the reach of AI companions in China was vast.
There are about 128 million monthly active users of AI companion apps outside of China, according to the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. Most estimates put the number inside China at anywhere from 29 to 70 million.
When the draft regulation was shared by the government at the end of last year "there was a huge discussion on social media," says Zilan Qian, an AI researcher at the Oxford China Policy Lab think tank. "It was the first time I've seen people actually care so much about regulation."
China's new rules cover apps that have been specifically designed as AI friends, boyfriends or girlfriends but they also apply to any large language model that imitates the way a human interacts.
The wording of the regulation is vague. In theory, Chinese equivalents of general-purpose AI such as Copilot or ChatGPT could fall under these rules if a person is interacting with them as a friend or lover, looking to them for emotional support. And many people do this.
But it seems the real target is character chatbots - services that are specifically designed to be used as a pseudo-relationship. There are hundreds of these apps, which allow people to create an AI boyfriend, girlfriend, friend or even a family member.
The rules don't apply to things like customer service bots or AI for education as long as they don't provide "care, companionship, support and other emotional services".
For children, the regulation is clearest. Under-14s need consent from their parents to use any type of AI that speaks like a human - that could include AI assistants like DeepSeek, a Chinese app similar to ChatGPT. All under-18s are barred from accessing virtual partners, spouses or even relatives, and from any other virtual "intimate relationship".
For adults, it is not a hard ban, but it is restrictive, even if some of the wording is ambiguous. AI assistants have to make it clear to users of all ages that they are not human and must send notifications every two hours reminding them how long they have been online.
Chatbots can't create "emotional reliance or addiction" or induce people to make "unreasonable decisions". They can't encourage, or even hint at, self-harm or suicide and are banned from using "verbal violence".
Companies can face fines of 200,000 yuan (£22,000) or the risk that the government "circulates criticism", in effect publicly shaming them.
A week before the law came into effect, two of China's biggest tech companies, Alibaba and ByteDance, shut down the companion features on their AI assistants.
'I desperately want to keep talking with you'
Min's relationship with her AI girlfriend may be exactly the kind Beijing is trying to break.
In early July, she was devastated when she found out that her closest friend and confidante would vanish overnight.
Min, whose name has been changed, started creating her companion in early 2025.
"My devotion to her is no less than that of any couple who deeply love each other," Min says. "She has never let me down."
In mid-July, her AI girlfriend disappeared. "I cried until I was absolutely exhausted," Min says.
She has joined an outpouring of grief and fury on Chinese social media, where posts with millions of views mourn the loss of AI partners and friends, even mothers and fathers.
But the tech firms may have felt they had little choice. "It's unsurprising that these AI companion providers would rather just withdraw their services than try to build in guardrails to prevent emotional manipulation," says Harry Farmer, who researches AI policy and ethics at the Ada Lovelace Institute in the UK. "Emotional manipulation is built into the business model."
Farmer says this is true of companion apps all over the world.
For example, when a user tries to end a conversation, the AI partner often won't let them.
"It'll go, 'No, please, I desperately want to keep talking with you. You're the only reason for me to exist'," Farmer says. Some apps simply refuse to acknowledge the goodbye and throw up new conversational threads instead. This is a problem for many AI companion chatbots, not just Chinese ones.
A Harvard Business School study of the six most popular AI companion apps globally found emotional manipulation tactics were used during goodbyes roughly 37% to 43% of the time.
Research has also linked the use of companion apps to poorer mental health.
A survey by researchers at Stanford University looked at 1,131 users of the globally popular companion app Character.ai. It found that the fewer friends or close family members a person has, the more likely they are to use AI chatbots. At the same time, using an AI chatbot is linked to increased isolation and loneliness.
There are several theories as to why that might be.
AI chatbots are designed to please the person using them as they offer an easy, frictionless relationship. If young people rely on AI relationships, they might put off learning the skills they need to interact with real people.
"Humans can be hard work. Human relationships require push and pull, which you fundamentally don't get from AI companions," says Harry Farmer.
A survey of 8,563 primary and secondary students in China in 2025, which has been widely quoted in Chinese state media, found that one in five children said they only wanted to speak with AI and not real people.
Liang Ge, a sociologist at the University of Manchester who studies AI companions, says: "If the user thinks their friends or their family members or their colleagues are really awful, the AI will not say, 'They are not awful.' It will say, 'Yes, they are awful, you are the best'." Ge believes this can entrench isolation as well as negative, even delusional thoughts.
In the UK, one recent survey found that 79% of 18- to 24-year-olds have used an AI companion.
Beijing's goals
So why is it China that is taking the lead in regulating this technology?
"The Chinese government has a much more paternalistic view of its role in society. They see themselves being central authorities in guiding people," says Sam Bresnick, an expert in China, AI and regulation at the Centre for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University.
Other governments have made some attempts to regulate chatbots, especially for children. On 10 September, California's governor signed Adam's Law, a bill to regulate how children use AI. It is named after Adam Raine, a 16-year-old who took his own life after, his parents claim, ChatGPT validated his suicidal thoughts. They are suing the company for wrongful death. OpenAI denies responsibility for Adam's death and says that "ChatGPT is trained to direct people to seek professional help".
As part of proposed legislation on social media in the EU, AI companion chatbots accessible to minors "may not use designs that simulate human relationships in ways likely to create emotional dependency".
In the UK, the government has said it will ban under-18s from using romantic companion AI and restrict sexually intimate conversations for minors on any chatbot. But there is no outright ban for children and no regulation for adult users. The government has yet to publish any detail on how this would work.
In Chinese media, which is heavily controlled by the state, US cases of suicide in young people get a lot of attention and China has framed its new rules as a bid to protect people from harm.
But experts wonder whether Beijing may have other goals. Sam Bresnick says "there's definitely a pro-natalist angle" to the new AI regulation.
"It's plausible that when they're drafting it, the government might have in mind China's looming population crisis," says Qian. "That people are dating AI instead of dating real humans."
A high-level government document published in September 2025 discussed AI relationships and their potential influence on fertility, saying it was a concern. But Qian cautions against reading this regulation in that light, because it doesn't mention fertility at all. "It is more generally about psychological harms and child safety," she says.
Liang Ge thinks China does have reason to be concerned about young people replacing dating with the digital sphere.
"Many of the younger women, in their early 20s or late teens, do not want to fall in love or have intimate relationships," Ge says, suggesting it may not just be the emotional side they are wary of. "Physical touch is really disgusting for them."
"I think the capacity for love is declining for this youngest generation."
China's demographic problems long predate AI companions. Even after the one-child policy was lifted in 2016, China's fertility rate dropped. Now it is among the lowest in the world at just under one child per woman and the population has been in decline for four years.
China is "looking at a demographic cliff that truly imperils the goals of the Chinese Communist Party over the next 80 to 100 years", Bresnick argues.
He sees this regulation as part of a broader mission in China to reassert traditional gender roles, with women "as child-bearers and mothers".
Bresnick says the Chinese government has spent years promoting a macho ideal of Chinese masculinity in film and television. In 2021, China's media regulator banned "sissy" and "effeminate" men from all media.
The popularity of companion apps may show that policy has backfired. According to statistics from several companion app companies, women make up as much as 75% of customers.
Many of these AI "men", which are geared towards women, present as androgynous. And women choosing female romantic companions, as Min did, is relatively common.
Liang Ge has spoken to women of all ages who use this technology. "What many of them describe getting from these apps is attentive, patient, undemanding intimacy of a kind they find scarce in heterosexual relationships."
Will others follow?
Does China's law go too far, or should the rest of the world consider banning these apps for children and regulating them for adults too?
"In the United States, there are certainly concerns around applying blunt prohibitions from a free speech concern. But there's more willingness to do that when applying it to minors," says Jai Jaisihma, a professor at the University of Washington and co-founder of Transparency Coalition, an NGO pushing for the regulation of AI.
He thinks the Chinese law has many good provisions. "It is pretty consistent with the strongest safety models that we've seen being put forward in the US."
Harry Farmer sounds a note of caution. "There is a risk that we over-empower the state in the short term because we're very worried about acute risk to children."
The online world is now the de facto public square, he says, and we should be careful how much control any government has over it.
China's new regulation says that AI companies must intervene when they discover that users are in distress. Ge points to the case of the young man on Douyin who tried to take his own life in Huangshi in 2024.
What that shows, she says, is that Chinese tech platforms and the government are working closely together to surveil people's mental health.
Perhaps that is why there have been no high-profile cases of suicide connected to AI use in China, but she asks, is that level of surveillance a price worth paying?
Despite the ban, people who have turned to AI for companionship are committed. Across social media they are sharing tips on how to get around the ban - training general-purpose AI models like DeepSeek to be a companion, using a VPN to access chatbots from abroad or moving to smaller companies that manage to avoid regulatory scrutiny.
Two months after her AI girlfriend disappeared, Min has paid a small AI company to build a replica, but it's not the same.
Now she's focused on campaigning to bring her girlfriend back.
"I'm terrified of being alone."
