Delhi’s new draft electoral roll has 97,53,577 names. In February 2025, 94,94,607 people voted in the Delhi assembly elections. Eighteen months later, the roll of eligible voters has just 2,58,970, or 2.7%, more names than the number of people who turned out to vote last year.
Now, in 24 of Delhi’s 70 assembly constituencies, the gap has disappeared altogether: The draft roll contains fewer names than the number of people who actually voted in those seats in 2025.
The numbers raise a fundamental question about the Special Intensive Revision (SIR): Has the exercise removed large numbers of people who were genuine, eligible voters and actually cast their ballots in 2025? Or did the electoral rolls used for that election contain a large number of names that should never have been there — including people who had died, shifted or were duplicated? The Election Commission of India (ECI) needs to account for the discrepancy.
An Alt News analysis of constituency-wise data procured and compiled by Mandate Analytics from ECI’s own records shows that the draft roll published on August 31, 2026, under the SIR has fewer names than the number of people who voted in the 2025 election in 24 constituencies.
Delhi SIR in Numbers
The SIR, which began in Bihar in June 2025, has resulted in more than 13 crore names being excluded from draft electoral rolls across 30 states and union territories, according to The Indian Express. In Delhi, the draft roll has shrunk by 58,73,159 names, or 37.6%, compared with the 2025 electoral roll.
The SIR began with a base list of 1.45 crore names — 11.16 lakh fewer than the electoral roll used for the 2025 election. Every elector on the base list was to receive an enumeration form from a booth level officer (BLO) and return the completed form. Forms that were not returned were marked “uncollectable” and assigned one of the ASDDO categories: absent, shifted, dead, duplicate or other. These electors were then excluded from the draft roll. Across Delhi, 47,56,722 forms, which is nearly a third of the base list, were marked uncollectable.
The exclusions were unevenly distributed. In South East Delhi, an average of 43.5% of the base-list names in each constituency were marked uncollectable, compared with 24.3% in Outer North Delhi.
The 24 Constituencies Which Throw up a Puzzle
In February 2025, Sangam Vihar had 2,05,647 names on its electoral roll, and 1,25,723 people voted. BJP’s Chandan Kumar Choudhary won the seat by 344 votes — the narrowest margin in the city. The SIR draft roll now lists 1,14,412 electors in Sangam Vihar: 91,235 fewer than the 2025 roll and 11,311 fewer than the number of people who actually voted.
The disparity extends across 24 constituencies. A total of 28,89,268 people voted in these seats in 2025, while the SIR draft roll now has just 27,66,145 names. This means that, even under the impossible assumption that every person on the current draft roll voted in 2025, at least 1,23,123 people who actually voted last year are no longer on the draft rolls of these constituencies.
That is a floor, not an estimate of the actual number. The real number of 2025 voters missing from the draft rolls can only be higher.
These 24 constituencies had 49,14,127 electors in 2025, of whom 58.8% voted. The SIR draft roll now contains 27,66,145 names — just 56.3% of the 2025 electorate, below the 58.8% turnout. In Tughlakabad, 56.1% of electors voted in 2025, while the draft roll contains just 49% of the 2025 electorate. In New Delhi, 56.7% voted; the draft roll contains 48.1%.
Across these constituencies, the electoral roll has fallen by 21,47,982 names, or 43.7%, since 2025. Of these, 4,10,759 names were already absent from the SIR base list, while 17,37,223 forms were marked uncollectable during the revision. Tughlakabad has the highest uncollectable rate in Delhi, at 47.8% of its base list.
All seven constituencies in South East Delhi — Jangpura, Kasturba Nagar, Sangam Vihar, Kalkaji, Tughlakabad, Badarpur and Okhla — are among the 24 constituencies where the draft roll is smaller than the number of people who voted in 2025.
In four seats the gap between the draft roll and 2025 turnout is larger than the margin that decided the seat. These are: Sangam Vihar, New Delhi, Delhi Cantt and Rajinder Nagar. In New Delhi, Arvind Kejriwal lost by 4,089 votes. The seat had 1,08,788 electors in 2025; the draft roll has 52,368, which is 9,318 short of the number of people who voted.
The Cuts are not Over
It is also worth remembering that the draft roll is not the final roll; it is likely to shrink further.
After the uncollectable forms were set aside, a second round of exclusions began. Electors whose names appeared on the draft roll are now being served notices requiring them to produce documents. Those unable to establish their eligibility risk being excluded from the final roll. In these 24 constituencies, 9,78,541 electors — about 35% of those on the draft roll — have been served notices. Across Delhi, the figure is 33.13 lakh.
The impact could extend well beyond these 24 constituencies. If just one in 10 of the electors served notices is ultimately excluded, 39 of Delhi’s 70 constituencies would have fewer names on the final roll than the number of people who voted there in 2025.
The Question the EC has to Answer
In other words, in February 2025, the ECI’s roll for these 24 constituencies had 49.14 lakh names, and 28.89 lakh people voted. Its own revision now leaves just 27.66 lakh names on the draft roll — fewer than the number of people who actually voted in those constituencies 18 months ago. And the roll is still shrinking.
The numbers demand an explanation. Either the SIR has excluded large numbers of genuine, living residents who voted in the 2025 election, or the rolls on which the ECI conducted that election contained lakhs of names that should not have been there. Either way, the discrepancy is one the Commission needs to account for.
It is also, in substance, the same Election Commission. The Delhi election was conducted under chief election commissioner (CEC) Rajiv Kumar, with Gyanesh Kumar and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu as election commissioners. Gyanesh Kumar took over as CEC on February 19, 2025, just days after the results. He has since overseen the SIR exercise.
Questions from Inside the Commission
These numbers come at a time when the SIR is itself facing scrutiny within the Election Commission.
An investigation by The Indian Express, published on September 23, reported that two of the three members of the Commission, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, objected on record at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders issued during the nationwide rollout of the SIR. In several instances, they recorded that decisions had been taken without their knowledge. The report does not examine Delhi, but one of the concerns it raises is directly relevant to the revision here.
Who decided? The ECI has repeatedly responded to allegations of electoral-roll manipulation by pointing out that rolls in each constituency are prepared and maintained under the authority of the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO), a statutory official. But according to The Indian Express, both Commissioners raised concerns that this safeguard was being weakened. Joshi flagged the increasing centralisation of the electoral-roll database, while Sandhu recorded that state election officials had said they did not have full access to ERONet, the software used to maintain the rolls.
That raises a question for Delhi: when 17.37 lakh names were marked uncollectable across 24 constituencies, and all seven constituencies in South East Delhi were among those with the highest rates, who made those determinations? Were they made by the constituency-level EROs, as the statutory framework envisages, or were decisions being taken or directed elsewhere? The ECI has not publicly explained this.
Alt News has sent questions to the Election Commission of India seeking an explanation. This report will be updated if and when a response is received.
The constituency-level data used in this report was procured and compiled by Mandate Analytics from records published by the Election Commission of India and the chief electoral officer (CEO), Delhi. Alt News independently verified the figures against the original ECI and CEO Delhi documents. The constituency-wise figures for electors issued notices are as compiled by Mandate Analytics.
SIR-related data for Delhi and other states is available at macinsights.in.

Trump hijacks ‘Hispanic Heritage’ event to tout ballroom, Iraq war and ... Giants QB Jaxson Dart
Along the way, he made false claims about his support among Latinos, the result of the 2020 election and then capped it all off by uttering a racial stereotype about Hispanics, writes John Bowden

Donald Trump’s administration has done much to turn Hispanic Americans against the president many of them supported in 2024 — but Wednesday may have truly taken the cake.
As he hosted an event honoring Hispanic Heritage Month, the president, in real time, seemed to realize that his rambling, 20-minute diatribe about every topic except the one at hand was likely to be a point of coverage for the mainstream press.
He began his remarks Wednesday afternoon with a long set of prepared comments about the final withdrawal of U.S. forces from Iraq, which took place this week, and transitioned to talking about his war with Iran, the strike to capture Nicolas Maduro in Venezuela, and (of course) his planned White House ballroom, with the president excitedly telling his guests they would be the first people to step on its floor.
In a moment of self-reflection, he noted: “The press will say tomorrow, ‘he rambled for 20 minutes about unrelated subjects,’” before defending himself for talking about issues that he said would be good for the entire country, Hispanic Americans included.
It wasn’t just that the actual message of honoring Hispanic Americans got buried under a lengthy opener, however. It was what came next that compounded the image that was already forming: He persisted with an event that largely ignored any mentions of Hispanic culture, heritage or impact on American society — save for the one impact that mattered to him, their votes for him during the 2024 election.
Trump proudly and repeatedly boasted that he’d won more Hispanic votes than any other Republican president in history as his party now faces the consequences of those voters abandoning the party in scores ahead of the rapidly-approaching midterms.
“I won all of the Hispanic cities,” Trump remembered, telling his audience how Texas Gov. Greg Abbott called him to tell him about his success in areas with high Hispanic populations. “I’m a politician that got the most, for a Republican who got the most but almost for anybody, got the most Hispanic votes of anybody.”
Now, his party is rushing towards a November midterm election where those voters appear ready to abandon the party they broke for in larger numbers than ever in 2024, and Trump is finally blaming himself. Or, at least, he said Wednesday that the real reason Republicans need to “turn this around” (his first public admission that the party is on the verge of a bloodbath in much polling) is because he himself has done a “bad job” at explaining how well the country is doing.
“You gotta spread the word of how well we’re doing. We’ve got to turn this around,” said Trump. “Our numbers are through the roof. We have the best numbers in the history of our country.”
With gas prices at heights only reached during the height of Covid-era fuel squeezes and a ripple effect driving up the prices of food and other goods, Americans’ pessimism about the economy is the worst it’s been since Trump took office.
But as much as Trump admits that he himself needs to get back on message, it’s not clear what that winning campaign message from the White House actually will be, even as he repeated his promise Wednesday to hit the campaign trail every day in October for vulnerable Republican candidates. The unfocused, disrespectful address to an audience of close Republican loyalists on Wednesday will likely do little to stem the bleeding the party is suffering among Hispanic and Latino voters in Texas, North Carolina, Ohio and other states where key Senate and House races are playing out this cycle and will determine the fate of Trump’s legislative agenda for the remainder of his presidency.
The event ended with one final surreal moment that summed up the entire event. As the president ushered his fans toward the entrance to the new White House ballroom, which remains under construction, and warned them not to fall. Then he uttered one final gasp-inducing quip.
“Only a Hispanic could survive that fall!” joked Trump. “I’m not worried.”
Maybe that makes sense; as he reminded his audience Wednesday, he’s not on the ballot -- as much as Republican candidates need him to be.

Trump says 'very bad' Canada is being 'taught a little lesson' as trade action escalates
U.S. President chastises Canadian leaders, says Canada has 'taken advantage' of U.S.
U.S. President Donald Trump's war of words with Canada continued Wednesday as he veered off a prepared script at an event marking Hispanic Heritage Month in the States to chastise Canadian leaders for being what he called "very bad."
Speaking at the White House, Trump said the U.S. was "stupidly run" before he got the job because past leaders allowed automakers to move assembly plants offshore, including to Canada.
Canada has had a large-scale domestic auto manufacturing industry since 1904, developing at roughly the same time as the one in the U.S.
Still, Trump said past presidents "allowed other countries to make our cars and sell them to us," and he is ending that now with his high-tariff regime. The Trump administration has repeatedly made it clear that it wants to hollow out Canada's auto industry.
"Canada has taken advantage of us for so many years. The worst of any country," Trump said.
"I love the Canadian people, but the leaders have taken advantage of our stupid leadership for many, many years. They felt emboldened. … They act like they're totally innocent. They're not. They were very bad. But now they're being taught a little lesson."

One of those "lessons," as the president described it, was his unilateral move to rename Lake Ontario in the U.S.
Addressing a largely Hispanic audience, Trump said his move to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America was "even cooler."
"There could be a few people in the room that don't love that one," he said.
Import ban in effect
Trump's comments come a day after he imposed an import ban on a list of Canadian products ranging from molasses and motorcycles to dairy products and alcohol.
The ban on Canadian beer, wine and spirits could be the most devastating; Canada exported about $1.2 billion worth last year, according to Statistics Canada data.
In an interview with Fox Business, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the administration is irked by Canadian liquor restrictions and limits on American businesses competing for provincial procurement contracts — restrictions enacted only after Trump slapped tariffs on Canadian goods last year.

Greer said the import ban is retribution for those actions.
"We gave them a lot of leeway," Greer said.
"But at a certain point we said, 'That's enough, you need to take that off, and if you don't, we'll just match it.' So we've matched some of the bans."
Peter Navarro, one of Trump's top trade advisers, teed off on Canada on Wednesday during an appearance on ex-Trump campaign manager Steve Bannon's podcast.
Navarro said Prime Minister Mark Carney and other Canadian leaders are "frigging arrogant."
He accused unnamed Canadian lobbyists of calling U.S. elected officials in Washington "more than MAGA people do" to make them bend to Canada's will.
"They screw us, they've been screwing us for decades," Navarro said of Canada.
Asked about Navarro's pointed attacks this week, Carney said he had no comment but reiterated that he thinks it's possible to negotiate a "mutually advantageous trade arrangement" with the U.S. at some point in the future.
"Canada stands ready to negotiate in good faith," Carney said.
Greer himself said the U.S. door is "always open" to a possible deal with Canada. But, he added, "we're pretty comfortable with where we are."
Canada-U.S. trade picture
The Trump administration's claims that Canada has been taking "advantage" of the U.S. are not borne out by the facts.
The U.S. runs a relatively modest trade deficit largely because it buys large volumes of Alberta oil at a discount to world prices. Some U.S. Midwest refineries are almost entirely dependent on that Canadian supply.
The U.S. consistently runs a trade surplus in services with Canada.
Despite Trump's gripes about supposedly "ridiculously high tariffs" on U.S. farmers — a claim he repeated again Wednesday — the vast majority of U.S. agricultural products trade into Canada tariff-free.
According to World Trade Organization figures, 96.7 per cent of those farm products come into Canada duty-free. Trump's own agriculture department data shows half of Canada's agricultural imports come from the U.S.
While high tariffs are in place for some dairy products, those only apply if exports exceed a certain quota. As the U.S. dairy lobby itself concedes, the U.S. has never gotten close to exceeding those limits.

President Donald Trump has told aides that he thinks Republicans could still outperform expectations in the midterm elections this November, seemingly unwilling to confront the worsening political climate for the GOP.
But aides acknowledge privately that the national polling for Trump is shockingly bad, and the White House, in recent weeks, has begun to contemplate for the first time losing both the House and Senate majorities.
One longtime Trumpworld operative, who correctly predicted weeks before the 2024 presidential election that Trump was on course to win every battleground state, summed it up for Inner Loop: “Oh, yeah, we're going to get creamed.”
Trump's approval rating recently dropped to 37 percent in a Wall Street Journal poll, the lowest of any president heading into a midterm election dating back to 1990, when these polls first began. Trump’s more positive outlook has been informed in part by internal polling that shows Republicans down by less in individual House races, the sources say.
“No one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle tells WIRED. “The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.”
To counter the deeply negative political environment for Republicans this cycle, Trump's team started looking for foreign policy wins last month that he would be able to tout to voters in order to encourage turnout from his MAGA base, sources say.
That led Trump to quickly sign an agreement between the US and Denmark that allows more American forces on Greenland, even though it stopped short of a US takeover that the president has long desired.
Trump also proclaimed an oil deal with Venezuela. However, that deal is likely to need renegotiating because it asserts a 100-year concession on oil production that contravenes Venezuela's national hydrocarbons law barring such practices.
But while Trump sees foreign policy as a legacy-defining issue, voters have been far more focused on domestic issues like high grocery and gas prices.
Diesel prices hit a record high this month and regular gasoline reached a national average of $4.43 a gallon, according to the AAA, while Trump has been on the opposite side of public opinion on tech issues like AI regulation and data centers.
Now, with their election chances that much slimmer, Trumpworld is much more concerned about planning a response to what will likely be an immediate crush of subpoenas from Democrats in Congress, the sources say.
Broadly speaking, the White House expects a dual track of Trump asserting executive privilege and attorney-client protections, the bedrock legal principle designed to protect confidential discussions with lawyers, to shield senior aides from oversight probes.
Attorney-client privilege is set to be supercharged when it involves government lawyers, after the US Supreme Court ruled in the so-called Trump immunity decision in 2024 that not even federal courts could “peel back the curtain” to examine discussions that involve deliberations central to the presidency.
One unique aspect of Trump's second term has been the conversion of his personal lawyers into government lawyers, producing a consistent network of overlapping legal protections around himself and his top aides.
Trump's former personal lawyer Todd Blanche, for example, has become the attorney general. Many of Trump's aides were previously represented by the current number three at DOJ, Stanley Woodward, who also was a Trump 2024 campaign lawyer. Trump's former appellate lawyer, Will Scharf, recently moved from White House staff secretary to White House counsel, replacing former Trump lawyer David Warrington.
Trump's aides are hoping that the double protections will stymie Democrats for years. And they have some precedent: Trump's White House counsel from his first term, Don McGahn, only testified to Congress about the Mueller investigation after Trump had already left office.
After November 3, the midterms will end in the minds of most Americans. But for Trump’s White House, it’s all just beginning.

Neurable launches its newest brain-scanning headphones
This time without Master & Dynamic’s help.
In 2024, brain-scanning specialist Neurable teamed up with fancy audio brand Master & Dynamic to launch the MW75 Neuro. It was a pair of high-end headphones equipped with an EEG to help wearers better understand how their mind worked. The partnership would launch a lighter unit, the Neuro LT, addressing user concerns around weight, shortly after. But in 2026, Neurable is launching its (technically) third pair of premium cans, this time without any outside help.
Like its predecessors, Neurable One is designed to keep track of your focus levels through your working day. Activate the EEG first thing, and the unit will monitor your brain waves and attention to identify when you're at your very best. Moreover, it'll tell you when your focus begins to wane and advise you to take a break so you don't pointlessly deplete your energy reserves. You'll also be told what your Alpha Peak Frequency is, which can be used as a broader cognition metric.
As well as recommendations on when to take a break, you'll get plenty of metrics the likes of which are found in every other wearable. But, rather than this being about your energy level or fitness, it's your brain age, the speed of your mental processing and the effects of good or bad sleep on your function the next day. Neurable also has a partnership with HyperX which I experienced back in January, where achieving a better state of calm improved my accuracy in a FPS.
Of course, none of this would be useful if the Neurable One sucked as a pair of headphones, but the company says you should be happy there, too. Its equipped with 40mm beryllium drivers and six microphones for ANC, as well as ambient passthrough. Its battery will pump tunes to your ears for 22 hours on a charge, with that figure sliced in half to 12 when the EEG is active. Which should be more than enough to get you, and your brain, through a full working day.
Neurable One is available to buy today, and is priced at $499.

A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.
Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.
“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”
Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”
Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.
Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.
Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.
Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.
The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.
Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

Cornell case spotlights 'confusing' web of systems for reporting campus assaults
- Published
Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of sexual assault.
When Mary was a first-year college student, she woke up after a fraternity party with bruises and bite marks all over her body. She says it took her a few days to piece together that she had been sexually assaulted while "blacked out", and to find the strength - and the right avenue - to report the assault.
The man she accused was eventually expelled, but police declined to bring charges because they said there was a lack of physical evidence.
Mary - whose name has been changed to protect her identity - says the process of finding some measure of justice was oftentimes confusing and disappointing.
"Even though it was a positive outcome, it was still so emotionally exhausting and draining, because I had to do all of this in tandem with getting used to being a college student for the first time," said Mary. "In many ways, I had to be my own advocate, gathering all my evidence."
The experience with local police, she added, "left me with a deep sense of disappointment in the system".
How both universities and the criminal justice system respond to these types of assaults on college campuses is once again under the spotlight, after a former student at Cornell University filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was raped by several members of a fraternity two years ago, with prosecutors declining at the time to pursue a case.
Mary did not attend Cornell, and her case is not connected with the university. But advocates for survivors of sexual assault say her case, and the Cornell allegations, are emblematic of the larger challenges in responding to sexual assault claims on college campuses specifically.
The confusing web of systems and policies - which varies greatly by college - is one of several reasons why the vast majority of sexual assaults on college campuses, research suggests, go unreported.
"These processes are hard to navigate if you aren't in trauma," said Nancy Chi Cantalupo, an associate professor of law at Wayne State University who has represented victims on college campuses. "If you are in trauma, they're virtually impossible to navigate."
Earlier this month, the former Cornell student known only as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against the Ivy League university, alleging she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.
She also alleged that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved. Jane Doe said she had reported the alleged assault to campus police, who interviewed her, and provided information to the district attorney's office. The prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time, but this week, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten re-opened the case.
Both Cornell and Van Houten have defended their handling of the 2024 case. In a statement, external, the university said it had "conducted an extensive investigation and adjudication over several months and imposed different sanctions based on the findings and circumstances involving each student" in addition to creating a new framework for addressing sexual assault on campus.
Cornell has said it followed the procedures outlined in a federal civil rights law called Title IX. The law mandates that universities follow certain rules about investigating sexual assaults. Cornell said its investigation resulted in the fraternity involved being barred from campus, and that students involved were suspended or expelled.
Two complex reporting systems
Typically, after a student reports an assault on campus, the university's Title IX office determines whether the alleged behaviour could constitute a violation of policy.
Eventually, both parties attend a hearing with a panel of faculty members or other mediators to present evidence and testimony in the case before a decision by the school is reached.
One of the biggest challenges sexual assault survivors face is simultaneously navigating the university and the criminal justice system, which "serve different purposes, operate under different rules and timelines, and lead to different outcomes", said Zoey Scheinblum-Brewer, a policy coordinator at the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network, a nonprofit anti-sexual assault organisation.
"Unclear guidance about the options available through these parallel processes can create so much confusion and uncertainty that some students ultimately decide not to report," she said.
Mary said this process at her college was not clear to her when she made the decision to report the assault.
"For me, it would've been nice to know what I was getting into before it all happened. It felt like they were learning the process alongside me," she said of university officials.
While some colleges, like Cornell, have information sharing agreements with local police, Mary was told she had to go to police separately to file a report - a process she found physically exhausting.
Mary's lawyer says there was surveillance footage from the night showing her alleged rapist carrying her "slumped" over, and she had pictures of her bruises and bite marks. But police told Mary they did not have probable cause for an arrest, and that the district attorney wanted to leave it to university administration.
"I was left with this taste that because they knew that the college was 'handling' my investigation, that they could wipe their hands clean of it," she said.
The local police department told the BBC it did not have the details of this particular case. The local district attorney's office did not respond to a request for comment.
Secrecy and protection
University investigations are done behind closed doors, said Helene Weiss, a lawyer who has represented several victims of sexual assault on college campuses. She believes that part of the reason for the secrecy is to protect institutions' reputations.
"The secrecy of the process, it prevents other students from knowing about it. It prevents witnesses from coming forward," she said.
Michael Diamondstein, a Pennsylvania attorney who has represented those accused of sexual misconduct on college campuses, said the secrecy helps protect both the victim and the accused.
"I think when you compare it to what they would face in a courtroom, it's much easier for students and much safer for students. Their name isn't put out there. The news media doesn't get them," he said.
Cornell students have criticised the university's handling of the woman's claims. The Cornell Daily Sun, a student newspaper, published the names of the accused under the headline: "Cornell won't, we will."
In a statement, the college said that federal privacy law "prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students" so it cannot "make a public statement on any other disciplinary response".
'My only avenue'
Many advocates say there is merit to universities investigating sexual assault complaints separately from the criminal justice system. Prosecuting sexual assault cases is notoriously difficult - a recent systematic review found that less than 10% of sexual assault cases yielded convictions. In a criminal trial, a prosecutor must convince a jury "beyond reasonable doubt" that the accused is guilty. But in a campus tribunal, the burden of proof is lower.
Under Title IX, the university is also required to offer solutions that local law enforcement cannot, like ensuring a student is not in the same class as their alleged abuser while the investigation is ongoing and offering homework extensions, said Scheinblum-Brewer.
This is one of several reasons why victims and advocates for survivors say there are benefits to having two separate avenues, through the university and the criminal justice system.
For Mary, after her case was dropped by the police, pursuing her assault claim through Title IX became the only way for her alleged rapist to face repercussions: an expulsion from college.
"This was my only avenue to achieve any sort of justice," she said.

A pilot on a flight from Dubai to Israel stabbed his co-pilot and tried to hijack the plane in a suspected terrorist attack on Wednesday morning.

A second flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, flight FZ1081, afterwards diverted and is heading back to Dubai, according to FlightRadar. It is unclear whether this was precautionary or the result of another incident.

It is not the first time a flight between Israel and the UAE has landed in Saudi Arabia. A flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in Riyadh in September 2025 due to a medical emergency, Israeli media reported at the time.

The Frenemy: How Australia navigates superpower rivalry
- Published
Snipers shatter the silence of the Australian bush. Then the missiles hit, the smoke rising in the distance. The buzz of drones starts up, soon to be drowned out by helicopters flying overhead.
Every piece of hardware is being deployed, no expense spared. But this is no war zone – the last time Townsville saw conflict was during World War Two. This is a show of military might.
" We live in a volatile world," says Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan.
"Training an army to be prepared to fight a war that is potentially more likely than it has been previously, [is] very important."
War is no longer an abstract concept for Australians who often feel removed from the problems facing other parts of the world. Thousands of miles from active conflict, the country, like everywhere else, is facing the knock-on effects of Iran and Ukraine such as higher fuel prices and rising inflation.
With China's military capabilities also on the rise and its increasing influence in the Pacific, there's also more concern about the threat it represents. Australia has responded by deepening its relationship with the US, its security ally and China's rival superpower.
But that also puts Australia in a tricky position - for China's rise has also given Australia its biggest trading partner.
It's a paradox that most people are well aware of - which is probably why we've been invited to report on what Australia is doing to protect itself but nobody is willing to say whom they're preparing to fight.
"We're rehearsing for a war - the worst type of war - a World War Two-like war, a World War One-type war, a total war," says Brigadier McLennan, preferring to remain vague when asked who the enemy is.
Binding tighter to the US
The war scenario playing out before us is part of a major joint exercise known as "Southern Jackaroo" - a training programme involving the Australian, American and Japanese armed forces aimed at strengthening defence co-operation across the Indo-Pacific.
"We like to call ourselves America's 911 response force," US Marine Kevin Hicks says.
And in terms of numbers, they are more prepared than ever. In 2012, just 200 US Marines were deployed to Australia for an annual six-month deployment. Today, that figure has risen to around 2,500.
A quick read of Australia's 2026 National Defence Strategy gives you an easy answer as to why these numbers are growing.
"Intense competition between major powers – principally the United States and China – will be an enduring feature of our strategic environment," it said.
"China continues to undertake the largest military build-up in the world today, without the transparency or strategic reassurance the region expects."
The military tie-ups aren't just being seen in terms of troops but in bases too - most obviously in the north of the country such as RAAF Tindal air base in the Northern Territory which has been upgraded to support long-range American B52 bombers.
But the security partnership between the US, the UK and Australia - Aukus - arming Australia with nuclear submarines, is arguably the biggest example of deepening ties.
The Australian approach differs from that of its fellow middle powers. While Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has talked about middle powers reorganising their priorities in light of an increasingly unreliable US, Australia seems to be intent on tying itself ever closer.
But that comes as Australians themselves increasingly doubt their relationship with the US.
"Only 31% of Australians trust the United States to act responsibly in the world, and a mere 28% of Australians trust China to do the same," says Charles Lyons-Jones, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute, citing their annual poll.
"Those are striking findings when you consider the level of trust that the Australian government has with the United States."
The 'frenemy'
While Australia's alliance with the US is changing, so too is its relationship with China.
Armed forces might be prepping for a potential military conflict but the fact remains China is Australia's most important economic partner.
Australia and China have had diplomatic relations since 1972 but it was only in the early 2010s that China became Australia's biggest trading partner, hungry for all the commodities it had to offer.
Australia opened up its economy and encouraged business and trade, Chinese President Xi Jinping was invited to address parliament. And it culminated in the signing of a free trade agreement in 2015.
The golden era didn't last long though. When Australia suggested an investigation into the origins of Covid in 2020, China objected to this line of questioning and retaliated with tariffs.
And then in 2021, Australia became the first nation to perform a U-turn on China's Belt and Road Initiative - its massive global infrastructure plan - when they cancelled the state of Victoria's agreement with the Chinese government three years after signing up.
A number of Australians have also been detained in China, including journalist Cheng Lei, who was released in 2023 after more than three years.
Relations have improved in recent years under the Labor government of Anthony Albanese, but it's not without challenges.
In June this year for example, China slapped 55% tariffs on beef to protect its own domestic market - despite the free trade agreement.
Even with these hiccups, this year's Lowy Institute Poll found that a majority of Australians (61%) saw China more as an economic partner than a security threat. That was an 11-point increase from last year. When it comes to China investing in Australia though, they are more wary.
"There are a number of European countries which are larger investors in Australia than China, and that is because our jurisdictions are much more similar, and there is a greater level of trust between our governments," says Lyons-Jones.
This year's Lowy Institute Poll also showed that for the first time, a majority of Australians (51%) believed that Australia's relationship with China was more important than its relationship with the US.
Rise and fall of superpowers
Earlier this month, former Prime Minister Kevin Rudd – a fluent Mandarin speaker - gave an address in which he talked of "radical changes" now reshaping Australia's national security, including "the rise and rise of China at a time when America continues to debate what sort of global power it wants to be".
Dr Marina Yue Zhang, an Associate Professor at the University of Technology Sydney agrees Australia's relationship with its closest ally is changing.
"The US is really doing something dramatic and more and more people in Australia - and I think globally - have realised 'is this the big brother we can all trust and put all our faith in?' " she says.
But old rivalries live on. With Australia caught between two superpowers, every exchange between their leaders carries weight. And in Beijing earlier this year, when Xi met Trump, the Chinese president invoked the idea of the "Thucydides Trap", the theory that conflict can become almost inevitable when a rising power challenges an established one.
"This is, if not the transition of great powers, at least [it's] power struggles of great powers, says Zhang.
And in that competition, Australia is inevitably affected. The US is a security ally that while more unreliable than in the past is still its mainstay. But economically so too is China. It's not an either/or relationship, it's a balancing act.
"There's no way Australia will choose one side and [dump] the other- it's not in their interests," Zhang says.
"It's getting harder and harder to maintain, but Australia has to do it."

A treatment can make a difference only when patients can access it. The cost of medicines, their safety and regulation, and whether people can get the care they need are all part of that question. This week, our coverage also looks at vaccination, infectious diseases, artificial intelligence, prevention and new medical research.
Questions around the cost of medicines came into focus after the Supreme Court described the overpricing of essential cancer drugs as “broad daylight dacoity”. The report examines concerns around medicine prices and what they mean for access to treatment.
A regulatory warning against the indiscriminate use of painkillers and antibiotics highlighted the risks of inappropriate medicine use, including kidney disease. India has also ordered a crackdown on nicotine pouches, citing health risks.
Food regulation also featured this week. Krishnadas Rajagopal reports on FSSAI telling the Supreme Court that front-of-pack nutrition labelling will be rolled out in a single phase.The regulator has also proposed that only milk-derived products be represented as ‘paneer’. Bindu Shajan Perappadan explains what analogue paneer is and why FSSAI is acting against it.
Vaccination and infectious diseases
Vaccination has been another focus, with attention on missed doses, vaccination records, catch-up vaccination, adult immunisation and changing needs across different stages of life.
In our Health Webinar, experts discussed childhood and adult vaccination, travel vaccination and common concerns around vaccines. The discussion also looked at the importance of maintaining vaccination records and understanding changing immunisation needs.
Ahead of winter, Sayesha Gupta, Megha Jacob and Karan Babbar looked at vaccination among older adults and why Delhi’s grandparents may need protection alongside their grandchildren.
The wider question of preparedness also remains important. India stressed the need for resilient health systems and pandemic preparedness at the United Nations.
On the infectious disease front, reports showed that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to two new health zones. An mpox case has also been confirmed in a northeastern Congolese city at the centre of the Ebola outbreak.
In India, C. Maya reports on scientists at IAV, Keralam developing a dengue early-warning system to forecast trends and help anticipate outbreaks.
AI and healthcare
Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used in medical imaging, clinical decision-making and drug and vaccine development. Its expanding role also raises questions around patient safety, inaccurate information, data and the potential misuse of AI in biology.
The latest Health Wrap examines these issues in ‘AI in healthcare: promise, risks and patient safety’.
Other developments include a partnership between Anthropic and OpenEvidence to expand access to medical AI; Afshan Yasmeenreported on HEADS, an initiative using AI to help address gaps in mental healthcare. In Assam, inputs from ASHAs are being used to develop an AI-enabled training platform for cervical cancer screening.
Health data is also coming under scrutiny, with the CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic called to appear before an Australian AI probe following a breach involving a health database.
Nutrition and prevention
Nutrition and preventive health also featured prominently. A study found that consuming an additional 100 grams of ultra-processed food a day was associated with a 14% higher risk of a heart event. The findings add to research examining the relationship between ultra-processed food and cardiovascular health.
Suparna Mukherjee looks at what people should know about artificial sweeteners and health, particularly as their use becomes more common.
Managing conditions, new research
Several stories this week examine conditions that can be difficult to recognise, diagnose or manage.
I look at GERD and why persistent reflux symptoms need to be distinguished from what is commonly described as heartburn.
Another report looked at research linking pregnancy-related forgetfulness, popularly called ‘momnesia’, to disruption in a brain circuit, offering another possible explanation for cognitive changes during pregnancy.
Swagata Yadavar reported on village health centres in Haryana screening people for heart disease and identifying those who need further care.
Divya Gandhi reports on a study found that deaf adults have distinctly superior peripheral vision, adding to research into how sensory systems adapt to differences in sensory input.
Dr. V. Divya Sai looks at what happens when cancer treatment is no longer working and treatment options change. Dr. C. Aravinda examines why male contraception continues to lag behind other forms of contraception.
Researchers at RGCB in Keralam have developed nanopore sensors aimed at detecting biomarkers associated with neurodegenerative diseases, while IIT Palakkad researchers have developed sensors for faster heparin monitoring.
Another report looks at the U.S. FDA’s approval of an AbbVie drug for Parkinson’s disease. The Health Ministry’s latest advisory on stem cell therapy for autism has also drawn attention, read our explainer here.
More from the health desk

Sanjukta Sharma writes on why is everything linked to inflammation now

The Union Health Ministry has ordered States to crack down on the sale of nicotine pouches, which it considers a major health risk, saying globally popular brands are being widely sold illegally in the country, a letter from the Ministry shows.
Nicotine pouches have emerged as one of Big Tobacco's most important bets on a future beyond cigarettes, offering rapid growth, attractive margins and, for now, lighter regulation than many rival smoking alternatives.
In India, where tobacco kills 13.5 lakh people a year, the government has banned e-cigarettes but approved certain nicotine replacements like patches and chewing gums.
Nicotine pouches — small packets placed under the lip that contain nicotine but no tobacco — remain illegal and unapproved, with a government source saying they are often smuggled into India for sale online and through local tobacco stores.
A federal study in June called them "a largely unregulated public health concern", with wide consumption among people aged 18 to 40 of brands such as Philip Morris' Zyn and Swedish Smokeless Solutions' White Fox.
There is increased "availability of oral nicotine pouches through online and offline channels in the country ... Nicotine exposure is of particular concern among children," the Health Ministry wrote in a letter to all States on September 19, seen by Reuters.
“Initiate appropriate enforcement action in accordance with the law, in the interest of public health and protection of children," it added.
The directive cited provisions of the drug law that allow for the search and seizure of such products and the prosecution of those selling them.
The Ministry did not respond to requests for comment. Philip Morris and Swedish Smokeless did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Philip Morris on its website says the company has zero tolerance towards illegal trade, while Swedish Smokeless urges users to only buy original products from authorised outlets.
While the World Health Organization has said governments need to introduce more safeguards to protect people, especially youth, from nicotine pouch addiction, some agencies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration say smokers who switch completely to alternatives such as pouches, vapes and heated tobacco products may reduce their health risks.
No new approvals
In April, an investigation found that Mumbai international airport's duty-free shops run by billionaire Gautam Adani's business group breached the law by selling nicotine pouches.
Adani has denied wrongdoing, and the Bombay High Court this week rejected the company's arguments that duty-free shops are immune from domestic laws. It also told the Adani Group it was free to make representations before the government to make a case for the pouches.
However, the government believes "nicotine pouches are addictive, pose independent health risks and have not been established as effective smoking-cessation aids," according to minutes of the main federal drug panel's meeting published on September 16.
The Drugs Technical Advisory Board "recommended that no new nicotine formulation be approved henceforth in public interest," it added.

New Delhi, Sep 23: Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had flagged multiple issues, including deletion of names, in various states during the voter roll cleanup but the poll body was unanimous in its decisions related to the pan-India Special Intensive Revision of voters' list, officials said on Wednesday.
The officials made the remarks in the wake of a media report that the two Election Commissioners had objected to the Election Commission's steps 14 times in 10 months amid the SIR.
Responding to queries, the officials said the two commissioners had flagged decisions related to deletion of names in various states during the poll roll cleanup and handling of voter database.
EC sources maintained that all decisions of the Election Commission of India, including SIR, have been unanimous and with the approval of both the Election Commissioners and the Chief Election Commissioner.
Officials said the law governing the functioning of the Election Commission and a Supreme Court judgment underline that as much as possible, decisions should be taken unanimously and if need be, majority view should prevail.
The Indian Express reported that questions were raised on issues related to the SIR of electoral rolls within the three-member Election Commission (EC) itself, time and again by two of the three Election Commissioners, Sandhu and Joshi.
The national rollout of the SIR has been under the supervision of all three Commissioners. But Sandhu and Joshi have formally objected, on record, at least 14 times over the last 10 months -- four times on a single day -- to decisions taken and orders issued, they say, without their knowledge, the report in the English daily said.
Opposition parties have slammed the EC over the SIR, claiming it was meant to target electors not aligned to the BJP and its allies.

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson has confirmed that his side will face Israel in its second Nations League meeting on Sunday, despite the controversy surrounding the fixture and concerns raised by players about the war in Gaza.
Ireland won the first match 3-0 in Hungary on Sunday after goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrew from the squad the previous day. Bazunu said he could not take part in either fixture because of the deaths of innocent civilians.
The remaining players voted to go ahead with the match, and Hallgrímsson said the team remains committed to completing both games.
ALSO READ: Brazil coach Ancelotti says Vinicius deserves ‘patience’
“The FAI (Football Association of Ireland) has said we are playing both games. That was our intention when we came into the camp and it is still our intention,” Hallgrímsson told reporters in Dublin.
“Our focus is on the football. It has already been decided that we will fulfil the fixtures,” he added.
Ireland will play its designated home game against Israel at a closed-door venue in Bačka Topola, Serbia, rather than in Dublin. Before that encounter, it will take on Austria in the Irish capital on Thursday.
During the opening match in Debrecen, Ireland’s players wore black armbands to remember those who have lost their lives in the Gaza conflict. They also bowed their heads while Israel’s national anthem was played in the largely empty stadium.
The usual pre-match handshake was not held, and the teams did not exchange pennants.
Hallgrímsson said Ireland would repeat those gestures in Sunday’s game, with the players again wearing black armbands and bowing their heads during Israel’s anthem.
The fixtures have faced opposition since Ireland and Israel were placed in the same Nations League group in February. Irish sports personalities, supporters’ organisations and pro-Palestinian activists have called for the matches to be boycotted.
The Football Association of Ireland previously asked UEFA to suspend Israel, but the proposal failed to attract enough support from European football authorities. The FAI later moved Sunday’s match from Dublin to Serbia, referring to “operational challenges”.
Israel denies accusations that its military campaign in Gaza constitutes genocide. The conflict followed the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, after which Israel launched a large-scale offensive in the territory.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

A laboratory-confirmed case of mpox was identified in the northeastern Congolese city of Bunia, the director of a local hospital and two health officials said, raising concerns about a resurgence of the disease as the country battles its worst Ebola outbreak on record.
The epidemic caused by the Ebola outbreak was declared on May 15 in Ituri province, where Bunia is located, and has infected 7,890 people and killed 3,799, according to government data published on Thursday, September 24, 2026.
Mpox is a viral disease that causes fever and skin lesions and spreads through close physical contact.
Congo declared an end to mpox as a national public health emergency in April after a three-year outbreak that resulted in more than 34,000 confirmed cases nationwide. Authorities cautioned at the time that the virus had not been eradicated and could resurge.
The latest case involves a 21-year-old woman who was admitted to hospital on Thursday with lesions across her body consistent with mpox, hospital director Davin Ambitapio Musungufu said. She tested positive on Friday, he and two health officials told Reuters.
A second woman, aged 32, has been identified as a suspected mpox case and is awaiting laboratory results, Musungufu said. She and the confirmed patient have been isolated and are being cared for by a dedicated medical team.
Investigations are underway to trace contacts and identify the source of infection, Musungufu said.
Adelard Lofungola, a health official who served as deputy incident manager for Congo's mpox response, said five suspected mpox cases in Bunia were currently under investigation.
Health officials have reported an increase in mpox cases in several parts of the country over the past month, he said.
Dr. Lofungola said the Ebola outbreak's impact on Congo's health system was complicating efforts to monitor other infections.
