Infantino should have no place in future of football - Pinto
- Published
The computer hacker who released documents which led to the Premier League investigation into Manchester City says Fifa president Gianni Infantino "should have no place in the future of the game".
City have been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-year period, though they continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.
The Premier League investigation was launched following information released into the public domain by the Football Leaks website in 2018, via German publication Der Spiegel, and following a separate investigation by European football's governing body Uefa.
In a message on X, external, Rui Pinto, creator of Football Leaks, repeated allegations from 2018 that Infantino intervened to help City and Paris St-Germain avoid financial fair play sanctions from European football's governing body Uefa.
According to a report by Der Spiegel, external, the clubs overvalued sponsorship deals to help meet FFP rules and, when facing sanctions over the matter, the allegations in the documents state Infantino helped arrange more lenient punishments for them in 2014.
A PSG statement at the time said it "has always acted in full compliance with the laws and regulations enacted by sports institutions" and it "denies the allegations".
"Since the introduction of Financial Fair Play, Paris St-Germain have been one of the most audited and scrutinised clubs in history," the club added.
"Back in 2014, there was a man who was already aware of the irregularities involving Manchester City," 37-year-old Portuguese Pinto wrote on Wednesday.
"The infamous Gianni Infantino, then Uefa general secretary, abused his authority, shared confidential documents and, in short, outmanoeuvred the investigatory chamber, doing everything in his power to ensure that both Manchester City and PSG would merely receive a fine, avoiding a deeper investigation that could have led to a Champions League ban.
"All of these details were also revealed through Football Leaks.
"Given his actions as Uefa general secretary and, more recently, as Fifa president, I can only say, in my humble opinion, that Gianni Infantino has become a cancer on football and should have no place in the future of the game."
When the allegations first surfaced, Uefa stressed that it was within the remit of the general secretary to assist in such matters, adding: "This may include discussions, meetings, assistance to help find solutions, and other interactions to assist the [investigating body] in its work."
Infantino similarly pointed to how his "job entails having discussions, having conversations, exchanging documents, drafts, ideas, whatever, on many, many, many, many, topics.
"So if then this is being portrayed as something bad, I think there's not much I can do more than my job in an honest way, in a professional way and trying to defend the interests of football."
BBC Sport has contacted Fifa following Pinto's latest statement.
Infantino has come under increasing pressure following his now-shelved plans to sell stakes in the World Cup.
European football's governing body Uefa accused Infantino of "criminal mismanagement" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, while the Swiss Football Association (SFV) is the latest association to withdraw its support for the Fifa president.
"The decision follows a comprehensive reassessment of developments over the past few months," an SFV statement read.
"From the SFV's perspective, various incidents raise fundamental questions regarding leadership, governance, transparency and decision-making processes within Fifa."
Both Fifa and Uefa are based in Switzerland.
Infantino will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.

Greetings from Syria, where time seems to melt as a glassmaker braves scorching temps
Our world as journalists can move fast; every day there's breaking news from all corners of the world, and we scramble to stay on top of multiple threads of information each day.
That is why I loved watching this glassmaker just outside the historic Old City in Damascus. In 100 degree summer heat, he patiently shaped cup after glass cup in the blistering furnace in front of him, seemingly impervious to the temperature.
Time seemed to matter less than the process of melting and stretching the hot, melted glass. He made cups and oil jars and decorative lamps in a variety of jewel colors, using techniques and styles that have not changed for decades. Watching his craft reminded me to slow down and enjoy the moment, too.
Even though his shop was right on the edge of the Old City of Damascus, it was largely empty. Syria's nearly 14-year civil war has ended, but the economy is still struggling, while inflation has ratcheted up the cost of living in the last year. Even a glass can be a luxury for some.

Hyogo Prefectural Police arrested a 46-year-old doctor on Wednesday on suspicion of dismembering and abandoning his wife’s body.

Most implants like pacemakers and insulin pumps work in isolation. To help them coordinate with each other, a team of Georgia Tech researchers built a networking system that sends signals through body tissue instead of antennas and radio waves.
Radio problems
Implants that communicate today mostly rely on radio protocols like Bluetooth Low Energy or near-field communication (NFC). Both are a poor fit for in-body data transfer, says Alex Abramson, a Georgia Tech engineer and co-author of the new study.
The first problem is power. “If you want an implant to remain in an active state such that it can respond within milliseconds, it’s very difficult to do that with the Bluetooth system,” Abramson said. According to the paper, Bluetooth components, when they’re activated, can cut an implant’s battery life by up to 90 percent.
The second problem is that radio waves don’t travel well through the body. “Bluetooth and near-field communication are attenuated quite a lot in the tissue,” Abramson said. He said that implant-to-implant radio communication systems run into attenuation issues if the signal has to travel more than one centimeter through the tissue. Then there’s size. Radio needs antennas, and commercial Bluetooth components require a device at least five millimeters wide. Implants thinner than three millimeters can be injected with a syringe at an outpatient clinic; bigger ones usually need surgery.
The fix Abramson’s team came up is called SWANS (Smart Wireless Autonomous Networking System) and was inspired by the way body’s own internal communication networks. “The nervous system can take a lot of inputs from all over the body, harvest all that data, and make a specific decision. And our system mimics that,” Abramson said. SWANS relies on ionic conduction just like neurons, which communicate by shuttling sodium and potassium ions through their membranes, creating voltage differences. “But instead of using nerves, we use normal body tissue to send those signals,” Abramson said.

Sixty-three per cent of the 3,253 Water Supply Schemes (WSS) taken up under the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) in Jammu and Kashmir are non-operational despite expenditure of around Rs 7,000 crore, a House Committee of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly has found, raising serious questions over planning, execution, procurement, quality control and monitoring of the flagship rural drinking-water programme.
The findings are contained in the voluminous 1253-page report of the House Committee constituted to examine alleged irregularities in the implementation of JJM in the Union Territory. The report was laid before the Legislative Assembly on September 21 by committee chairman Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi. The committee was constituted on April 9, 2025, to examine alleged irregularities in implementation of the Mission.
“The result is that 63 per cent of 3253 WSS involving an expenditure of Rs. 7000.00 crore are non-operational,” the report states. It adds that even the 37 percent of schemes claimed by the Jal Shakti Department to be functional were “not fully operational”.
The committee said the institutional mechanism established to oversee JJM had failed to discharge its responsibilities effectively, resulting in inadequate planning, supervision and monitoring.
“The House Committee is of the considered view that there has been complete abdication of authority,” the report said, referring to the Apex Level Committee, Executive Committee and District Level Committees.
The panel attributed the failure to achieve the Mission’s objectives within the stipulated timeframe to what it described as “gross negligence” on the part of these committees and the officers who manned them.
According to the report, 37 per cent of schemes claimed by the Jal Shakti Department to be functional were also “not fully operational” in several cases.
The committee also questioned official figures relating to Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTCs), saying discrepancies emerged between departmental records and ground conditions during field inspections.
The panel said records supplied to it contained what it described as “false claims” regarding the number of FHTCs provided in habitations and the number of habitations covered.
“On spot visits, the House Committee came to know that far less than the number of FHTC indicated in the record, have actually been provided benefit of the Safe and Adequate Drinking Water of the prescribed quality,” the report said.
The committee also questioned the department’s claim that 81 per cent of rural households in J&K had tap-water connections as of March 2025, saying the figures required physical verification.
The House Committee was headed by Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi. Its 13 members were Mohammad Yousuf Tarigami, Ali Mohammad Dar, Altaf Ahmad Wani, Aijaz Ahmad Jan, Rajiv Jasrotia, Ranbir Singh Pathania, Tanvir Sadiq, Javaid Riyaz Bedar, Muzaffar Iqbal Khan, Rafiq Ahmad Naik, Arjun Singh Raju and Iftikar Ahmad.
The committee subsequently undertook field inspections to assess the implementation of JJM works. It inspected schemes in Rajouri and Poonch, among other areas, before finalising its findings.
One of the major concerns highlighted by the committee was the failure to establish the sustainability and adequacy of water sources before executing schemes.
The panel found instances where expenditure had been incurred on pumping systems, storage facilities, transmission networks and distribution infrastructure without adequately establishing the viability of the underlying water source.
In WSS Shirpora Bangil, the committee found high sulphur and iron content in the source and said this had rendered the scheme useless. It termed the expenditure “unfruitful” and directed fresh testing of the source.
“Providing of FHTC is immaterial in absence of safe and viable source,” the committee observed.
The report also cited schemes affected by land and source disputes. These included WSS Dachnipora in Pahalgam, WSS Lelhara, WSS Syed Mantaqi Khrew and WSS Greenland Wuyan. In WSS Bugam Dooniwari, the committee said Rs 10 crore had been spent without benefiting the targeted population because of a source dispute.
The committee has also scrutinised the decision to shift from GI pipes to HDPE pipes during JJM implementation.
It noted that the Jal Shakti Department, Jammu, authorised Executive Engineers in April 2023 to use HDPE pipes instead of GI pipes depending on site feasibility. However, an earlier technical committee had recommended modification of DPRs before the change.
The panel said the national-level communications cited in support of the shift did not mandate compulsory replacement of GI pipes with HDPE pipes and questioned why the decision was taken several years after the Mission’s launch.
It said the decision had significant financial and operational implications and “ought to have been taken by the Apex Level Committee”.
The report also records allegations made by retired IAS officer Ashok Parmar concerning procurement orders and changes in pipe specifications. Parmar alleged that procurement orders worth Rs 4,000 crore were placed without approval and that HDPE pipes were ordered in violation of approved DPRs. The committee recorded these as allegations and evidence presented before it, rather than independently establishing every allegation.
The committee separately examined tube-well projects and raised concerns over tendering, technical qualifications, quality assurance and functionality.
It said some tube wells had failed to meet desired standards and noted submissions that water from certain sources was unsuitable for human consumption. The committee observed that quality-assurance mechanisms appeared to have been inadequately enforced.
The panel also questioned the effectiveness of third-party monitoring agencies hired for audit and inspection of JJM works. It said field observations regarding faulty execution indicated that such agencies had failed to discharge their obligations adequately despite being paid for monitoring and audit work.
The committee has recommended constitution of a High-Level Committee to conduct a comprehensive audit of JJM and retrofitting schemes, including procurement of DI, GI and HDPE pipes and execution of civil works.
It has recommended identifying officers and engineers responsible for irregularities and initiating action against those found responsible under applicable rules.
The panel has also called for scrutiny of officers who served on the Apex Level, Executive and District Level Committees from their constitution until March 31, 2025, with their actions and omissions examined against the respective terms of reference.
A comprehensive technical, financial and administrative review of tube-well projects has also been recommended, covering functionality, water quality, payments released, pending liabilities and possible additional expenditure.
The committee said the problems identified were not confined to isolated technical failures but indicated “possible systemic deficiencies in planning, procurement, quality control, contract administration and project oversight”.
Its central finding is that the success of JJM cannot be measured merely through construction figures or tap connections recorded in official databases. The ultimate test, the committee said, is whether households are actually receiving safe and adequate drinking water.

Researchers have documented the first confirmed snakebite envenomation and subsequent human deaths in India caused by the venomous Caspian cobra (Naja oxiana), which have never previously been reported in the country, according to a case report published in Epidemiology International, a peer-reviewed journal.
The study titled ‘First Report of Deadly Bites by Caspian Cobra (Naja oxiana) From India’ by Bharti O.K., Menon J.C., Phull A., Joy S., Sharma V. and Malhotra A. details two fatalities and two survivals from bites by the species, also called the Central Asian cobra, in Himachal Pradesh’s Chamba’s Pir Panjal mountain range.
“Envenomation and subsequent deaths from the Caspian Cobra (Naja oxiana) have never previously been reported from India. While collecting data for the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) project on snakebites, we came across two deaths due to the bite of N. oxiana,” said Omesh Kumar Bharti of Himachal Pradesh’s Directorate of Health Services, who led the study.
“Deaths due to N. oxiana have never been previously reported from India. Naja oxiana is primarily found in Central Asia, with high human mortality resulting from envenoming. This species has been reported from Pakistan and Kashmir and was recorded in 2019 from Tissa block of Chamba district, Himachal Pradesh. Naja oxiana has been shown to have rapidly expanded its range from Iran towards the northeast and it has been observed to be slowly expanding its range in Chamba towards lower elevations as reported by local rescuers,” noted the study.
The first death occurred in July 2020 in Ullansa village, when a 40-year-old man was bitten twice on the leg while spraying an apple orchard. He was taken to a nearby faith healer. However, his condition continued to worsen and on the third day after the bite, he was taken to the Civil Hospital Bharmour, where he was seen by the doctor and was found to lack a detectable pulse. A second victim, a 62-year-old man from Bhanjraru village, was bitten in July 2021 while walking to work and collapsed within half an hour. He died before reaching Civil Hospital Tissa; a post-mortem attributed the death to the venom’s neurotoxic effects, the study said.
Snakebite envenoming (SBE) remains a major cause of preventable mortality in rural India. The big four species, namely the spectacled cobra (Naja naja), Russell’s viper (Daboia russelii), common krait (Bungarus caeruleus) and saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus), are responsible for the majority of snakebite envenomation and deaths in the country. The commercially available anti-snake venom (ASV) correspondingly covers these species only, it said. The study also noted that the available anti-snake venom (ASV), designed to counter the ‘big four’ species responsible for most snakebite deaths nationally, does not effectively neutralise the venom components of N. oxiana.
The researchers said that there is a need to create greater community awareness about the danger of this species of snake in affected areas and educate them about ways to reduce the risk of being bitten.

Ronaldo leaves Portugal camp after coach denies rift
- Published
Cristiano Ronaldo says he has left Portugal's international camp and will explain the reasons why "in time".
It comes after head coach Jorge Jesus earlier said there was no rift with the captain, following claims the five-times Ballon d'Or winner had refused to train.
Ronaldo has said he considered retiring from international football after the World Cup in the summer but opted to continue as he chases down 1,000 career goals.
He was included in Jesus' 25-man squad for the current international break and started the opening Nations League game against Wales.
However, the Al-Nassr forward did not feature in Portugal's 2-1 win over Norway in Olso on Sunday and did not join his team-mates in going over to the visiting fans at the final whistle.
Instead, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United player headed to the changing rooms - prompting reports he was unhappy with the manager.
Speaking to media before Portugal's Nations League match against Denmark on Thursday, Jesus said: "There was no incident whatsoever.
"Any player - and I was a player myself - when you spend 20 or 30 minutes warming up and then don't get on, no-one is happy about that."
Jesus said he had told Ronaldo before the match he would not be starting, but might be brought on later in the game.
"Afterwards, as coach, I decided not to bring him on. It's nothing to make a fuss about," he added.
Former Benfica manager Jesus also dismissed suggestions Ronaldo had refused to train on Tuesday, saying the 41-year-old instead had to do individual exercises for "mobility" and "strengthening" but would train as normal on Wednesday.
However, Ronaldo did not join his team-mates on the pitch in Denmark with Portuguese media sharing a video of him leaving Parken stadium alongside two members of the backroom staff.
And the player later took to Instagram to announce his departure.
"After the press conference of the national team and following a conversation with the president of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team training camp," he wrote.
"In time, I will tell all the Portuguese the truth about the reasons that motivated me to leave."
He added he wished his team-mates good luck in their forthcoming games.
Goncalo Ramos scored the winner against Norway and Jesus had said the AC Milan striker would again be preferred to Ronaldo against Denmark.
"If I need [Ronaldo], he'll come on. If I don't need him, he won't."
The Portuguese Football Federation later confirmed Ronaldo's departure in a statement which added: "Preparation for the two matches against Denmark and Norway continue as planned with the 24 remaining squad members.
"The entire delegation remains totally focussed on the national team's next fixtures and on achieving the established objectives."

Engineering education needs to move beyond writing code and equip students to understand how entire software systems work, according to speakers at Inc42’s inaugural ‘The CTO Summit 2026’. Speaking during the panel ‘The Great Engineering Reset: Teams, Talent & Leadership After AI’, the participants called for greater emphasis on logical thinking, philosophy, and systems design to prepare engineers for work increasingly shaped by AI. Moderated by Accel VP Anagh Prasad, the panel featured Naukri.com CTO Arvind Heda, Acko cofounder and CPTO Vishwanath Ramarao, and IDfy CEO Ashok Hariharan. The discussion examined how AI is changing engineering roles and team structures, with automation taking over more routine coding and quality assurance work. Hariharan said this shift raises a longer-term question: how will engineers develop the expertise to design and manage complex systems if they spend less time building them? Drawing on his “old-school engineering background”, he recalled how earlier generations of engineers had to grapple with problems such as memory management. Over time, tools and software layers made those underlying processes less visible to developers. “There's a lot of crap code that gets written,” he said, warning that AI-assisted development could amplify existing quality problems if engineers assume the tools can do everything for them. The concern extends beyond the code being produced today to the capabilities engineers will develop over the coming years. Hariharan joked that engineers can advance into leadership roles before fully understanding the responsibilities of a lead or manager, eventually becoming VPs. “I think we are in danger of the same kind of thing now,” he said. Hariharan said engineering teams have fewer mid-level engineers, leaving a skills gap between senior architects and junior developers. This raises a question about how junior engineers will learn to design systems. “How do you teach systems design when they don't necessarily code on a daily basis?” he asked. The growing demands of testing also surfaced in a separate discussion at the CTO Summit on how AI is changing coding and review. Cashfree Payments CTO Ramkumar Venkatesan said the company’s spending on virtual environments for testing now exceeds its spending on AI tools. For Hariharan, the shift towards AI-generated code increases the need for architects who understand deployment, security, and scaling. Automating routine implementation work does not remove the responsibility to ensure that the resulting systems are reliable and secure. “I think there’s a huge number of security flaws that are going to be exposed. I am pretty sure that’s a fear every CTO has,” he said.

On July 19, as Sahida Fakir stepped out of her Navi Mumbai home to buy dinner, she was allegedly picked up and detained by Mumbai police’s Chembur crime branch. Four days later, her husband Jumman Fakir learnt that she was forcibly pushed across the border into Bangladesh on suspicion being an illegal immigrant.
Even as Sahida remains steeped in uncertainty, away from her family in Bangladesh to this day, a writ petition filed in the Supreme Court was heard by a Bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana on September 17. The court sought a response from the Centre within four weeks.
A native of Gobindapur village, Swarupnagar block in West Bengal’s North 24 Parganas district, Sahida was not given any opportunity to established her Indian citizenship before being detained, her husband alleged.
Alt News spoke to Sahida Fakir, who narrated to us the harrowing experience of being pushed into no-man’s land at midnight and wading through a marsh to reach the Bangladesh side. According to her, she was picked up by the Mumbai police and kept in a detention centre for four days before being pushed out of India. In this duration, the police didn’t produce her before a magistrate.
“When I was pleading with Mumbai police officials to let me go, they just sneered at me and said we need to fill up the empty seats of the deportation airplane,” she alleged, asking, “How can they be so inhumane? What is my fault? Being a Muslim who speaks Bengali?”
Jumman told Alt News that he reached Chembur crime branch office on July 19 and attempted to prove his wife’s citizenship by furnishing her documents. “The police said that they would need few days to verify her documents and, if necessary, would ask for additional documents. I went to the office again on July 22 with more papers, but the next day, they informed me that she had been pushed into Bangladesh. When I asked how they could do such a thing without giving us any opportunity to prove our citizenship, I was thrown out of the office,” he claimed.
According to Jumman, after almost a week, Sahida called from Bangladesh to inform him that she had allegedly been expelled from India through either the Assam or the Northeast border, and that she was currently living with a family from Satkhira that provided her shelter. “She called me from an unknown number and was crying inconsolably. A family from Bhadiyali village in Kalaroa Upazila of Satkhira was sheltering her, and the Bangladesh police posted two armed guards for her protection outside the residence,” he said. “I get to speak to her occasionally by calling the Bangladeshi family’s number. She is a thyroid patient. Local journalists had arranged some food, clothes and medicines for her, however, that stock is fast depleting.”
The couple has lived in Mumbai for the last 20 years — Jumman works as a car cleaner while Sahida worked as a domestic help. Their elder son Sahin Fakir lives in their native village in Bengal’s North 24 parganas district while 13-year-old Samim Fakir lived with his parents in Mumbai. After Sahida’s pushback, Jumman and Samim left Mumbai and returned to Swarupnagar.

What The Documents Say
According to Sahida’s citizenship documents, including her birth certificate, her Aadhar card, voter card, PAN card, accessed by Alt News, she was born in November 1988. On October 19, 1995, the Bithari-Hakimpur Gram Panchayat, under the Swarupnagar Block, issued her birth certificate (serial number 6382).
Sahida’s father, Aminuddin Gazi, is listed in the 2002 SIR electoral roll (Part 89, Serial 514, Swarupnagar assembly); her grandfather, Badsha Gazi, is also listed in the 1952 electoral roll for Swarupnagar assembly. See below:
On January 29 this year, the Bithari-Hakimpur Gram Panchayat issued a family genealogy stating that Badsha Gazi’s son, Aminuddin Gazi, had 14 children, including Sahida. Sahida’s name also appears in land records accessed by Alt News. Although Jumman’s name appeared in the final SIR list, Sahida was placed in the “under adjudication” category. However, she had appealed against her exclusion.
Following her ‘unofficial deportation’ to Bangladesh in July, Sahida’s family was able to obtain a certificate from Swarupdaha Free Primary School on August 9, which states that she studied there from 1994 to 1998. Her transfer certificate, issued by Jamia Islamia Girls’ High Madrasa located in Swarupnagar block for Class 8 in 2008, is also available.
Sahida’s Account
Speaking to Alt News, Sahida said, “I was kept at the Chembur detention camp for four days. My phone, the money that I was carrying to buy chapatis for my family and my Aadhaar card — everything was snatched away. I begged the police, fell at their feet to let me contact my family, only then did they allow me to make a call for a few seconds. After I informed my husband, he came to the Chembur crime branch office to furnish all the documents to prove my Indian citizenship, but the police didn’t even bother to see or check them,” she alleged.
“After spending four days at the detention centre, they stacked several others and me onto a bus with dark curtains, so we couldn’t see where we were going. If anybody even tried to pull the curtains slightly, the Border Security Force men would beat and abuse them. We later realised that it was the airport. From there we were boarded onto an aircraft, and they took us somewhere on the Assam or Northeast border. I don’t know any of these places, but heard it from other people in our group,” she further alleged.
According to Sahida, she was placed in a group of around 200 people who were also pushed into Bangladesh.
“After we landed, we were taken to a detention centre. From there, we were packed into buses in batches. The bus took us to several other camps. They kept us waiting in some camps for 10 hours, and in some for about 3-4 hours before moving us out. Finally around 1 am, the BSF pushed all of us back into no man’s land,” she claimed.
“We were in a marsh with the muck reaching my neck in some places. I had to wade through the mud on no man’s land to finally reach the Bangladesh side of the border by daybreak,” she added.
The others told Sahida that they could be at the Feni border, near Chattogram of Bangladesh.
Following this, according to the petition submitted in the Supreme Court by her son, Sahin, Sahida somehow managed to reach the Petrapole-Benapole border area after a few days. There, the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) apprehended her, but due to humanitarian reasons, she was provided shelter and was finally able to contact her family on July 31, the petition said.
“A farming family from Bhadiyali village has sheltered me, and despite their financial constraints, they are doing their best to feed me. But do I deserve this hopeless situation? Why do I have to survive on other people’s grace? I have diabetes and thyroid issues. Since July 19, I haven’t had my medicine. My family’s life has been turned upside down. My husband had to flee Mumbai, leaving his meagre employment and my younger son had to leave his studies,” she lamented.
Alt News contacted an officer from Chembur crime branch, who refused to comment on the matter, stating that they are “officially required not to speak on such matters.”
We also reached out to the officer-in-charge of Kolaroa police station in Bangladesh. He refused to comment.
Legal Tangle: Contentious SOP, Loopholes in Govt Order
On August 17, Sahin moved the apex court with a petition challenging his mother’s apprehension, detention and forcible expulsion to Bangladesh, demanding that she be brought back to India. The petition argued that the Mumbai police’s actions directly contradicted the provisions of Article 21 of the Constitution.
The petition also challenged the legality of the Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) dated May 2, 2025, titled ‘Procedure for deportation of illegal Bangladeshi nationals/Rohingyas’, and the ‘Immigration and Foreigners Order, 2025’, insofar as it permits or facilitates removal of persons apprehended within India without the safeguards prescribed by law and the Constitution.
The SOP from May 2025, published by the Union ministry of home affairs (MHA), establishes guidelines for ‘deportation/removal/expulsion’ of Bangladeshi nationals and Rohingyas. According to the SOP: “All State Governments/UT Administrations shall set up a Special Task Force in each District under the police of the State/UT to detect, identify and deport/send-back illegal immigrants from Bangladesh/Myanmar settled in the State/UT concerned.”
“If the suspected Bangladesh/Myanmar national claims Indian citizenship and residence of a place in any other Indian State/UT, the concerned State Government/UT would send to the Home Secretary of the State/UT and District Collector/District Magistrate of the District from where the suspected person claims to hail, the details including name, parentage, residential address, details of near relatives etc. The State Government/ UT/Collector/District Magistrate concerned in turn will ensure that an appropriate report is sent to the deporting State Government/UT after proper verification within a period of 30 days,” the SOP reads.
It is important to note here that the SOP doesn’t mandate an FIR under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, if a suspected Bangladeshi or a Rohingya is apprehended and due investigation, enabling anybody under suspicion of being an illegal immigrant to be simply expelled from India.
A Supreme Court advocate, requesting anonymity, told Alt News that the SOP is inhumane as it empowers the State and the border guarding forces such as the BSF to push back suspected ‘Bangladeshi and Rohingya’ infiltrators into ‘no man’s land’ without any judicial process. The SOP also mandates the handover of suspects to the relevant border guarding forces of Bangladesh and Myanmar, thus enabling the Indian border guarding forces to exercise their powers arbitrarily.
As contention around this SOP rose, the Indian government initiated ‘The Immigration and Foreigners Order, 2025’ — published in the Gazette of India on September 1, 2025, effectively overriding the provisions of the earlier SOP. According to this order, if a suspected foreign national is apprehended without his/her travel document, such as a passport, then that person’s nationality has to be first ascertained by that person’s Nation. After it has been proved beyond doubt that the person is an illegal immigrant, the deportation process will take place.
As per Chapter 3, Article 12(4)(c) of the said Order, it is clearly mentioned: “In the absence of a valid passport or other travel document, the authorities referred to in sub-paragraph (3) may immediately take appropriate steps for getting the nationality verified and for issuance of travel document in favour of the illegal migrant from the Embassy or High Commission of the country concerned in India through the Ministry of External Affairs and necessary steps shall be taken by such authorities to deport the illegal migrant from the country as soon as the travel document is received.”
Based on Sahida’s account of her ‘deportation’, however, it becomes clear that provisions of the Order were not followed. Further, even though certain provisions of the previous SOP were applied, the process, or rather the lack of it, in which she was pushed into Bangladesh, contradicts the rest of it.
In a similar case reported by Scroll.in, 66-year-old Dablu Sheikh and his three sons were picked up from their home in Suti, Murshidabad, under suspicion of being Bangladeshis. They have been missing for over 40 days. Sheikh’s father, Sk Samjani, was also a voter in the Suti Assembly constituency in 1966 and 1995, the report stated, adding that the inspector-in-charge of Suti police station said the four persons were illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators, and thus had been deported to Bangladesh. The officer further said that no FIR was registered against the four men under the Foreigners Act, as they were detained following the Union government circular from May 2025, and directly sent to the Jangipur holding centre. The report suggests that they were deported to Bangladesh from the holding centre.

A court in Japan has ruled that the human voice has legal protection after a landmark case involving a well-known actor and a TikTok account that he claimed had cloned his “lustrous” baritone voice in its AI-generated videos.
Tokyo district court said on Wednesday that voices should enjoy the same protection as publicity rights, at the end of a closely watched legal action brought against TikTok by Kenjiro Tsuda – best known for voicing the character Kento Nanami in the anime Jujutsu Kaisen.
But the court dismissed Tsuda’s request that the operator of TikTok remove the videos, noting that the user had deleted them soon after the suit was filed last November. “The unauthorised use of a performer’s voice … can be considered an infringement on publicity rights,” said the presiding judge, Aya Takahashi.
The lawsuit is believed to be the first in Japan seeking to defend an individual’s vocal identity against AI-generated copies. Japan’s voice actors, many of whom achieve star status through their “appearances” in anime, are increasingly worried that AI mimicry is threatening their livelihoods and the industry as a whole.
An actor’s voice “is the result of years of rigorous training and apprenticeship”, Yuko Sasaki, executive director of the Japan Actors Union said ahead of the ruling.
Tsuda, 55, claimed that the 188 TikTok videos uploaded on an anonymous account between July 2024 and September last year had been narrated by a “deep” and “lustrous” voice that could only be his. In response, the platform argued that the videos contained a “generic male voice” and that any perceived similarities to Tsuda’s voice were highly subjective.
The verdict is the first in which a Japanese court has declared that the human voice is protected under publicity rights, a reference to the ability to control and profit from aspects of an individual’s identity, in Tsuda’s case his distinctive voice.
The protection applies “if the purpose of using the voice is exclusively to take advantage of its commercial appeal”, Takahashi said, describing a voice to be “as symbolic of one’s personality as portraits are”.
The TikTok account, whose picture resembled Tsuda’s Jujutsu Kaisen character, combined images and AI-generated speech about urban legends, the occult and conspiracy theories.
At one point, the account had more than 200,000 subscribers and, according to the legal complaint, the clips would have earned its owner between ¥500,000 (£2,395) and ¥75,000 in monthly revenue, the Kyodo news agency said.
Describing the content as “sordid”, Tsuda’s legal team claimed the account had only attracted attention because it had cloned the “attractive voice of a popular actor”.
TikTok said in a statement it would “respect the court’s judgment while considering what steps to take after scrutinising [the ruling’s] details”. It added: “We will continue to sincerely work on the balance between technology development and rights protection.”
In 2024, actors in Japan launched a campaign called “No More” to oppose the unauthorised use of their faces and voices in AI-generated content.

The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh has called for a nationwide National Register of Citizens (NRC). The Sangh, which is an ideological fountainhead of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has said that identifying citizens was necessary to address “population imbalance” and protect the country’s “unity, integrity and security”.
“When solutions (to population imbalance) are discussed, it is said there should be a National Register of Citizens (NRC),” RSS publicity in-charge Sunil Ambekar was quoted as saying while speaking at an event at the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA) on Wednesday, 30 September.
Ambedkar, as reported by Indian Express, said there was a need to identify people who had been “wrongly included” in electoral rolls and to ensure citizenship for those who had come to India from neighbouring countries under the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA).
His remarks came amid a massive political row over the functioning of the Election Commission following a report by The Indian Express, which said that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections at least 14 times over 10 months regarding decisions and procedures related to the Special Intensive Review exercise.
In support of his argument, Ambedkar said India’s partition was due to a population imbalance. He added that in our neighbouring countries that became Islamic states after 1947, many people who were left behind were from SC/ST and economically weaker sections and they continued to face persecution.
“For those who have come back, ensuring their citizenship through CAA is necessary. Identifying such people through the NRC is necessary. If people have been wrongly included in the voter list, it is necessary to identify them,” he said.
The National Register of Citizens (NRC) is a government register intended to contain the details of people recognised as Indian citizens. An NRC was prepared in 1951, following the Census of that year. The exercise was subsequently given particular importance in Assam because of concerns over migration and the Assam Accord of 1985.
The NRC has not featured in the political agenda after nationwide protests against the CAA and the proposed NRC in 2019-20. Prime Minister Narendra Modi had said in December 2019 that his government had not discussed the NRC since coming to power, while the BJP subsequently dropped the proposal from its 2024 election manifesto.
However, a debate around NRC has renewed with the ongoing Census exercise. The Census questionnaire contains several questions that were also part of the 2020 NPR (National Population Register) schedule, including nationality and details of parents, Aadhaar and voter ID. The statutory framework provides for verification of the Population Register for preparation of the National Register of Indian Citizens, including identification of cases where citizenship may be considered doubtful.
The government has not officially announced anything about a nationwide NRC. The NPR exercise, which had been scheduled alongside the 2021 Census, was postponed during the Covid-19 pandemic and was not re-notified when the Census process was revived.
Assam has a special NRC process under the Citizenship Rules. The updated Assam NRC used documents and records establishing a person's presence in Assam, or that of an ancestor, on or before 24 March 1971. These included the 1951 NRC and electoral rolls up to that date, along with specified supporting documents.
The RSS has for years maintained that a nationwide NRC should be carried out. In 2019, then RSS general secretary Suresh Bhaiyyaji Joshi had said it was the government’s responsibility to prepare an NRC to identify those who were not Indian citizens. RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat subsequently said in 2021 that the NRC was intended to determine who were genuine citizens and should not be viewed as a Hindu-Muslim issue.
AIMIM chief and Hyderabad MP Asaduddin Owaisi on Saturday alleged that the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls was a “backdoor NRC”, claiming that the exercise would eventually be used as a basis for implementing the NRC.
Many opposition leaders, including former Bengal CM Mamata Banerjee has also linekd SIR with NRC.
Owaisi said that the issue of standing “shoulder-to-shoulder” with other parties would be decided in the future, but reiterated his opposition to the SIR exercise.
“Whether we stand shoulder-to-shoulder or not is a matter for the future. However, we have been saying from the very beginning that SIR is a 'backdoor NRC'. I reiterate that the country's Home Minister has constituted a commission—headed by a retired Supreme Court judge—tasked with examining the demographic changes in areas where the final NRC was implemented; the Home Minister has stated that they will review the final NRC list,” Owaisi told ANI.
Amid speculation of talks regarding a nationwide NRC, Owaisi had earlier said that NRC would be “100 times worse.” The Hyderabad MP alleged that the exercise had already caused immense trouble, particularly to minorities, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and migrants.
“NRC is going to be 100 times worse. We’ve already seen how disastrous the NRC has been in Assam. It has caused immense trouble, especially for minorities, SC/STs and migrants,” Owaisi said in a post on X.
Owais said the NRC would force everyone to stand in line and prove their citizenship and questioned how people dependent on ration for food would be able to find documents and establish their citizenship.
“NRC will force everyone to stand in line and prove their citizenship. In a country where 80 crore people depend on ration for food, you want them to find documents and prove their citizenship? To what end?” he said.
Owaisi alleged that the government wanted people to remain at the mercy of government officials during the process.
“We are now seeing a tragedy play out with SIR, wherein ordinary people are being forced to attend hearings with documents,” he said.

It is sometimes called "momnesia," "mommy brain," "pregnancy brain" or "baby brain" — the forgetfulness, mental fogginess and cognitive changes that many women may experience during pregnancy. For instance, a woman might walk into the kitchen and forget why she did, or perhaps misplace her car keys in the bathroom.
Scientists know it is a real biological phenomenon, and now have found a possible explanation, identifying a specific brain circuit that becomes disrupted under the sustained high levels of oestrogen that accompany pregnancy.
They conducted experiments using laboratory mice designed to mimic the sustained elevated oestrogen experienced during pregnancy, finding that this led to temporary memory impairment in the animals without mood changes.
Underlying this in the mice, they found, was how the high oestrogen affected a neuronal pathway between two brain structures — the hypothalamus, which acts as a control center and integrative hub, and the hippocampus, which is central to memory formation.
High oestrogen increased the activity of hypothalamus neurons, which in turn suppressed activity in the hippocampus and impaired memory, they found.
"Momnesia" becomes most evident in late pregnancy and may continue into the postpartum period but usually dissipates after childbirth. Short-term and long-term memory can be affected, including spatial, social and verbal memory such as having difficulty remembering names or words, or struggling to recall familiar information.
"It is not serious or medically disabling, although it does affect daily functioning and confidence," said Zheng Sun, a professor of medicine at Baylor College of Medicine specialising in endocrinology and molecular biology and one of the leaders of the study published in the journal Science Bulletin.
"Typical examples include forgetting why one entered a room, misplacing an item, losing the thread of a conversation or needing reminders for appointments. It is widespread. About 80% of pregnant women notice those changes, but that figure largely reflects self-report and subjective experience rather than objective testing," Dr. Sun said.
The findings suggest that the phenomenon does not represent a general decline in cognitive ability.
"The important point is that pregnancy does not simply make someone 'less intelligent.' The effects appear to be more subtle and specific to certain cognitive tasks," said Yanlin He, director of the Brain Glycemic and Metabolism Control Laboratory at Louisiana State University's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and another of the study leaders.
Mouse experiments
The mouse experiments shed light on what is happening in the brain. Oestrogen is a hormone that governs a woman's pregnancy, menstrual cycle and puberty, spurring physical changes that help the body support the fetus, foster fetal development and prepare for childbirth. Its levels increase during pregnancy, peaking in the third trimester.
The researchers found that a protein called "oestrogen receptor alpha" transmits estrogen's signals into cells in the hypothalamus.
This region has abundant brain cells called GABAergic neurons that typically transmit calming signals to other parts of the brain. The study showed that high oestrogen levels over-activate the inhibitory signals by these neurons in the mice, and this directly affected the hippocampus.
The researchers performed memory tests including object and location recognition, finding impairment in mice given high oestrogen levels compared to those that were not.
When the researchers experimentally turned off the hypothalamus-to-hippocampus neuronal pathway, the mice no longer experienced oestrogen-induced memory problems. But experimentally activating the same pathway impaired memory in the mice, even without higher amounts of oestrogen present.
"When we genetically removed estrogen receptors from these hypothalamic neurons, estrogen-induced and pregnancy-induced memory problems in mice were also reversed. We suspect that a similar circuit may play a similar role in humans, although you cannot do this type of invasive study directly in humans," Dr. Sun said.
The researchers complemented the mouse experiments with a study assessing memory performance in 70 women, including some across different stages of pregnancy and some who were not pregnant, using tests of long-term, short-term and working memory. These tests revealed memory impairments that manifested during late pregnancy, correlating with high circulating oestrogen levels.
"Importantly, higher circulating estrogen levels were associated with poorer performance on several memory-related measures even after accounting for other potential contributing factors. This provides human evidence consistent with the mechanism we identified in mice," Dr. He said.
"However, we should emphasise that we did not directly manipulate or measure this specific neural circuit in pregnant women. Therefore, the human findings support the hypothesis but do not establish the same level of causality as the mouse experiments," Dr. He said.

Thirteen-year-old S. Ishaan completed a double crossing of the Palk Strait on Wednesday, setting a record as the youngest S14 para swimmer to achieve the feat.
The Chennai swimmer covered approximately 64km in 18 hours and 50 minutes, starting at 5 p.m. on September 29 and finishing at 11.50 a.m. on September 30. He swam from Dhanushkodi in Tamil Nadu to Talaimannar in Sri Lanka and back to Dhanushkodi.
The crossing followed a 5km sea swim in Goa and a 10km swim in Kochi. In preparation, he trained in different sea conditions, gradually progressing from swimming near the shore to sessions farther out at sea.
Ishaan has also built a competitive record in the pool. At the Junior and Sub-Junior National Para Swimming Championship in Bengaluru in June, he won gold in the sub-junior boys’ 100m backstroke, 100m butterfly and 200m individual medley events.
In 2025, he won gold in the 100m butterfly and silver in the 200m individual medley at the National Championships.
Across National and Tamil Nadu State competitions over the past two years, he has collected eight gold and two silver medals.
Ishaan was diagnosed with autism, intellectual disability and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder at two, according to his mother, Sharmila. He competes in S14, the category for swimmers with an intellectual impairment.
Sport initially became part of his routine to develop coordination and help him follow instructions. His mother noticed that he was more attentive in the water.
“He is very happy when he is swimming, as compared to when not in the pool,” Sharmila told Sportstar before the sea swimming attempt.
She introduced him to skating, running, badminton and table tennis as well, without initially aiming for medals. His swimming coaches subsequently identified his potential for competition and began preparing him for races.
Sharmila, an IT engineer, said she had left her job to support his development, adapting activities at home to his interests and working towards small achievements.
The sea crossing was also intended to give Ishaan a sense of joy after he encountered rejection and difficulties interacting with other children.
Sharmila said she wanted him to develop the skills and mental strength to manage daily life independently. Taking on new challenges through sport was part of preparing him for life beyond the pool.
“He needs a tough mindset to accept everything,” she added.

At Madison Square Garden in New York City on November 9, 2017, at the G-Shock 35th Anniversary Celebration, G-Shock creator Kikuo Ibe showed off three sapphire-crystal prototype watches: one clear, one ruby, and one sapphire blue. Because machining sapphire was so difficult at the time, each watch took over a month to produce.
These were built with, for the time, high-end Casio features such as Tough Solar power and Multiband 6 radio-controlled timekeeping—but as they didn’t meet the G-Shock shock-resistance standards, the trio was never intended for sale. They were primarily a symbol of innovation for the Japanese brand, which started in 1983 specializing in super-tough performance timepieces.
Now, nine years later, in what Casio is calling the culmination of an “eight-year project” (so presumably the ball started rolling soon after the excited reception Ibe’s crystal concepts got on stage at MSG), G-Shock is launching a three-watch collection using blue sapphire as an expression of what happens when G-Shock toughness meets Japanese engineering. The flagship model, and by far the most expensive, is the $80,000 MRG-D5000, the first-ever retail G-Shock with an outer case and bezel hewn entirely from blue sapphire crystal.
The collection is called the “Blue Rose Project” because the blue rose is viewed as a symbol of making the impossible possible since it doesn’t exist in nature. It sees the super-expensive MRG-D5000 released alongside the $9,500 MRG-B5000SA-2, and the GMW-B5000SB-1A for $850.
Only 20 of the $80,000 MRG-D5000 full-sapphire G-Shocks will be made, putting these rugged “luxury” timepieces somewhat implausibly in the same price bracket as a Patek Philippe or Porsche Macan. This is quite the flex from a company that also sells its watches for less than $90.
The 2017 concept watches required metal bracing to hold the crystal sections together, which is partly why they couldn’t pass G-Shock’s rigorous toughness tests. The new MRG-D5000, however, is a fully functional G-Shock, taking construction lessons from the MR-G engineering team who found that dividing the outer case into multiple interacting components could disperse impact more effectively than a conventional single-piece construction.
G-Shock fans will have already seen this technique employed in the titanium MRG-B5000 from 2022, but this “Multi-Guard Structure” has now been reengineered specifically for sapphire crystal, with Casio claiming the construction takes inspiration from traditional Japanese timber-frame techniques, using interlocking pieces rather than placing stress around screw holes or other details that could result in cracking.
While the MRG-D5000’s bezel and outer case are entirely machined from blue sapphire crystal ingots grown over several months, sadly—unlike the 2017 concepts—the strap isn’t matching sapphire but instead a rubber strap that repeats the brick pattern seen on the watch face in raised detail. To round off the luxe makeover, the MRG-D5000’s MR-G mark, “Shock Resist,” and other lettering on the face are in 24-carat gold.
The G-Shock development team responsible for the new collection tells WIRED the fundamental challenge was building a “near-unbreakable” watch using an inherently brittle material. Making watch cases from sapphire is not new in the high-end watch world, and many distinguished makers, including Richard Mille and Hublot, have released pieces made of the crystal.
To make the sapphire case work for a G-Shock, however, Casio had to develop a brand-new, dedicated shock-resistant structure, with the Multi-Guard construction using virtually invisible seams, alongside a completely screwless assembly method to hit the required shock performance. To do this, the outer case assembly required the development of completely new, dedicated jigs and fixtures, a process apparently so demanding that only one person at Yamagata Casio (the primary “mother factory” for Casio) can currently perform it.
All three new watches, along with the proper G-Shock resistance to knocks and drops, are water-resistant to 200 meters, solar-powered, and feature radio-controlled timekeeping, world time, stopwatch, countdown timer, five daily alarms, and a full-auto LED backlight.
If the $80K G-Shock is too steep an investment, the MRG-B5000SA-2 with two two-carat facet-cut blue sapphires and a grade-5 titanium exterior is limited to 500 pieces. The cheapest GMW-B5000SB-1A2 marries a full-metal black exterior with four round brilliant-cut blue sapphires.

Google promised Gemini 3.5 Pro in June, but it spent the summer trotting out smaller Flash models. Now, Google is ready to take on the frontier again with Gemini 4 Argon. The company claims this new AI offers industry-leading performance in coding, knowledge work, and cybersecurity, but you aren’t allowed to use it yet.
While most of us will have to wait to test Gemini 4, Google says engineers inside the company are already using the new model extensively. Argon reportedly used “fleet-wide telemetry data” to help Google save 300 TiB of memory across its data centers. Meanwhile, Argon agents have been working to migrate C/C++ codebases to Rust across Google, including thousands of lines in the core re2 and libgav1 libraries and more than 800,000 lines in the Fuchsia OS Zircon kernel.
Google has also come armed with a raft of benchmarks to back up its claims. On the software engineering DeepSWE v1.1 benchmark, Gemini 4 Argon hits 77.9 percent, which is higher than GPT-6 Astra, Fable 5.1, and Opus 5.5. Google promises similar power across a range of long-horizon tasks, pointing to Argon’s industry-leading score in the economic analysis Vals Index test.
Since this model is still in limited testing, Google has not announced API pricing yet. The company has, however, confirmed that Gemini 4 Argon will support a much higher output limit of 1 million tokens. That’s up from 64,000 tokens in previous Gemini models. Google says this allows users to complete more daunting tasks in a single step.

Gujarat trio allegedly held captive in Ethiopia released, no ransom paid: Police
Three members of Gujarat family who were taken captive in the East African nation of Ethiopia reached Mumbai on Thursday after being released
The three members of a Gujarat family who were taken captive in the East African nation of Ethiopia while on their way to the US through an illegal migration route reached Mumbai on Thursday after being released, with police saying no ransom was paid for their release.
The three, Rutvik Jansari, Mamta Chavda and Mayuri, from Mehsana and Gandhinagar, left for the US on September 20 with the help of agents. They last contacted their kin on September 22, according to the complaint lodged with the Gujarat Police.
A man identifying himself as “Khan” allegedly contacted the family and demanded ₹1 crore ransom for their release. Jansari’s grandfather, Kanubhai, said they had paid ₹60 lakh after the three were taken captive, but the abductors continued to demand ₹1 crore.
Inspector AM Ghelot of the Langhnaj police station, where the missing persons complaint was filed, told HT that the three were released after police negotiated with the people holding them captive. He said the police told the captors that the families were not in a position to pay the ransom and persuaded them to release the three.
“We explained to them that the financial condition of the families whose relatives they had held captive. We tried to reason with them on phone. Following the negotiations, they released the three and put them on a flight to India,” Ghelot told HT over the phone.
Ghelot said no ransom was paid for their release. He said the police had informed the central government and the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) about the case, but he did not have information on what role they played in securing the release of the three.
The three reached Mumbai airport on Thursday noon and are on their way home to Mehsana, Ghelot added.
The alleged abduction is the latest in a series of cases involving perilous routes for illegal immigration from Gujarat.
In October 2025, four people, including a couple from Gandhinagar, allegedly headed to Australia, claimed they were held captive in Tehran before they were released after the Indian government’s intervention and returned home.
A family from Gujarat’s Mehsana attempting to illegally enter the US from Mexico was among at least 16 people on a boat that capsized in waters off Torrey Pines State Beach in May 2025. In January 2022, a family of four from Dingucha (Gandhinagar) froze to death while trying to cross from Canada into the US. A year later, a Mehsana family drowned in the St Lawrence River during a similar attempt.
Despite deportations, illegal immigration continues. Smuggling networks charge exorbitant fees to transport migrants through complex international pathways. Alternative routes include hazardous sea passages to Europe.
In December 2023, French authorities grounded a chartered Legend Airways flight from Dubai to Nicaragua carrying 303 Indians, including 66 from Gujarat, exposing a human trafficking operation.

Christa Pike execution latest: Satanic killer survives two lethal injections and rushed to Tennessee hospital
Pike was due to be the first woman put to death in the state in more than 200 years

Tennessee has failed in its attempt to execute Christa Pike, who survived and was rushed to hospital late Wednesday, despite being administered two doses of a lethal drug.
Pike, 50, was due to be the first woman put to death in the state in 206 years, after a court overturned a late stay of execution. Experts say her survival is unprecedented.
Officials administered pentobarbital to Pike twice, but she was later heard snoring. Witnesses say the curtain to the execution chamber was drawn and reopened on two separate occasions before the procedure was halted and they were asked to leave.
The attempted execution took place at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville at about 8 p.m. local time.
Pike was being executed for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student she tortured and killed when she was 18.
The execution had already been delayed for hours after a panel of the Sixth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals issued a stay to allow further review of her legal challenges.
The U.S. Supreme Court later lifted that stay at Tennessee's request in a 6-3 decision, allowing the execution to proceed before Pike's death warrant expired at midnight.
Pike could be left with brain injury, medical expert says
Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine in Atlanta, Georgia, who has been retained by Pike’s legal team, has told the BBC the convict is unlikely to have received a sufficient quantity of pentobarbital in her blood to cause the apnoea and cardiovascular failure intended for her execution.
“It’s very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury,” Zivot said of the possible consequences of last night’s episode.
‘Nothing about today was normal’
Media witnesses have held a press conference describing what they saw after Pike was administered with the injections.
Be warned, you might find the reporter’s account below distressing to hear.
Christa Pike's failed execution is Tennessee's second botched attempt in months
The failed attempt to execute Christa Pike is the second botched lethal injection in Tennessee this year, after officials spent about an hour trying and failing to establish IV access on inmate Tony Carruthers in May.
Maria DeLiberato, an attorney for Carruthers, said at the time the medical staff repeatedly stuck his arms and feet with needles, then attempted unsuccessfully to insert a central line through his collarbone and shoulder. Carruthers groaned in pain and bled from puncture wounds, she said.
Governor Bill Lee halted the attempt after more than an hour and later granted Carruthers a one-year reprieve.
More than 40 doctors and nurses wrote to Mr Lee afterwards, calling for executions to be paused and for health workers to be removed from the process, arguing Tennessee's rules conflict with medical ethics guidelines set out by the American Medical Association, which bars doctors from participating in executions.
Nine Republican state lawmakers have joined defence attorneys in demanding a moratorium on the death penalty and an overhaul of the state's execution methods.
Since 2020, 170 people have been executed across 17 states, mostly in Florida, Texas and Oklahoma, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Six states have recorded botched lethal injections in that time.
What is pentobarbital and why did Biden ban it?
Christa Gail Pike survived on Wednesday after being given two doses of the lethal drug pentobarbital, according to her lawyers.
Pike, 50, was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and was taken by an ambulance from the prison, her attorneys said. She was being treated at a hospital, but they said they hadn't been told about her condition.
She had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. Wednesday for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said in court filings late Wednesday. The Biden administration had previously removed pentobarbital from the federal protocol for single-drug lethal injections over concerns about the potential for unnecessary pain and suffering.

Christa Pike: What is pentobarbital and why did Biden ban the lethal injection drug?
'I met Christa Pike 20 years ago. This is why she shouldn’t be executed'
I met Christa Pike 20 years ago. This is why she shouldn’t be executed
Pike's execution was an unprecedented failure, death penalty expert says
Robin M Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced is "singular and unparalleled."
Seven other people have survived medical problems due to an execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.
Pike said she never intended to kill Colleen Slemmer
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens. Pike believed Slemmer had insulted her and was trying to take her boyfriend away from her.
The murder drew intense media attention in Knoxville, Tennessee, after Slemmer's body was found with an inverted pentagram, a symbol associated with satanic groups, carved into her chest.
Pike denied carving the symbol herself. Two other residents of the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the killing both before and after it took place, and had shown them a piece of Slemmer's skull.
In a clemency petition, Pike said she had intended to beat Slemmer, not kill her, but was unable to "put the brakes on".
"I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid," she said in a statement. "It took me numerous years to even realise the gravity of what I'd done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."
Slemmer's mother said that she wanted the execution to go ahead, telling the Associated Press she had waited decades to see Pike's sentence carried out.
Tennessee governor halts all executions after failed attempt
Tennessee governor Bill Lee said in a statement that he had ordered “a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred” and the remaining scheduled execution would not take place this year.
“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” he said.
Pike's legal team say she was put through 'unnecessary agony'
While the execution was under way, Pike's legal team filed an emergency motion in the Tennessee Supreme Court to immediately stop the process, saying that after receiving the two doses she was still alive and experiencing "unnecessary agony”.
They said the prolonged nature of the attempt had caused her "superadded physical and mental suffering".
"Ms Pike has lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring."

You can get Microsoft 365 for free through an eligible Education plan, free web and mobile versions of Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and other apps, or a 30-day Microsoft 365 trial with full desktop apps and 1 TB of OneDrive storage.
Microsoft 365 (formerly Office 365) is a subscription service that gives you access to various Microsoft products. This includes productivity apps like Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and OneNote; 1 TB of OneDrive cloud storage; and tools like Teams, Forms, and Loop.
As of writing, a paid subscription starts at $1.99 a month or $19.99 a year for Microsoft 365 Basic and goes up to $19.99 a month or $199.99 a year for Microsoft 365 Premium. Whether getting a subscription is justified depends on which of the included apps and services you use and how much.
If you’re not too sure about that and don’t want to buy a subscription right away, you can get Microsoft 365 for free using the following methods. Which method to pick depends on whether you’re a student/educator and your requirements.
Get the Microsoft 365 Education Plan
Microsoft 365 Education is a special plan for students and educators that provides free access to Microsoft 365 apps and services. You need a valid school, college, or university email address to be eligible. You’d have one if you’re a student or educator at an accredited institution with a Microsoft Education license.
To check if you qualify, visit the Microsoft 365 Education portal, type your institution-issued email address, and hit Next. If you’re eligible, you’ll be prompted to log in with the same email address. Or you may receive a verification link in your inbox. Subsequently, you’ll be able to use the Microsoft 365 apps within the browser or download them to your devices, based on the plan your institute offers.
Microsoft 365 Education is currently available in three plans: A1, A3, and A5. Your institute will most likely offer an A1 plan since it’s free, though some may offer an A3. The major difference between them is that A1 is web-only, whereas A3 supports downloads, so you can use the apps even when you’re offline.
If you don’t have an institute-provided email address or it isn’t eligible for the Education plan, you can get Microsoft 365 for free using the next method.

Use Microsoft 365 for the Web or Native Mobile Apps
Unless you have advanced needs — creating and running macros (VBA) in Excel, multi-device installation rights, or fully offline mode — you don’t really need a Microsoft 365 subscription. The online version of Microsoft 365, which offers access to basic versions of its apps, along with 5GB of free cloud storage, should serve your needs just as well.
All you need for this method is a Microsoft account and a web browser. In your preferred browser, visit the Microsoft 365 online portal and sign in with your Microsoft account. Create a new Microsoft account if you don’t have one.
Next, click the app launcher icon in your dashboard and select the app you want to use. This will open the app in a new browser tab, where you can create a new document or work on an existing one in your OneDrive storage. Any changes you make to the document are automatically saved to the cloud. Keep in mind, though, that the app’s functionality halts completely when you lose the internet connection.
Just like Microsoft 365 for the web, Microsoft also offers mobile apps for many of its productivity apps. So, if you just want to work on a Word, Excel, or PowerPoint document, you can download their mobile apps on your phone or tablet and use them. Just note that these apps offer limited functionality, similar to the web version. However, unlike their web versions, mobile apps support some offline functionality, allowing you to view a cached version of the document or edit local documents, even without an active internet connection.
Get the Microsoft 365 Free Trial
Microsoft offers a 30-day free trial to Microsoft 365. This trial gives you full, unrestricted access to the service, including complete offline capabilities and the ability to download desktop apps to your PC or Mac. You also get 1 TB of OneDrive cloud storage.
A free trial is great for someone who wants full-blown access to Microsoft’s productivity suite for a brief period. It also makes sense for those who want the Microsoft 365 service without committing to an upfront payment.
To subscribe to a 30-day Microsoft 365 free trial, you need a Microsoft account and a valid payment method. Open a browser and go to the official Microsoft 365 free trial page. Click the Start Free Trial button, and log in with your Microsoft account when prompted. If you haven’t taken a free trial with this account previously, you’ll be asked to add a valid payment method. Complete the checkout process. You now have complete access to Microsoft 365.
Set a reminder to cancel the subscription before the 30 days are up. If you forget, Microsoft will convert the trial to a monthly or annual subscription and charge you for the same on your added payment method.
Identify Your Use Case to Find the Right Method
You can use any of the above methods to get Microsoft 365 for free. However, not all of them offer the same level of access. As such, it’s important to identify your use case before choosing a method.
For example, if you want a full-blown Excel experience for a few weeks, the free 30-day trial makes more sense. Meanwhile, you might want to subscribe to the Microsoft 365 Education plan if you’re a student or educator and want desktop access to productivity apps for a longer period. Or use their mobile apps on your phone or tablet if you only need to view or maintain a few Excel sheets.

'Hero' pilot stabbed by other pilot on Israel-bound plane, Israeli PM says
- Published
A pilot has been arrested after he stabbed the other pilot on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv and "apparently tried to crash the plane", Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said.
Passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control of the Flydubai aircraft, landing it safely at an airport in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia, with more than 170 people on board.
The passengers, who were almost all Israeli, arrived later on Wednesday in Tel Aviv on a repatriation flight.
The stabbed pilot, named as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, has been taken to hospital but is reported to be in a stable condition. Netanyahu praised him as a "true hero" of "extraordinary bravery".
"Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster," Netanyahu wrote on X.
"He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals."
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar was in a stable condition in hospital.
No motive for the incident has been given and the pilot was under investigation in Saudi Arabia, Netanyahu told Fox News on Wednesday night, before he was expected to be taken back to the United Arab Emirates (UAE), where the flight took off from.
Israel was "likely" to contribute to the investigation, the prime minister added.
US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has also called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack", without giving any details.
Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben-Gurion Airport in Israel.
Around two and a half hours into its journey, data from flight tracking website Flightrader24 reported a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia, dropping more than 17,000 feet (over 5,000m) in less than two minutes.
Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code reporting a hijacking.
Around 20 minutes after these codes were signalled, the plane looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.
Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.
Shortly after the incident, the Israeli and Saudi Arabian air forces dispatched fighter jets, while Netanyahu held urgent consultations.
Initial media reports suggested a fight had broken out between the aircraft's two pilots, causing the rapid descent and landing.
However, in the hours after the plane touched down in Tabuk, eyewitness accounts and a statement by Netanyahu confirmed one of the pilots had stabbed the other and, according to the Israeli prime minister, "apparently tried to crash" the aircraft.
He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member entered the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".
Two on-duty crew travelling on the flight were then able to land the plane safely, Flydubai said.
In an address on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu called the situation "a very serious security incident" and said Israeli security forces were "maintaining close contact with the relevant authorities to ensure the continued safety of the passengers".
Unlike Israel's defence minister, Netanyahu did not give a motive for the incident.
"I salute these heroes who demonstrated extraordinary resourcefulness and courage," he added. "They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster."
Flydubai said in a statement that "an altercation occurred in the flight deck" and the flight was "successfully secured by on-duty Flydubai crew travelling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk airport".
An airline spokesperson added: "Our immediate priority is to ensure the ongoing safety, health, and wellbeing of all passengers and crew members involved in this incident and support the official investigation."
The passengers who had been on board flight FZ1073 arrived in Tel Aviv at around 18:40 local time (15:40 GMT). They were greeted at the airport by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags.
A number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane," a paramedic from Israel's ambulance service told the BBC.
One passenger, Yaniv Hayun, met Netanyahu and told him how he and others on the flight had restrained the attacker.
"The pilot who was stabbed was simply very close to the door, so it was hard for us to open it," Hayun said in a video posted on social media by the prime minister's office, but before the stabbed pilot - now identified as Machchhar - collapsed, he was able to open the door.
Yaniv said he put the attacker, who was trying to disable the plane, in a chokehold before other passengers helped pin him down.
He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane and after it levelled out, another pilot took over control.
Zvika Meness, another passenger, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan News that he and other passengers tied the attacker up "with his own zip ties and with the multimedia headphones".
He said: "There are children and families here who have been through a very severe, highly traumatic event."
