The Best Kids’ Mattresses, Put Through the Toddler Test
Featured in this article
Kids, especially toddlers, aren’t mattress reviewers. They don’t wake up and tell you the pressure relief is lacking or that they appreciated the vegan foam and airy woven top. Instead, as a parent, it’s your job to become the observer, paying attention to the little things, like how easily they can climb into bed, whether they stay asleep, if they seem comfortable while moving around, plus how well the mattress can handle inevitable spills, jumping, and tumbling.
For the last few months, my toddler daughter tested each mattress in this guide in her bedroom on a Simply Sori Montessori twin bed frame. I narrowed down the mattresses tested by looking for beds specifically designed for children and prioritizing a mix of constructions, price points, and features. I paid close attention to everything from how well she slept, how easily she could climb onto the mattress, the edge support for myself during bedtime stories, and how cool each cover felt on a warm summer day. Some mattresses stood out for specific features, while others offered impressive value or the ability to grow with your child. Regardless of the specific accolade, every pick here earned its spot through toddler testing.

Also Tested
Nolah Nurture Kids Mattress for $919 (Twin): My biggest complaint with the Nolah Nurture Kids Mattress is, unfortunately, the reason I had to stop testing it. It was just short enough that it didn’t fit in my daughter’s twin bed frame, leaving a solid 8-inch gap between the bottom edge of the mattress and the foot of the bed frame. Every other twin mattress I tested fit the frame without any issues, making the Nolah the odd one out. It’s a bummer, because the mattress otherwise had a lot going for it. It’s got the flippability of many mattresses we tested, and its hybrid design was very comfy, with great edge support. If it’d fit the bed frame properly, I think it would’ve been a contender.
FAQs
What’s the Difference Between a Kids’ Mattress and a Regular Adult Mattress?
Many kids’ mattresses have firmer sleep surfaces for younger children and specific features like flippable designs, waterproof and stain-resistant covers, or reinforced edges that stand up to roughhousing. Kids’ mattresses also typically have a lower profile, which makes it easier and safer for kids to get in and out of bed.
They’re also available in smaller sizes, most commonly twin and full, which are typical for kids’ bedrooms and smaller bed frames. A full-size mattress can make sense for a child who needs more room but still benefits from the features mentioned above. Once your child reaches their teen years or no longer needs these features, an adult mattress may make more sense.
Why Are Many Kids’ Mattresses Flippable?
Many kids’ mattresses are designed to grow with your child. They typically have a firmer side for younger children as they transition from a crib mattress and a softer side for older kids. Being able to adjust firmness by flipping the mattress can save you from replacing it after a few years when your kid’s wants change.
What Do Mattress Certifications Mean?
You’ll probably come across several mattress certifications while shopping. Here’s what the most common ones mean:
- CertiPur-US applies to polyurethane foam and verifies that the foam has been independently tested for emissions, durability, and certain chemicals, including formaldehyde and specific flame retardants.
- GreenGuard Gold certifies that a mattress has been tested for low chemical emissions, known as volatile organic compounds (VOCs), which can cause irritation in the nose, eyes, throat, as well as other ailments.
- Global Organic Latex Standard (GOLS) verifies that latex is responsibly sourced and processed according to environmental and production standards.
- Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS) certifies organic textile materials like cotton and wool. It ensures the materials meet strict environmental and manufacturing standards, with no VOC emissions or off-gassing.
We have more info about mattress shopping terms.
Should I Buy a Foam or Hybrid Mattress for My Child?
Foam mattresses are usually lighter and easier to move, which helps when you’re changing sheets or rotating the mattress. Hybrid mattresses combine foam with coils, which can boost pressure relief, edge support, and airflow to help prevent overheating. Neither is inherently better; it comes down to your little one’s needs and what feels most comfortable.
How Long Does a Kids’ Mattress Last?
A quality kids’ mattress should last anywhere from 7 to 10 years, depending on how heavily it’s used. Replace a mattress if you notice sagging, permanent body impressions, or tears. Also, if your child has outgrown the mattress’s size, it’s probably time for a new one.
What Should You Look for in a Mattress?
- Materials: Kids’ mattresses use many of the same materials as adult mattresses. You’ll commonly see memory foam for cushioning, higher-density foam for support, latex for a responsive, bouncy feel, and steel coils for extra support, airflow, and edge support. You’ll also see materials like Tencel, which is a plant-based fiber often used in mattress covers because it’s soft and breathable. Cotton and wool are often found in natural or organic mattresses. When researching mattresses, you might also see materials described with the brand’s proprietary names, whether it's gel-infused memory foam or a stain-resistant treatment. When shopping for and comparing mattresses, look past the marketing name to see what the material actually is and what purpose it serves.
- Firmness: There’s not much strong research or official medical guidance on mattress firmness for children. However, the American Academy of Pediatrics does specify that infants should sleep on a firm, flat mattress to reduce the risk of sudden unexpected infant death (SUID). When it comes time to transition out of the crib and into a “big kid bed,” it stands to reason that a firmer mattress will be more comfortable and familiar to a young child. Mattress firmness for kids of any age is ultimately a matter of preference, not a medical mandate, but we recommend consulting your child's pediatrician for additional advice.
- Pressure Relief: A mattress that properly supports a child's weight can help with body development and spinal alignment as they grow. It can also help prevent restless nights and lead to better sleep.
- Edge Support: This refers to how reinforced a mattress's perimeter is. As a parent who loves reading with my daughter, the last thing I want is for the mattress edge to sink in as I sit next to her. It also helps protect a child from falling out of the bed.
- Shipping, Trial, Warranty: Most online mattresses ship compressed in a box and are delivered directly to your door, and some brands offer in-home delivery and setup. A sleep trial gives you a window to test the mattress at home and return it if it isn’t a good fit. Be sure to pay attention to the fine print, though; some brands charge return or processing fees. The warranty covers manufacturing defects for a set period but typically not normal wear and tear, spills, or damage.
- What Else to Consider: Be sure the mattress fits your child’s bed frame. Also consider the height, especially if the mattress will be used on bunk beds and trundles. If you’re hoping to keep a mattress for several years, a flippable model can offer more flexibility. Also consider the practical stuff: stain-resistant and water-repellent covers can come in handy for inevitable spills or accidents.
Should I Buy a Mattress in a Store or Online?
All of the mattresses I tested for this guide were purchased online, and most were shipped vacuum-sealed in a box. Many come with sleep trials so you can test them at home and return them if they don’t work for you.
Buying online often makes it easier to compare prices, materials, and certifications without driving from store to store. That said, shopping in person lets you get a sense of a mattress’s firmness before committing.
How I Tested
My almost 2-year-old daughter tested each mattress in her own bedroom over several months, sleeping on them in the same Simply Sori Montessori twin bed frame. Because toddlers don’t provide detailed feedback on things like lumbar support and motion transfer, I took a more observational approach by paying attention to how well she seemed to sleep and how easily she could climb into bed.
I also tested each mattress from a parent’s perspective by sitting on the edges, climbing into the beds for nighttime cuddles, and monitoring things like how easy it was to set up, whether my daughter seemed hot while sleeping/after waking up, how supportive it felt, and how the mattress held up to normal toddler behavior. I also considered each mattress’s construction, materials, and price.
I narrowed down the mattresses by focusing on models designed and marketed for children rather than smaller versions of adult mattresses. I wanted to test a range of price points and constructions, as well as explore features relevant for kids, like flippable designs, stain resistance, and lower heights.

The winter season in Delhi usually results in poor air quality, outbreaks of seasonal influenza, a heavy burden on hospitals and increasing medical expenses. Hidden within the yearly air quality reports is a health problem that is preventable, and yet costs the city’s citizens lakhs. Among the elderly, especially those who have diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart disease or a suppressed immune system, a viral infection can develop into bacterial pneumonia and require hospitalization. Industry estimates suggest that the average cost of a hospital stay is about ₹50,000, while intensive care can amount to ₹1 lakh. A single such incident can erase months’ worth of income and cause households relying on pensions and daily wages to slip down the income scale.
The battle against pneumonia
India has achieved real advances in the fight against pneumonia, mainly as a result of introducing the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) as part of the Universal Immunisation Programme in 2017 and through Mission Indradhanush. Free three-dose vaccinations are provided to infants, and by 2023, vaccination rates among infants in India had reached 83%, according to the WHO/UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage (WUENIC).
The grandparents of these infants, however, are almost completely unprotected: National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) 80th Round Data on Health reveals that vaccination coverage among people aged 60 and over is only 0.40 per cent. While one generation is covered by the national programme, the other is left to avail of vaccines from a private market they may struggle to afford.
This gap is most significant in Delhi, since in the winter, the conditions can turn common respiratory infections into serious health issues.
Toxic winters
In December 2025, the city experienced its most toxic month in six years, with an average Air Quality Index of 351. Colder months naturally place a greater strain on the respiratory system. Winter air, which tends to remain stagnant, traps particulate matter near the ground: prolonged exposure compromises the lungs’ defensive abilities.
Government records show that there were more than 2,00,000 cases of acute respiratory illness and 30,000 hospital admissions in just six Delhi government hospitals between 2022 and 2024. When the pollution lasted throughout December 2025, doctors reportedly noted a 20% to 30% increase in the number of patients with respiratory problems, including some who had never before had such a condition.
These figures do not reflect the full extent of the problem, as they exclude people treated in private clinics, those who take medication on their own, infections that have never been confirmed by a laboratory test, and cases recorded as pneumonia rather than influenza.
Vaccine present, policy absent
What makes the number of hospitalisations and their resultant expenditure tragic, is that a a significant portion of this could perhaps be avoided with a vaccine that is already available. The 2026 Indian consensus guidelines concerning immunisation in adults recommend pneumococcal vaccination based on age and level of risk. It recommends the PCV20 vaccine for all adults between the ages of 18-49 years with chronic medical conditions or those considered at risk based on their health and lifestyle, or a single dose of the vaccine for all adults aged 50 and above. The guidelines also include adults who have immunosuppression and chronic diseases. For residents of Delhi, in winter when pollution makes the air toxic, this could mean the difference between a minor ailment an episode of hospitalisation.
India has no National Adult Immunisation Policy, and as a result, vaccination rates rely on individual awareness, access to a doctor, and the ability to pay out of pocket, a situation that systematically excludes older people in lower-income families. While this a critical problem ahead of winter in Delhi, it is not merely a Delhi problem: in 2022, India was estimated to whom were 149 million people aged 60 and over, a large number of whom are still economically active and support households.The Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (2017-18) showed that of Indians aged 45 and over, only around 0.6% had received a pneumococcal vaccine, a figure that has not changed much since then.
The burden in lives
The figure for deaths due to pneumonia recorded by India’s Medical Certification of Cause of Death in 2024 was 35,987, making it the leading cause of respiratory deaths, although it remains relatively out of the spotlight compared to other causes. Even this figure is an under estimate since the system covers only about one fifth to one quarter of all registered deaths nationally, and older people who die at home rather than in a hospital where certification takes place almost never get included at all.
Data on a year-by-year basis from Delhi shows that this is not an isolated occurrence but a consistent pattern, affecting precisely the group for whom a vaccine is already available but for whom no public system provides it.
Pollution raises the stakes
It is impossible for Delhi to solve its problem of air pollution by vaccination, and there is no suggestion here that it should. Reducing emissions at the source must continue to be the main course of action. However, the two measures operate at different stages of the same risk pathway. In the winter of 2025, the AQI reached 450 at a number of monitoring stations and people suffering from respiratory and cardiac conditions were told to remain indoors, a recommendation that is not a policy. When pollution increases baseline vulnerability, the removal of an additional infectious trigger becomes all the more important.
Before winter sets in this year, there is a concrete option available. Delhi could provide free pneumococcal vaccination to adults aged 60 and over who have recorded comorbidities via its present dispensary and mohalla clinic network and then assess both the uptake and the hospitalisation outcomes. The cost of each dose, at a few thousand rupees, is significantly lower compared to ₹65,000 for a hospitalisation episode.
Delhi already vaccinates the grandchildren; the medical case for vaccinating the grandparents is no different, it is merely administratively missing.
(Sayesha Gupta is a research student at the economics department, Jesus and Mary College, University of Delhi, sayeshagupta08@gmail.com; Megha Jacob is assistant professor of the department, mjacob@jmc.du.ac.in; and Karan Babbar is an assistant professor of economics at XLRI Jamshedpur, phd17karanb@iima.ac.in)

WASHINGTON — About half of rural voters identify with Make America Healthy Again, a sprawling political movement championed by the Trump administration, but most said President Donald Trump’s health care policies have not benefited their communities, according to a new poll from The Associated Press in partnership with KFF.
About 8 in 10 rural voters — an important voting bloc for Trump and fellow Republicans — said the Trump administration’s policies have had a negative effect or no impact on the health of people where they live. Most MAHA supporters, 68%, also feel this way, according to the national survey of more than 2,000 rural registered voters.
The findings signal an apparent disconnect between the Trump administration’s MAHA-branded policy priorities and rural America’s perception of their reach and effectiveness.
Iowa pastor Mike Jager, 58, is a registered Republican and considers himself part of the MAHA movement. The Trump administration’s health policies have had “minimal” impact on the health of his community, Jager said, but he added that Trump’s health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., is moving the needle “in the right direction.”
“It’s a beginning,” Jager said. “It’s a big ship to try and turn around and course-correct.”
Kennedy has used the MAHA label to support various agendas, including abandoning long-standing vaccine guidance, researching ultraprocessed foods and investing in regenerative agriculture.
Jager lives in Sumner, Iowa, “less than a quarter mile from where the corn ends and the city begins.” He’s seen family members and neighbors develop diseases that he believes resulted in part from exposure to agricultural chemicals and consumption of unhealthy, processed foods.
In the June Republican primary for governor, Jager voted for Zach Lahn, a businessman and farmer who ran on a MAHA platform and beat out Trump-backed U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra. He plans to vote for him again in November.
Many rural voters are prioritizing health issues
About two-thirds of rural voters who support MAHA said it’s “extremely” or “very” important to them to vote for a candidate who does, too, while only 4 in 10 rural voters overall said the same.
Trump sought to seize on MAHA support during his campaign for another term two years ago. Now, amid tight midterm races, Kennedy has campaigned to galvanize the movement’s support. In May, he attended a MAHA bill signing with Iowa Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds, and in August, he went fishing with Lahn, posting about it on social media.
Yet the survey indicates voters are noticing “this weird split in the Trump administration” between what Kennedy messages and what Trump says and does, said David Peterson, a political science professor at Iowa State University.
In Iowa, concerns about what’s causing rising cancer rates are “a big deal,” he said. For many people who identify with MAHA, being healthy includes taking on corporate agriculture and pharmaceutical companies that they think cause cancer, he added.
In the poll, views on health care access and costs largely diverged along party lines. Most Democratic and independent voters said the Trump administration’s health care policies have had a negative impact on their health care costs and the health and well-being of people in their communities. Republicans were likelier to say there hasn’t been an impact.
Talking on the phone from her 200-acre farm in Carroll County, Iowa, 71-year-old Donna Klocke said that her husband had died from cancer and that she has neighbors who also have cancer.
“It’s just very prevalent,” Klocke said. “We’re in a farming community. We use chemicals and pesticides and all kinds of things that aren’t necessarily good for us.”
Klocke, a Democrat, said the MAHA movement is a good idea because she cares about being healthy, but she does not consider herself part of it and will not be voting for a candidate who represents the movement.
Kennedy, who was an anti-vaccine activist before entering politics and has sent mixed messages to Americans about getting the measles vaccine, scares her.
“Measles are coming back and polio,” Klocke said. “It’s the measles that really gets me. It’s like, do you not understand how dangerous it is?”
Survey reflects angst over health care
Nearly half of rural voters said their communities don’t have enough doctors or other health care providers, and even more said there aren’t enough mental health workers specifically. The share of rural voters who said their community does not have enough hospitals increased to 35% from 21% in a similar question asked in a KFF-Washington Post survey in 2017.
And as with the general population, health care, gas and grocery costs are top pain points. At least 6 in 10 rural voters said they were worried about health care costs.
The level of worry varied based on coverage, with rural voters enrolled in employer plans or Medicare less likely to be worried. The survey found that 80% of working-age rural voters on Medicaid were very or somewhat worried about health care costs. Last year, Republicans passed a tax and spending bill that cut over $900 billion in projected Medicaid spending over a decade and mandated new eligibility requirements.
In the tiny community of Lipan, Texas, west of Dallas, Kim Solis and her husband have a handyman-and-home-remodel business and get their insurance on the marketplace. Since Trump returned to office, their premium payment jumped from zero to $166 a month. Their copays went up, and their deductibles each increased by $2,000.
Solis, 62, said she worries what will happen if they get a big medical bill.
“Certainly, we’d be in a world of hurt trying to take money out of savings or getting it out of our 401(k) just to be able to do something about it,” she said.
Most MAHA voters are also MAGA — but not all
Like the general population, rural voters said they trust their own doctors and health care providers for health information over government agencies or officials, according to the poll.
Trust in Kennedy and Trump fell largely along partisan lines. About 10% of rural Democratic voters reported having a “great deal” or “fair amount” of trust in Kennedy, compared with 74% of rural Republican voters. About 5% of rural Democrats and 69% of rural Republicans said they trust Trump a “great deal” or “fair amount” for reliable health information.
While Make America Great Again and MAHA identities are “linked in a lot of ways,” the rising costs of health care and groceries pose a challenge for those committed to the MAHA principles that Kennedy promotes, said Peterson, the Iowa State professor.
Buying healthy food “becomes, ‘I can’t afford to do that because of Trump’s policies,’” he said.
In Stamping Ground, Kentucky, Alma Johnson, 65, works night security at a horse farm.
Johnson voted for Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024 and said she “pretty much” likes how Trump is running the country. But she said she is not a MAGA devotee, preferring to “think for myself.”
MAHA, however, is an easy sell for Johnson because, she said, she doesn’t think people should be able to buy junk food in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP.
Still, she said she hasn’t seen much impact from the Trump administration’s health care policies, including the new food pyramid.
“It takes a long time to change people, their habits, their thoughts or the things they do,” Johnson said.
The poll of 2,241 U.S. adults registered to vote in rural areas of the country was conducted Aug. 12-24, 2026, using a sample drawn from the probability-based SSRS Opinion Panel. The margin of sampling error for the full sample is plus or minus 3 percentage points. In collaboration with AP, KFF researchers worked to design the survey sample and questionnaire, analyze and report findings.
This report is a collaboration between The Associated Press and KFF Health News. KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling and journalism.

Quick Answer
Snapchat’s distinct navigation uses custom icons across its main features: the bottom bar accesses Snap Map, Chat, Explore, Stories, and Spotlight. In chats, color-coded arrows and squares signal message types (pink for audio-less snaps, purple for video/audio snaps, and blue for text chats), while outlined versions show opened status or screenshots.
Snapchat successfully positioned itself as “the social media platform for Gen Z”. With its ephemeral nature and best retention features such as Snapstreaks, Snapchat is one of the most popular social media platforms currently.
However, I took my time to understand the platform better and finally became a user. But still, I am far from being a snapper, a word I use for those who are obsessed with Snapstreaks, including my close friends.
Despite being a user for months, I still find the Snapchat interface harder to navigate. Part of the reason is that it is completely detached from the common interfaces used in other social media platforms.
Moreover, Snapchat uses its own terms, such as Planets, Best Friends, and Chats, which can confuse new users. So, as part of our icon explanation series, in this guide you will learn everything about icons and their meanings on Snapchat. For quick reference, here is the Snapchat legend, followed by various icons on each screen and what they mean.
Table of Contents
Snapchat Icons Legend
Snapchat Icons and Symbols and Their Meanings
Snapchat Bottom Navigation Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Open Snapchat > View the bottom navigation bar
Snapchat is still one of the apps that uses a bottom navigation bar, which lets you switch between different Snapchat core features such as Snap Map, Chat, Stories, Discovery, and Spotlight
- Snap Map: Snap Map is an interactive feature that lets you see your friends’ current locations and also locations with the most Snap activity
- Chat: The chat icon lets you switch to the Chats tab
- Explore: Using this icon, you can browse various Snapchat lenses and filter options
- Stories: Takes you to the Snapchat stories tab
- Spotlight: Spotlight is another name for the short video feed in the Snapchat app, just like Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts
Snapchat Chat Screen Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon
Now, moving on to the chat feed, which many of us also spend more time on, you will find various icons and symbols. This screen can be confusing for the user with various symbols. Here is what each symbol means.
- Add Friends: This is the same add button that you see on other screens, where it lets you discover or add new friends
- More Options: This option opens additional chat screen options, including the ability to create new chats, create new groups, manage them, manage friendships, and also customize friend emojis and more.
- Viewed Snap Without Audio: This means you have viewed your snap without audio
- Snap Reply: If you see a reply, it means you can reply to a friend with a snap again
- Unopened Snap With Audio: If you see this icon, it means it is an unopened snap with audio
- Chat: The chat icon lets you start a new conversation with your friend.
- New Chat: The new chat icon lets you create a new chat with any of your friends
Snapchat Chat Status Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon
Snapchat also uses various colored arrows and squares to represent the type of snaps. If you see a pink arrow icon, it means you sent a snap without audio. If you see a purple arrow, it means you sent a video snap; in other words, you sent a snap with audio or video.
If you see blue, it means the chat was sent; in other words, you sent a chat message. If you see gray, it means your chat is waiting for the person to accept you.
If the arrow turns into an outline pink arrow, it means the recipient has opened your Snapchat without audio. If you see purple, it means the recipient opened your Snapchat with audio or video, and it’s the same for the blue outline arrow.
If you see a square-shaped icon in pink, it means you received a new snap without audio. If you see a purple square box, it means you received a new snap with audio or video.
If you see a blue square-shaped icon, it means you received a chat message. If you see the outline messages, it means you have viewed all the chats and messages.
If you see a double-arrow outline pink arrow, it means someone took a screenshot of the snap without audio, and it is the same for the other arrow types, including video and chat.
If you see a reload symbol, it means someone replayed your snap without audio. If you see a purple arrow, it means someone replayed your snap with audio or video.
Snapchat Chat Call Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon > Open a conversation
Chat screens can be confusing initially with the various arrow and square icons, but it consists of a similar interface to other chat applications, such as the ability to voice call and video call, and also an input bar with various options to send a message
- Camera: It opens the camera to send a snap as a reply
- Voice Call: Snapchat also supports voice calls. Tapping on this icon, you can make a voice call to your friend.
- Video Call: Along with the voice call, Snap also supports video calls. You can tap on the video icon to start a video call with your friend.
Snapchat Chat Toolbar Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon > Open a conversation
Snapchat uses different icons to represent various inputs for the message toolbar. Here is what each of the icons means.
- Camera: It opens your camera to send a snap quickly
- Voice Note: You can also quickly record a voice note and send it as a message
- Stickers: This is a sticker icon that lets you add stickers, Bitmoji, and other reaction options
- Notifications Off: If you see a bell icon with a cross, that means you have turned off notifications for the chat
- Photos: Lets you send your memories or camera roll photos to your friend
- Games: This icon opens the games you can play in the chat
Snapchat Chat Message Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon > Open a conversation
More icons from the chat interface, and here is what each of them means
- Reply: You can reply to your conversation in a thread to a message in your friends’ chat
- Stickers: Lets you access stickers, Bitmoji, and other emoji reactions
Snapchat Friendship Profile Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon > Open a conversation > Tap on your friend’s profile
Snapchat friends’ profiles can also be confusing for new users. It also consists of various icons similar to your profile page. Here is what each of them means.
- More Options: It opens more options for the friend you are viewing, including the ability to manage pin chat, manage location history, and much more
- Share Profile: You can share your friend’s Snapchat profile with others
- Send Snap: You can also send a snap to your friend from a Snapchat profile
- Chat: You can also initiate a conversation directly from your friend’s network profile
- Voice Call: You can also have a voice call with your friend by tapping on this icon
- Video Call: You can have a video call with your friend by tapping on this icon
- Activity Indicator: The green dot represents the activity indicator. If you see a green dot, it means your friend was recently active. However, unlike WhatsApp or other platforms, it does not mean that your friend is currently active
Snapchat Snap Map Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Snap Map icon
Snap Map shows your friends list and snap activity visually. It also includes various icons that can confuse beginners, especially when it shows Ghost Mode and other map settings.
- Ghost Mode: If you see this icon, it means your location is hidden from friends on Snap Map. You can tap on the icon to allow or disallow your location.
- Map Settings: It lets you manage your location and see your location. It also controls whether Snapchat can access your location.
- Satellite View: Snapchat supports both heat map and satellite view. You can switch to satellite mode using this icon.
- Explore Layer: The Explore option lets you see Public Snap and Activity Hotspots
- Battery Status: The battery icon shows a friend’s phone battery status. Remember that they should enable this option from their settings.
- Compass: It is a digital compass that lets you check the direction and reorient the map
- Friend Finder: It lets you search for and find friends who are visible on a Snap Map.
Snapchat Camera Screen Icons
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Camera icon
The Snapchat camera is the default screen that opens every time you launch Snapchat. It consists of various icons and symbols meant for different purposes. While we haven’t highlighted the multi-state capture button, which is the primary shutter button, you can use it to capture snaps. Remember that long-pressing will record a video.
- Search: This is a global search option that lets you search for your friends or groups. Recent search results also appear here.
- Notifications: View all your Snap notifications here
- Add Friends: You can find and add new Snap friends here. Tapping on this icon brings up your friends discovery page.
- AI Snaps: You can create AI snaps from here. Snap offers various lenses created using AI, which require a Snapchat+ subscription.
- Camera Zoom: While taking a snap, you can use this toggle to zoom in or zoom out the camera
Snapchat Camera Screen Icons
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Camera icon
Snapchat camera screen consists of various icons, so it’s hard to explain. In this part, let’s explore all the camera tools, which include the ability to switch cameras, control the flash, add music, HD mode, and much more.
- Profile: This is a global profile icon. Tapping on this takes you to your profile page.
- Notifications: Again, the same global notification icon that lets you see all your Snap notifications in one place
- Memories: Open your saved snaps and memories using this icon
- Switch Camera: While taking a snap, you can switch to rear or front camera options
- Flash: Lets you turn on or off the flash depending on your need
- Sounds: Let’s show you access various music options or sounds to add to your Snap
- HD Mode: Using HD mode captures snaps using a higher-quality camera mode
Snapchat Lens Category Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Camera icon > Open Lenses
If you want to quickly send a snap to your friend inside the chat, it also offers various options along with the camera interface. On the bottom navigation, you can find all the personalized options such as your favorite reactions and much more.
- Recents: This icon lets you view the lenses you recently used
- Favorites: View your favorite lenses that you previously saved as favorites
- For You: Snapchat uses your data to browse lens recommendations for you. You can access them by tapping on this icon.
- Reactions: Lets you browse Lenses specifically made for reactions
- Aesthetic: You can access aesthetic-style Snapchat lenses by tapping on this icon
Snapchat Profile Screen Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Profile icon
Snapchat profile screen is one of the most confusing screens, with various icons. Here’s what each one means.
- Back: You can use the same global button to take the user to the previous screen or to the home screen
- Share Profile: Using this share icon, you can share your Snapchat profile or the Snapcode with others
- Bitmoji Outfit: It opens a Bitmoji outfit screen where you can customize your current outfit
- Settings: It opens Snapchat global settings
- Birthday: If you see a balloon icon next to the date on your profile or in your friend’s profile, it represents their birthday date
- Snapchat+: If you want to upgrade to Snapchat+, you can tap on this. Snapchat+ is a Snapchat subscription that brings additional features. You can see the full differences here.
- Snapscore: You can view your current Snapscore from here
- Zodiac Sign: You can open your Snapchat astrological profile by tapping on this zodiac sign
Snapchat Friends and Stories Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Profile icon > Scroll down
Scrolling down to the bottom of the profile page also shows more options with different icons. Here is what each of them means.
- Back: The same global back button takes you back to your home screen or the previous screen
- Settings: Takes you to the global settings screen.
- Add Friends: You can add friends from here. Tapping on this icon takes you to the friends discovery page.
- My Friends: Here you can view all your Snapchat friends and also manage them from here.
- New Story: You can add a new story on Snapchat by tapping on this icon.
- More Options: Lets you view additional Snap story options.
Snapchat Add Friends Screen Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Add Friends icon
Snapchat friends discovery screen is one of the minimal screens found on Snapchat, with a less confusing approach. It follows a similar approach to other user discovery screens but uses slightly different terms. Here is what each of them means.
- Back: This is a global back button that takes you to the previous screen
- Scan Snapcode: With the Snapcode, you can scan a Snapcode saved in your photos and add them as friends. You can simply tap on the scan code icon in Discovery, and a photo library opens. You can select the photo with the Snapcode.
- Add Friend: To add a friend, you can simply click on the Add button
- Dismiss Suggestion: If you don’t like any suggestions or want to hide them, you can tap on the X icon

Link between technology and young people’s mental health ‘more complex’ than portrayed, study finds
A new report by the National Mental Health Commission has found the link between digital technology and the mental health of young Australians is “more complex than often portrayed”.
The study focused on Australians aged 5 to 25 found mental health symptoms may be prompting people to use social media in harmful ways, rather than technology causing mental health symptoms.
It calls for a greater focus on creating safe digital environments for children, rather than simply limiting screen time.
The commission’s chief executive, David McGrath, said policy needs to be “guided by evidence and not assumptions”:
This landmark Australian study helps move the conversation beyond screen time and towards understanding the real experiences children and young people are having online. The evidence shows those experiences are complex, it is important that policy responses reflect that complexity.
The report shows digital technology is neither simply good nor bad. What matters is how children and young people are using it, what they’re experiencing online, and whether digital environments are designed with their wellbeing in mind.
Shoebridge says people are sick of ‘messaging without substance’
David Shoebridge, the new Greens leader, says Australians are “sick of the messaging without substance”.
Shoebridge spoke to RN Breakfast this morning, saying the Greens are in a “terrific position” with robust support while the other major parties have seen their support “getting decimated and ripped apart”. He said the Greens would continue to work to “not just deliver some message and some pathetic, half-baked pretend reform”.
He told RN:
People are sick of the messaging without substance. What they’re asking for is they’re asking for a political party that’s going to go and fight for them and take on the 1% and take on the corporations. They want to see us fighting for that.
Shoebridge added the rise of One Nation was a challenge to politics across the board, saying he wants the Greens to grow the party and bring members in amid a shift in the political landscape.
We have an incredibly united membership base. We have an incredibly united party across the country. And I expect that to be how we operate as a party room, how we operate as a leadership team and how we operate as a growing movement.
Debit and credit card surcharges will be eliminated from today as part of Reserve Bank reforms that will do away with extra checkout fees on Visa, Mastercard, and Eftpos payments.
The RBA made the changes after reviewing Australia’s card payments system, which the bank’s governor, Michele Bullock, said was no longer fit for purpose.
Businesses have already made swift rule changes as they decide how to handle fees they are no longer permitted to pass on to customers.
The ATO has joined them, saying that as a government agency, it had decided it would not be appropriate for the “cost of credit card merchant fees to be transferred to the community”.
Guardian Australia has asked the ATO what it means by saying the fees would be transferred to the community.
While most Australians do not pay tax with a credit card, the ATO says it understands the changes may require some adjustments from the small group of individuals and businesses who do make their payments this way.
Taxpayers with a direct debit arrangement linked to a credit card must update their payment method before their next instalment due after 30 November to ensure compliance with their payment plan, the ATO says.
The agency said:
The ATO is committed to helping taxpayers transition to alternative payment methods and will continue to support those experiencing financial hardship or other circumstances that make it difficult to meet their obligations.

Telcos ready temporary disaster roaming before summer
Josh Taylor
Telstra, Optus and Vodafone will from today be able to move users over to one of their rivals’ networks in areas where coverage has dropped out due to natural disasters such as cyclones, bushfires or floods.
The capability will mean users in those areas will still be able to call, message, and get basic access to the internet if the other network is up at no additional cost.
This is beyond the existing capability for networks to hand over emergency triple zero calls to other networks when the call can’t get through.
The industry has flagged there will be some scenarios - such as power outages – when switching will not be possible.
The switch-on for temporary roaming will be managed by the three carriers, and will happen automatically for customers when activated.
The temporary disaster roaming can be activated in up to three affected areas at the same time, with up to 15 mobile sites included per area, and activated for 24 hours at a time. The disaster areas must be at least 400km apart.
Metropolitan areas are excluded from the roaming arrangement.
From today, children under nine years old with mild developmental delays and autism can access early intervention services through a program called Thriving Kids, which is administered by state and territory governments.
The change was announced by the Albanese government in August 2025 and will slowly move children off the National Disability Insurance Scheme. It will fully replace the NDIS for these children by 2028.
Unlike the NDIS, participation in Thriving Kids won’t require a formal diagnosis, potentially speeding up services and saving families money.
The health minister, Mark Butler, recently told parents there would be no gap in government support for their children.
More than one-quarter of big companies operating in Australia paid no income tax in 2024-25, according to the Australian Taxation Office’s latest corporate transparency report.
The report says companies mostly cited an accounting loss – when expenses outstrip revenue.
Guardian Australia has previously reported how some multinationals, including the Singtel-owned Optus and coal miner Adani, regularly pay no tax, citing infrastructure investments and operating expenses .
About 27% of entities in the report reported zero tax, which was a similar figure to the year before.
In total, 4,299 entities earning at least $100m in total income paid a combined $87.5bn in tax in 2024–25, led by Australia’s large mining sector.
The ATO acting deputy commissioner, Michelle Sams, says the agency is “increasingly focused” on making sure digital businesses and supply chains, including data centres, paid their share of tax.
We look very closely if there’s no tax being paid in significant industries, including things like data centres, to make sure that the level of tax being paid reflects the economic activity that’s happening in Australia.

Investigators probe why co-pilot stabbed captain of flyDubai flight to Israel
The suspect, an Omani citizen, is under arrest and Saudi authorities are working with countries, including Israel, to determine a motive
Investigators worked on Thursday to determine why an Omani pilot stabbed the captain of a flight to Israel, causing the plane to plummet dangerously before others on board landed it in Saudi Arabia.
Passengers on the FlyDubai plane – which was carrying 174 people, mostly Israelis, from the United Arab Emirates to Tel Aviv – have described how the bloodied Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door to let them in before they grappled with the co-pilot and stabilised a descent so sharp that the plane’s rudder was torn away.
“We felt helpless, suspended in mid-air, and I didn’t know who to turn to. But it was all instinct to survive,” Asaf Rajuan, who was among those who intervened, said in a statement shared by Israel’s presidency.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung delivers a speech during the 78th Armed Forces Day at a military base in Gyeryong, South Korea, on Thursday.
| Pool / via AFP-Jiji
Seoul – South Korean President Lee Jae Myung urged North Korea on Thursday to return to dialogue, a day after Seoul’s military demanded an apology over a blast in the demilitarized zone that severely injured three South Korean soldiers.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war since the 1950-53 Korean War ended in a truce, not a peace treaty.
Three South Korean officers were severely injured in the Sept. 21 explosion inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), the heavily mined buffer dividing the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice. One lost his foot.

Private equity (PE) giant TPG has now offloaded more shares of listed logistics giant Shadowfax via an open-market transaction for ₹113.6 Cr. According to BSE data, the PE major, via its entity NewQuest Asia Fund IV (Singapore), sold 40 Lakh shares of the logistics giant at ₹284.03 apiece to rake in the amount. There was no clarity on who lapped up the shares that flooded the market. The block deal was undertaken at a premium of 1.3% to the stock’s last closing price on Wednesday. This is not the first time that TPG has sold its stake in the company in the past two months. In September, the PE firm offloaded Shadowfax shares worth ₹200 Cr. A month prior in August, TPG also pared stakes worth ₹300 Cr in the company a block deal. The bulk deals come as investors look to book profits amid a sharp jump in Shadowfax’s share prices. The stock hit an all-time high ₹291.90 on September 24. Overall, shares of the company have surged 14.22% in the past month, and are up more than 143.97% in the last six months. This jump has come on the back of healthy performance by the startup on the financial front. The logistics major reported an 8X surge in its consolidated net profit to ₹65.4 Cr in Q1 FY27 as against ₹8 Cr in the year ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue jumped 65% YoY and 10% QoQ to ₹1,358.1 Cr in the quarter ended June 2026. Following the results, Shadowfax also revised its FY27 revenue growth forecast to 38-40%, a significant jump from the 28-30% guidance projected just a quarter ago. Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Bansal and Vaibhav Khandelwal, Shadowfax operates a logistics network serving ecommerce, quick commerce and D2C brands. The company was listed on the stock exchanges earlier this year. It currently operates across more than 16,372 pincodes and plans to increase its network of dark stores from 47 to 100 by March 2027 as it looks to strengthen its quick commerce business. Shares of Shadowfax closed Wednesday’s trading session 0.09% lower at ₹280.5 on the BSE.

United Nations, Sep 23: In his inaugural speech at the UN General Assembly, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said world leaders must set up global standards to oversee artificial intelligence because “fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance”.
Burnham said the UK will try to persuade other countries to adopt rules on transparency and access to AI models - and, even tougher, to get tech companies to sign on, too.
He said AI has immense potential but will also be “a source of disruption to the way we live and work - and a multiplier of risk”.
Burnham also said Russia and other states are using AI-augmented misinformation and disinformation to corrode democracy, something he said Britain has faced in the decade since it voted to leave the European Union.
He said he has asked British security chiefs to set up a National Centre for Information Defence to counter the threat.
Burnham also chaired a meeting at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday on the Israel-Palestine issue, alongside French President Emmanuel Macron, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan.
He said the two-state solution to Israel-Palestinian conflict must be kept alive.
Burnham said failure to deliver a two-state solution will “corrode trust” in politicians who have talked about the issue but not taken action.
He told delegates from dozens of countries that the UK has banned trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank because the “E1” settlement expansion plan is “a deliberate attempt to block a two-state solution.”
“We all live in an era of low trust in politics. Many people in this room, many politicians around the world, have spoken for decades about a two-state solution. But if we fail to back those words with deeds, we will further corrode trust in the political, diplomatic and international process,” the UK prime minister said. (AP)

The Embassy of the State of Palestine to India has questioned the description of the 1918 Battle of Haifa as the “liberation of Haifa”, saying that Indian soldiers who participated in the battle were serving under British command as part of an imperial military campaign that resulted in the occupation of Palestine.
In a five-page position paper titled “Rewriting of India–Palestine history: The battle of Haifa: liberation or occupation?”, the Palestinian Embassy said the terminology surrounding the battle required “careful and scholarly reflection” and argued that the event should be understood within the historical context of British military occupation of Palestine.
The Embassy said Palestine, including Haifa, was under Ottoman rule before 1918 and that British forces defeated the Ottoman Empire during the First World War, bringing Palestine under British occupation. Indian soldiers participated in the campaign as part of the British Indian Army, under British command.
It argued that describing them retrospectively as having “liberated Haifa” risked attributing to India a sovereign military decision that the country did not possess in 1918, when it was still under British rule.
The paper pointed to contemporary British terminology, saying military and parliamentary records referred to the operations in Palestine using terms such as “capture”, “take”, “fall” and “conquer”. It also noted that following the British military campaign, Palestine was administered under the Occupied Enemy Territory Administration (OETA) until its replacement by a civil administration in July 1920.
The Embassy also cited India’s own historical records, including the 2014 publication Indian War Memorials Around the World, saying it does not describe the event as the “liberation of Haifa”.
According to the paper, the publication records that the “fortified town of Haifa fell to a cavalry charge by the Jodhpur Lancers” and that the 15th Imperial Service Cavalry Brigade “broke through and took the town”.
It also referred to the Teen Murti Memorial in New Delhi, stating that the memorial was established during British colonial rule to commemorate Indian soldiers who served and died during the First World War, and was not originally intended to commemorate relations between India and Israel.
The Embassy said the memorial refers to “Palestine and some of its cities” among the places associated with the military campaigns in which Indian soldiers served.
The paper further cited official Indian records to state that 491 Indian soldiers are recorded at Ramleh War Cemetery, 109 at the Gaza and Deir el Balah War Cemeteries and 47 at the Haifa Indian Cemetery, besides soldiers commemorated at other cemeteries and memorials across historical Palestine.
The Embassy questioned why Haifa had become the centre of a commemorative narrative when Indian soldiers had fought across a much wider region, including the Suez Canal, Gaza, Jerusalem, the Jordan Valley, Damascus and Aleppo.
It also said the first formal Israeli public ceremony commemorating the Indian soldiers was held in 2010, nearly a century after the battle.
The paper argued that Britain, rather than India, was the principal military power behind the campaign, as it financed, armed and commanded the operation. It questioned why the “liberation of Haifa” narrative centred on Indian soldiers while Britain’s role was not similarly emphasised.
The Embassy also stressed that the soldiers described as “Indian soldiers” served in the British Indian Army and came from different regions, communities and religions across British India, whose geographical and political boundaries differed from those of the present-day Republic of India.
The position paper placed the soldiers’ participation within the wider history of British colonial rule, noting that Indian troops were deployed in military campaigns far from their homeland.
It also referred to the Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, arguing that the broader record of British rule should be considered when interpreting the role of Indian soldiers in the First World War.
The Embassy cited Mahatma Gandhi’s opposition to the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine at the expense of its indigenous population, including his statement that “Palestine belongs to the Arabs in the same sense that England belongs to the English.”
It further pointed out that India voted against UN Resolution 181 in 1947, which proposed partition and allocated Haifa to the proposed Jewish state, and questioned how the 1918 battle could subsequently be presented as a foundation for India-Israel historical ties.
The Embassy said describing the 1918 occupation of Haifa as a liberation “raises serious questions and concerns in Palestine”. It maintained that Haifa should be recognised as a Palestinian city at the time and that the battle took place in the context of the British military occupation of Palestine.
At the same time, the Embassy said its position was expressed with “full respect” for the sacrifice and memory of Indian soldiers and for India’s sovereign right to commemorate its history and fallen soldiers.
It called for historical remembrance of the Battle of Haifa to remain grounded in accuracy, balance and respect for the historical experiences of all concerned, while emphasising that the document represented the Palestinian Embassy’s perspective and was intended to contribute to discussion on the historical and legal questions surrounding the battle.

When Away launched the Carry On suitcase in 2016, it created the must-have travel accessory. It went viral for its sleek, simple polycarbonate design (plus a dash of smart social marketing). Its pioneering ejectable portable battery earned it the “smart luggage” moniker, and other bag makers quickly copied the concept.
A decade later, Away is launching the Series 3—its third generation. The battery is gone, but the features that attracted and retained a loyal following remain, with a heavy focus on invisible tech.
“We didn’t like to be called ‘smart luggage’,” Sarah Amidi, Away’s senior vice president of Brand, tells WIRED at the company’s design studio in New York City’s SoHo district. When the first Carry On was conceived, charging solutions weren’t as ubiquitous as they are today, Amidi says, which created a unique travel pain point for Away to tackle. It may have seemed gimmicky, but a quickly accessible USB port to charge a phone made sense. The ejectable design was forward-thinking, given evolving regulations around traveling with batteries.
While the battery hasn’t been available in Away luggage since 2023, Amidi says tech isn’t entirely gone; the company is looking at how technology can play the right role in luggage design. Instead, with the Series 3, Away has become more of a traditional luggage maker than a disruptor. “We design it to last the next 10 years,” Amidi says.
On the surface, every piece from the Series 3 Classic and Flex (expandable) series will look familiar to Away fans, and that’s intentional. Instead of a new design, Amidi says the company strengthened its carry-on by putting it through rigorous testing. In fact, the Series 3 launch was delayed because it didn’t fully meet expectations.
“We asked, what features solve friction and earn their place,” Amidi says. “We didn’t want to add things just to add things that take away from capacity or add weight, and we couldn’t make polycarbonate any better.”
Reinventing the Wheel, Sort Of
Amidi says the shell design still works today (with the battery option gone, it also shaved off weight and added more room), so Away looked at two areas that could use some work: the wheels and telescoping trolley handle—what travelers often complain about in luggage.
For the WhisperGlide 360 spinning wheel design, Away added an extra ball bearing and improved the threading to make them glide smoothly and quietly. Away also brought its StopLock Brakes system, first introduced in its top-opening TopSide luggage, to the Series 3. As the name suggests, flipping a switch quickly locks the wheels, effective even on slight inclines.
When I asked why quiet wheels would even matter in, say, a busy airport, Amidi refers to a time when she needed to quietly sneak out of the house for a trip without waking her family. She says these are the kinds of new travel pain points Away is looking to solve with tech.
Then there's the Infinite Height Trolley handle, which offers five times more stopping points than before—a more personalized experience for travelers of varying heights. Hooks in the trolley handle might seem like a simple design touch, but they’re handy for holding a jacket, purse, or bag of airport fast food (each hook can hold up to 11 pounds, but Away has stress-tested it up to 40 pounds).
Other improvements include redesigned interior covers that open outward to give better access, more pockets for small items, a pouch for a Bluetooth tracker, and accessories to help keep the luggage looking clean. The compression system, a signature Away feature, remains the same.
Personalization is a key selling feature. In addition to the standard colors, the Series 3 comes in purple (Electric Iris), chocolate, and chartreuse. The handles and wheels are removable and can be customized in different styles (also handy for repairs). There's also a D-ring to attach accessories like luggage tags and charms, if that’s your thing. For many people, it will be.
The Series 3 Classic style is available in carry-on, bigger carry-on, medium, large, and trunk sizes. The expandable Flex style is available in the same sizes except trunk.
Away also unveiled the Signature Bags collection, which includes a tote, weekender, commuter backpack, duffle, and underseat bags. An evolution of Away’s Everywhere series, the durable nylon is now lighter and softer, Amidi says, with updated hardware like zippers—including a reverse coil zipper in the laptop compartment for better protection—hidden pockets for easy access to often-used items, and a water bottle pocket. The laptop compartment has moved to the outside of the bag, allowing quick access during airport security checks, for example.
Overall, Away's new luggage doesn't offer anything groundbreaking. Many of these features are available in bags from other companies, and in some ways, it feels like Away is playing catch-up. But Away is leveraging its strength with a well-regarded product that already works, with a few tweaks to make it better. It’s this, not batteries, that has made it a cult favorite among travelers.

Concerns over the safety of drinking water have resurfaced in parts of Uri area of north Kashmir’s Baramulla district after residents of Gawalta village found a dead snake inside a pipeline supplying water to the locality, raising questions over the maintenance and monitoring of the public water supply network.
The incident comes weeks after a similar complaint from Karkroo Mohalla in Nambla, where residents had reported finding dead rats inside a water storage tank and supply pipelines.
Both incidents have generated severe resentment among the local population, who accused the Jal Shakti Department of not taking care of the water tanks, pipelines and other components of the supply network.
In the fresh incident, the residents said the Sokad-Gowlta Water Supply Scheme had remained non-functional for several days, leaving the village without regular drinking water.
They said that despite repeated requests to employees of the Jal Shakti Department, the problem was not addressed promptly.
“With the supply remaining disrupted, the local residents inspected the pipeline themselves on Monday and found a dead snake lodged inside it,” said Arif Hussain, a local resident.
The presence of the snake triggered concern among residents over the possibility of contamination and the overall hygiene of the water distribution system.
The residents of Gowlta have now urged the department to conduct an immediate inspection of the entire supply network, clean and disinfect the pipeline and ensure that only safe water is supplied to households.
They have also sought an inquiry into how the reptile entered the pipeline and demanded preventive measures, including regular inspection and sanitation of water infrastructure.
Residents said repeated complaints involving contamination or poor maintenance were a major issue in the area and the concerned authority should ensure monitoring of drinking-water schemes in the Uri area.

Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under Donald Trump’s hardline immigration policy.
However, the authorities in Bujumbura, the country’s economic capital, said Burundi will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial details.
Washington has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to some half a dozen African nations as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely, under opaque deals that Senate Democrats say have cost tens of millions of dollars.
In many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. But rights groups say the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections.
Mutoni said preparations were underway to arrange accommodation, living conditions and integration into local communities in Burundi. “Receiving them requires serious planning – where they will stay, what they will eat and how they will live alongside the local population,” she said.
“If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law will be respected,” she said, regarding potential citizenship.
Burundi aimed to both strengthen diplomatic relations and provide hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson added.
The US state department did not immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available.

Does Horner have a chance of Ferrari job? F1 Q&A
- Published
Mercedes' George Russell took his first victory since June by holding off Max Verstappen to win the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
Verstappen's Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar completed the podium on his return after missing three races with a broken wrist.
Championship leader Kimi Antonelli finished fifth in Baku, meaning his advantage over team-mate Russell has narrowed to 66 points.
This weekend, Formula 1 heads to Malaysia, the host of the Bahrain Grand Prix - an event originally due to take place in April but which was postponed because of the war in the Middle East.
Before the race in Sepang, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
Does Christian Horner really want the team principal job at Ferrari, or even have a shot at it? - Ben
This topic has become a subject for conversation in recent days following an interview Horner did with the Times, external as he promotes his new book.
Horner said: "At this stage in my life, there's only one team for which I would accept non-participation in ownership."
Asked whether he would take a job there, he replied: "Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula 1. It's the dream. And arguably it's the sleeping giant of Formula 1."
Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur made his views about Horner's intervention pretty plain after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix when he said: "Mr Horner is looking for a job - that, everybody knows - everywhere."
Vasseur said the speculation surrounding the team meant Ferrari were "not working in the perfect serenity".
Horner's comments seem to make it clear that he would consider a job offer from Ferrari. But the key questions are under what conditions he might accept it, and whether he would be offered it in the first place.
Horner has made it very clear over the years that he believes an F1 team needs one person in charge and in overall control.
It's highly unlikely he would get that at Ferrari, where chairman John Elkann and chief executive officer Benedetto Vigna will always have more authority than any team principal.
Even at Red Bull, where Horner had theoretical leadership at the F1 team, he was ultimately answerable to headquarters in Austria and that is what led to his removal in the end.
It's hard to imagine how Elkann and Vigna could or would countenance any situation where they were removed from any input into the F1 team.
And it's even harder to imagine a situation where that was not the de facto position even if a team boss had been given assurances they would be left alone.
Then there is the question of whether Ferrari would want Horner.
Horner comes with baggage. All of the above for a start, and on top of that there is the cloud under which he left Red Bull.
There is no doubt that he was a remarkably successful team principal there, the team winning eight drivers' titles, six constructors' championships and 124 grands prix in his two-decade tenure.
However, the team unravelled in his final 18 months in charge, in the wake of the accusations of sexual harassment and coercive, controlling behaviour that were made against him by a female employee.
Red Bull dismissed those allegations after two internal investigations led by external lawyers.
But they were a key factor in Adrian Newey leaving his position as chief technical officer - along with internal politics in which Newey felt his role had been diminished by Horner.
Newey was followed out of the door by long-time sporting director Jonathan Wheatley and head of strategy Will Courtenay.
Horner was finally dismissed following a slump in form which Red Bull bosses concluded the team did not appear to be capable of arresting under his leadership.
In the Times interview, Horner says that the only justification he was given by Red Bull for his sacking was "it was more Christian Horner Racing than Red Bull Racing".
He adds at other points in the interview: "I am a bit of a Marmite character. I know I'm not everybody's cup of tea. It's impossible to be." And: "I'm the cure and the problem."
Clearly, any decision as to whether Horner is the person you want to lead your F1 team would need careful consideration.
It's also worth mentioning that Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton has made it pretty clear over the past few years that he has little time for Horner.
Why hasn't the FIA made a decision on the final two races of the season? They've cancelled the final rounds of the World Rally Championship and World Endurance Championship because of the Middle East conflict. Surely they should be confirming the changes in the calendar now? - Nigel
To start with a point of order, it is Formula 1 that decides the calendar - as in, the commercial rights holder - not the FIA, the governing body. The FIA's role is effectively only to rubber-stamp F1's decision.
As things stand, F1 is planning to end the season as the calendar was originally scheduled - with Las Vegas followed by Qatar and then Abu Dhabi, external over the last two weekends in November and the first in December.
Although the war continues between the US/Israel and Iran, the advice F1 has been getting is that the situation in those two countries is stable, and there is not a high risk of attacks on civilian infrastructure.
The UK Foreign Office, for example, does not advise against travel to Qatar and Abu Dhabi., external It simply says the situation there "remains unpredictable" and that "there is a risk of more attacks and unforeseen escalation in the region".
And the two countries consider themselves open for business.
However, F1 has a contingency plan.
Imola in Italy is preparing to host a race on the weekend of Abu Dhabi.
If the two Middle Eastern races cannot happen as a result of an escalation of the situation in the Gulf, Imola would step in and hold the season finale on 4-6 December.
But unless and until that happens, there is no confirmation of changes to make, as there are currently no changes.
Why wasn't a virtual safety car called when Valtteri Bottas crashed right at the end in Azerbaijan? This was obviously a dangerous situation as the car was buried in the barrier. And it almost cost George Russell a well-deserved victory - Steve
Valtteri Bottas crashed at Turn 15 on the penultimate lap of the race, meaning his Cadillac was in the barriers there when leaders George Russell and Max Verstappen came around their last lap less than a second apart.
Normally, a car in the barriers on a street circuit means at least a virtual safety car.
However, in this instance a spokesperson for governing body the FIA says that race control "determined that it was safe to let the leaders race to the line - they were able to cut the apex at T15, as it's a relatively slow corner".
In the event, the Bottas incident, the FIA says, was "successfully managed by localised double yellows".
Whether this was the correct course of action, and whether the decision was influenced by wanting to prevent the grand prix finishing under caution, will remain a subject for debate.
On the one hand, it allowed the race to continue and be exciting to the end.
On the other, slowing for the incident caused a technical issue for Russell's Mercedes.
"I lifted off the power and when I went back, I had no turbo, so then I had no power," Russell said. "Max almost got me at the line."
Russell was able to mitigate this loss of power from the internal combustion engine because, it being the final lap, he could use up all his battery on the run to the flag, rather than have to keep it balanced for the following lap.
So he managed to hang on - but by less than 0.2 seconds.
Had he not, the decision by race control would have come under a great deal more scrutiny than it did.
I love your explainers. Please can you analyse the data explaining the jump Williams have made with their upgrades. It seems more significant than Aston Martin's much written-about 'leap'? What are the percentages, averages etc. - John
First of all, thanks very much for the compliment.
This is a complex topic. There is no doubt that the lighter chassis and aerodynamic upgrades introduced by Williams in Baku marked a step forward.
It was their best qualifying performance of the year in terms of positions, even if in percentage terms they were actually slightly closer to the front in Miami back in May.
But it's too early to judge the Williams upgrades - and Aston Martin provides a clue as to why.
This year, there is quite a swing in competitiveness for certain teams depending on circuit type.
Regardless of the upgrades, Williams always expected Baku to be one of their stronger circuits - short-duration corners and long straights suit their car.
But they struggle in long-duration corners, so it will be interesting to see how they go this weekend in Malaysia, because Sepang is full of them.
Likewise, Aston Martin have specific weaknesses.
Their aerodynamic upgrade in Hungary improved their chassis performance by in the region of two seconds a lap.
Hence their significant improvement there and in Zandvoort, where Fernando Alonso drove superbly to take two points for ninth place.
But, despite its upgrade for Zandvoort, the Honda engine remains the worst on the grid, in terms of overall power, driveability and energy management.
So, it's no surprise that on two hugely engine-dependent circuits such as Monza and Baku, they would struggle.
On that basis, Aston Martin can be expected to be relatively more competitive again in Singapore, with its low power-sensitivity, and where Alonso is usually outstanding.

In what seems like an alternate universe in hindsight, Russia and the European Space Agency began discussing collaboration on next-generation crewed spacecraft two decades ago. Under the agreement, Europe would have provided a service module to power a crew capsule carrying up to six passengers.
Europe ultimately decided not to pursue a crewed spacecraft project at the time, and Russia’s state-backed space corporation, Roscosmos, chose to move ahead with a crewed spacecraft on its own. This project—always seemingly more of a Potemkin village than an effort encompassing real hardware—has gone under various guises over the years:
- PPTS (Perspektivnaya Pilotiruemaya Transportnaya Sistema / Prospective Piloted Transport System): The initial conceptual project name used in 2009
- PTK NP (Pilotiruyemy Transportny Korabl Novogo Pokoleniya / New Generation Piloted Transport Ship): The official technical designation used until 2016
- Federatsiya (Federation): The official name chosen following a public contest and announced in January 2016
- Orel / Oryol (Eagle): A new name adopted in September 2019 when Roscosmos was under the control of Dmitry Rogozin
Actual hardware tests, maybe?
Beyond the name changes and a flood of renderings, after nearly 20 years of work, then, is anything actually happening with the Eagle spacecraft?
For starters, the relatively new chief executive of Roscosmos, Dmitry Bakanov, appears to have jettisoned the “Eagle” name of the spacecraft favored by Rogozin. In a recently published Interfax story, the spacecraft is referred to as PTK NP.

Mom arrested after 4-month-old baby Luna found dead in South LA dumpster

A 19-year-old woman suspected of leaving her dead 4-month-old daughter in a dumpster in South Los Angeles could soon face formal criminal charges as police prepare to present the case to prosecutors.
Takiyah Babers was arrested Tuesday on suspicion of murder after Los Angeles Police Department officers questioned her near the area where the infant had been discovered.
A GoFundMe has been set up for the infant’s family to help to pay for memorial services.
Babers was being held on $2 million bail at the Century Regional Detention Facility in Lynwood, according to Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department inmate records.
Police said the investigation would be presented to the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office for consideration of criminal charges.
The baby was found unresponsive in a dumpster in the 5200 block of Alba Street at around 10:30 p.m. Monday.
Paramedics rushed the girl to a hospital, where she was pronounced dead. Authorities did not immediately publicly identify the infant, but Babers' foster parents told reporters at the scene that the baby's name was Luna.
Police detained Babers the following morning while investigating the infant's death. The LAPD later identified her as the baby's biological mother.
"This case will be presented to the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office for filing consideration," the department said.
Authorities have not disclosed how the infant died, and a possible motive has not been announced.
The baby's death prompted an outpouring of grief in the neighborhood, where community members created a makeshift memorial near the dumpster. Dozens of candles were lit and flowers were placed at the scene, while balloons were tied to the dumpster where the child had been found.
Herman Johnson, Babers' foster father, told Fox11 that the discovery had left him devastated.
"That was the sweetest little baby in the world. To be found in a Dumpster, dirty Dumpster, it just broke my heart," Johnson said. "I don't know what to do. I don't even know what to say."
Johnson said he questioned Babers on Tuesday morning after learning that an infant had been discovered in a trash bin nearby.
According to Johnson, Babers initially told him that the baby was sleeping. She later allegedly said the infant was at the home of the baby's father, but Johnson said that also turned out not to be true.
Babers' foster mother, Laura Lacy, told reporters she had not suspected anything was seriously wrong before the baby's death.
She said she "had no idea [Babers] was feeling that way to discard" the infant.
Babers had not been scheduled to appear in court as of early Wednesday morning.
The circumstances surrounding the baby's death remain under investigation. Police have not announced whether investigators believe the infant died before being placed in the dumpster or disclosed any findings about the cause or manner of death.
Anyone with information about the case was urged to contact the LAPD's Abused Child Unit at 213-486-0530.
