Reversing a downward trend over the past two months, monthly electric two-wheeler (E2W) registrations bounced back in September. As per Vahan data, total E2W sales for the month of September stood at 2.07 Lakh units, up 12.2% month-on-month increase from 1.84 Lakh units registered in August. Important to note that Inc42 had reported 1.72 lakh E2W registrations for August based on the data available on August 31, while the latest Vahan data puts the month at 1.84 lakh units, a 7% upward revision. From a year-on-year (YoY) lens, September’s total registration almost doubled 1.05 Lakh units registered in September 2025. The top three traditional OEMs — TVS Motor, Bajaj and Hero MotoCorp — together accounted for around 61% of September registrations, with all three recording month-on-month growth. In contrast, new-age players such as Ola Electric, Ather and BGauss saw more mixed performance. While Ather’s registrations rose 4.9%, Ola declined 3.5% and BGauss was broadly flat. The September rebound also comes against a broader strengthening of India’s electric mobility market. As per reports, total EV registrations rose 64.6% YoY to 3.15 Lakh units in the month. In this, E2Ws accounted for the bulk of this growth. The growth could partly reflect the build-up to the festive season, when automakers and dealers typically step up inventory and promotional activity. Established two-wheeler manufacturers are also expanding their EV portfolios and distribution reach, making electric scooters more accessible to mainstream buyers. This shift towards mass-market products could further support volumes as manufacturers target buyers beyond the early-adopter segment with more affordable models and wider retail networks. While Ather launched its ₹99,999 scooter, Konarc, in late August, Ola Electric launched the S1Z scooter, priced at ₹79,999, around the same time. Incumbents Maintain Lead E2W market leader TVS Motor led the charge in September as well, with its market share now at 26%. The original equipment manufacturer (OEM) recorded 53,989 E2W registrations in September, an almost 10% MoM increase from 49,284 units recorded in the month prior. After capturing over a quarter of the Indian E2W market, TVS Motors has now embarked on an international expansion effort which includes establishing and expanding presence in countries like Nepal, Kenya, Sri Lanka and now, Indonesia, where it is planning to set up a manufacturing facility. With its current monthly manufacturing capacity at 40,000-45,000 units currently, it plans to raise that to 50,000-plus units in three to four months. Meanwhile, Bajaj Auto is hot on the trail, strengthening its position further in September with 48,383 registrations recorded in September, a 17% jump from 41,341 units recorded in August. Its total market share now stands at 23.4%. The OEM is on track to launch an electric motorbike in the coming months, and is meanwhile expanding its market position through its portfolio spanning premium to mass-market offerings. HeroMotocorp, while failing to re-enter the top three ranking, saw registrations soar 27% in September to 24,306 units. The OEM is nevertheless planning to launch its own electric motorcycle in 2027 alongside new e-scooter variants, while doubling down on manufacturing. Ather, Ola Lose Market Share In comparison to larger OEMs, Ather Energy saw tepid growth in September, with registrations inching up 5% MoM to 30,479 units from 29,068 in August. Its market share, meanwhile, fell 110 basis points to 14.7% during the month. Important to highlight that Ather’s overall sales have now crossed the 8 Lakh mark, making it the fourth OEM in the country to achieve the milestone. It expects sales momentum to accelerate as its newly launched affordable scooter Konarc picks up, and could make up for half of its sales within two years. Meanwhile, Ola Electric continued its downward trajectory in terms of registrations, which dipped 3.5% MoM to 13,449 units in September. The September decline comes as Ola attempts to rebuild its distribution network through dealer-led stores, targeting a network of more than 500 outlets, while also pushing cheaper products and its in-house Bharat Cells. E-scooter maker E-Sprinto recorded a blockbuster 16X MoM increase in registrations during the month to 1,997 units.The OEM is planning to substantially increase its presence on Indian roads in coming months, buoyed by plans to launch an affordable family scooter with a claimed range of 130 km on a single charge. Meanwhile, electric motorbike maker Oben also recovered substantially in September, registering 1,417 units in September, a 120% MoM surge from 642 units in August. On the other hand, its rival electric bike maker Ultraviolette saw registrations dip over 12% MoM to 536 units. The startup raised $85 Mn in equity funding during the month as it plans to shore up manufacturing and enter new markets in US, Latin America, and Southeast Asia. Besides Ultraviolette, River raised $120 Mn in August to expand its manufacturing as well. The e-scooter maker saw its registrations increase 6.4% to 5,549 units. Simple, which raised $180 Mn earlier this week, saw its registrations dip 19% MoM to 1,351 units in September. It plans to focus on a new manufacturing facility, higher production, an expanded distribution and service network, and the next generation of products. The startup recently launched the Simple Wave, an affordable family scooter series starting at ₹1.10 Lakh.

South Korea has demanded an apology from North Korea over a landmine blast that injured three soldiers, saying they were hurt by North Korean mines on the southern side of the border.
Kang Hyun-woo, the director of operations at South Korea’s joint chiefs of staff, demanded an apology and “responsible measures” from Pyongyang over the blast, which occurred on 21 September during a search operation south of the border.
He also called for an immediate halt to North Korea’s mine-laying and border fortification, which he said violated the armistice and the spirit of inter-Korean agreements. North Korea would bear “all responsibility” for any future developments, he said.
The incident echoes a 2015 mine blast in the demilitarised zone between the countries that seriously injured two South Korean soldiers and prompted Seoul to resume propaganda broadcasts over loudspeakers. North Korea responded to the move with artillery fire across the border before expressing regret during high-level talks.
The US-led UN command (UNC), which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war, said on Wednesday that a joint investigation with South Korea’s military had identified a live North Korean anti-personnel mine on the southern side of the military demarcation line (MDL), the de facto border.
The UNC said an armistice violation had occurred and that it was addressing the issue through “established armistice mechanisms”.
The explosions occurred about 10 metres south of the MDL on the western front, as troops searched an area where North Korea was suspected of laying mines.
Two blasts went off about a minute apart, seriously injuring a battalion commander, whose foot was reportedly severed at the ankle, and an engineer. A third officer was present and has minor injuries from the explosion.
On Monday, South Korea’s military said interim findings showed the blasts were “highly likely” to have been caused by North Korean mines
North Korea has denied involvement. In a statement carried by state media on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong-un, called the incident “an obvious self-staged farce”.
“Our soldiers have never once crossed the border,” she said, warning that if South Korean troops fired directly at North Korean soldiers, border units would carry out “immediate and merciless retaliation”.
Chris Green, a senior consultant at the International Crisis Group, said the investigation findings would not settle the matter politically because the North would always have “guaranteed plausible deniability”.
There are no working communication channels between the two Koreas. Pyongyang severed ties in 2024, declared South Korea a hostile state and has since laid mines and built fortifications along the border. “Accidental escalation on the Korean peninsula is always just a few steps away and it’s fewer steps now than it was in 2015,” Green said.
The blast presents a challenge for South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, who has sought to revive diplomacy with Pyongyang. Last week, he told the UN general assembly that Seoul would be a “pacemaker” for peace, and urged Washington to ease sanctions in exchange for a freeze on North Korea’s weapons programmes.
The incident has also fuelled political tensions at home. Opposition politicians questioned whether the investigation had been delayed to avoid overshadowing Lee’s UN speech, a suggestion the presidential office denied.
The conservative People Power party has also called for the return of the propaganda loudspeakers, which were switched off and dismantled under Lee last year.
The mine blast adds to other diplomatic difficulties facing Lee. On Monday, Seoul demanded an apology from Ukraine after its president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, disclosed the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
Seoul said the two sides had agreed to keep the transfer secret, citing the men’s safety and diplomatic and security considerations. Some critics said the secrecy was about not upsetting Pyongyang.

An investor lawsuit against UnitedHealth Group will move forward after a federal judge on Wednesday declined the company’s motion to dismiss allegations that it juiced its earnings to the tune of $3.3 billion in 2024 to conceal weakness in its Medicare Advantage business.
It wasn’t all good news for the California Public Employees’ Retirement System, or CalPERS, though. U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Bryan dismissed most of the pension fund’s allegations that UnitedHealth’s leaders deceived investors about multiple aspects of their business in order to artificially inflate the company’s stock. Bryan agreed with UnitedHealth that most of the company statements CalPERS cited weren’t specific enough or represented typical promotional “puffery” that investors wouldn’t act on.
One of the lawsuit’s central allegations was that the Minnesota-based conglomerate concealed an illegal practice of making its Medicare Advantage patients appear sicker on paper to siphon more money from the government. On that front, CalPERS cited the company’s statements that home visits kept its members healthy and that its clinicians made independent clinical decisions. In fact, reporting has since shown that UnitedHealth used those visits to add diagnoses to patients’ records for which they received no follow-up care and pressured its doctors to do the same using bonuses. .

The cost of borrowing money is moving unrelentingly higher, with profound implications for savers, borrowers and the U.S. government's fiscal outlook.
The big picture: The bond market moves over the last few weeks have pushed most risk-free interest rates north of 5%.
Barring a rapid reversal, expect pain to come in interest-sensitive sectors like housing, new stress on federal government finances and greater risks of financial disruption.
It is better news for savers, who have taken paper losses on existing bonds in recent weeks but can now deploy cash safely with the best prospective returns seen in decades.
Zoom out: It is clearer than ever that the era of cheap borrowing and abundant capital that lasted from 2008 to 2021 is well and truly over.
Every individual looking to take a home mortgage or car loan is in competition with the voracious capital needs of the AI giants and the U.S. government.
While the Federal Reserve has gotten out of the business of forecasting its next moves, it is now looking out of position. Its leaders increasingly believe that it has set its policy rates too low to control inflation amid a growth boom, and are now looking to adjust course, which means last week's rate hike won't be the last.
Rate hikes may not deter much AI investment or government borrowing, which leaves all other interest-sensitive sectors to bear the brunt of bringing the economy into better balance.
Zoom in: The surge in rates has been driven for the most part by a rise in real yields — implying a stronger growth outlook, not an outburst in expected inflation.
Investors can now buy a 30-year inflation-protected Treasury security that pays 3.26%, the highest since 2002. This time five years ago, that number was negative.
The forward earnings yield of the S&P 500 is about 5%. With the 30-year nominal Treasury bond yielding around 5.5%, bonds look more attractive relative to stocks than they have in ages.
State of play: The recent surge in longer-term rates is poised to push 30-year fixed-rate mortgages to near 8%. Mortgage News Daily on Thursday clocked the 30-year rate at 7.45%, or 7.55% for jumbo loans.
Mortgage rates got that high briefly in the fall of 2023, but the last time they were above that level on a sustained basis was in 2000.
Over time, the housing market can find a balance. But in the near term, surges in rates just mean pain as the market freezes up.
People can't afford to buy houses with 7.5%+ rates, and sellers don't want to cut their prices, so there is a standstill, as witnessed in the fall of 2023, until either rates fall or prices adjust.
The intrigue: Higher rates, if sustained, will make America's fiscal situation considerably thornier.
The U.S. government's debt service costs were already projected to reach new highs in the coming years — but that burden will be much worse if the rate surge of the last few weeks is sustained.
By the numbers: In projections that the Congressional Budget Office produced last February, net interest costs are already at $1 trillion this year and on track to reach $2 trillion by 2035, meaning that much of federal spending is needed just to service old bills.
But those projections assumed 10-year Treasury yields were in the ballpark of 4.3%. They're now nearly a full percentage point higher than that.
In startling numbers that CBO released this week, in a scenario in which interest rates were 1 percentage point higher than its baseline, debt held by the public would grow to 222% of GDP in 2056, 47 percentage points higher than the baseline.
Reality check: Higher interest rates don't flow through to government debt service costs immediately. Longer-term bonds gradually mature over time.
So a reversal in rates would help the fiscal arithmetic (at least so long as it wasn't caused by a recession or productivity slump).
The bottom line: If the 5% world is here to stay, it commands a rethinking of the U.S. government's tax and spending policies, the price of assets, and more generally what we consider normal in an era of steep global demand for capital.

To establish a comprehensive framework for registration of allied and healthcare professionals (AHP) in both the State Registers and the Central Register, the National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions (NCAHP) under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare notified the Registration of Allied and Healthcare Professionals Regulations, 2026 on August 31, 2026, and published it in the Gazette of India on September 15, 2026.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
Under the new regulations, all allied and healthcare professionals spanning 57 vocations across 10 broad disciplines, including physiotherapists, dietitians, lab technologists, forensic psychologists, among others, will soon have to register in the State and Central registers to practise in their chosen fields.
Registration certificates, including digital certificates featuring the Unique Identification (UID) number and a secure QR code, will be issued to the professionals by the Commission or the respective State Council. This will facilitate identification and verification of registered professionals and support greater transparency in the delivery of allied and healthcare services. The registration and payment of the fee will be processed on a dedicated online portal developed by the Commission.
“These regulations mark a leap towards streamlining the allied and healthcare workforce. Unless and until the professional gets the UID, he/she will not be able to practise/work. There is a penalty of up to 6 months to two years’ jail term under the NCAHP Act-21 if the professional practices without registration,” Dr. Yagna Unmesh Shukla, chairperson of NCAHP said.
“The regulations also aim to bring uniformity in the registration of allied and healthcare professionals and ensure renewal. With this registration, the actual number of qualified professionals will be available, as well as the difference between qualified and non-qualified professionals, which is also one of the key objectives of the NCAHP Act-21,” she added.
Public access
Highlighting that the registration process is the first of its kind in the history of allied and healthcare professions, Dr. Shukla says that the regulations provide a real-time synchronisation between the State Registers and the Central Register through an integrated online system.
Further, the Central and State Registers will be accessible to the public through the websites of the Commission and the respective State Councils, which will display the prescribed particulars of registered professionals.
Since only persons meeting the prescribed eligibility requirements, including recognised qualifications and the applicable exit examination requirements, will be eligible for regular registration, this will provide an important safeguard for patients and service users by promoting the practice of appropriately qualified professionals.
The public will be able to verify the registration status and relevant details of allied and healthcare professionals through the websites of the Commission and the respective State Councils. Professionals residing in a State or Union Territory where a functional State Council has not yet been established may register directly with the Central Register.
A key feature of the Regulations is the flexibility they give to allied and healthcare professionals to register in one State and practise in another State. “This will mitigate the hassles professionals face when applying for registration in another state. All they now need to do is fill out the form and inform the state in which they reside of the state where they intend to practise, so that this information remains on record. Since each registered professional is provided with a UID number, all their records are documented, facilitating the smooth transfer of registration details from one state to another,” Dr. Shukla said.
Apart from registration certificates, including digital certificates featuring the UID and a secure QR code, registered allied and healthcare professionals will also have access to a Good Standing Certificate. It will help professionals pursue any foreign education or profession or participate in student exchange programmes outside India. “There is a big difference between registration and a Good Standing Certificate. Registration is the licence to practise in India, whereas a Certificate of Good Standing is issued by the State Council when required by various countries for professionals who wish to work or study in those countries,” Dr. Shukla says.
Registration of foreign-qualified professionals
The Regulations establish a pathway for Indian citizens holding foreign qualifications in allied and healthcare. A foreign-qualified allied and healthcare professional will be considered eligible to apply for registration provided his qualification is recognised by the Commission, or he has completed the prescribed credential equivalency evaluation, and has also passed the relevant exit examination, where applicable. “It is important to have an equivalence process of foreign qualified professionals in place for the safety of the patients,” Dr. Shukla adds.
There is also provision for temporary registration for eligible foreign-qualified Indian professionals for specific, time-bound purposes, including postgraduate or specialty education, fellowships, clinical research, observerships, advanced workshops, expert visits, and voluntary community service. Such registration remains subject to the conditions laid down in the Regulations and applicable regulatory guidelines.
Validity period
Under the regulations, the registration will remain valid for five years, renewable upon the fulfilment of Continuing Professional Development (CPD) requirements through approved online and offline modes. This means that professionals must upgrade themselves professionally (15 hours per year) by attending seminars, conferences, workshops, training programmes and faculty development programmes.
“It is important for professionals to update and upgrade themselves in their respective professions. Since the regulations are being implemented for the first time, flexibility in the CPD programme is being permitted. This explains why 50% of these participations in online mode are being considered,” Dr. Shukla said.
Additionally, the Commission is making efforts to introduce provisional registration for professionals currently practising in the allied and healthcare sector who lack the prescribed primary qualifications. Such professionals will be provided with an option to undergo a bridge course to attain eligibility for regular registration. The Commission is making concerted efforts to introduce provisional registration for professionals currently practising in the allied and healthcare sector who lack the prescribed primary qualifications.
“Those who are practising for many years and are not qualified as per the provisions of the Act will be registered under the Provisional Registration Act and will have to undergo a prescribed Bridge course within the given time period to attain eligibility for regular registration,” Dr. Shukla said.
Interim registrations
The Regulations have also introduced provisions for interim registration for students enrolled in recognised institutions who are undertaking internships, clinical training, observerships, or practical coursework required to complete an allied and healthcare qualification. Interim registration must be initiated by the recognised institution and obtained from the concerned State Council. No fee will be charged for interim registration applications, the NCAHP regulations stated.
(Rajlakshmi Ghosh is a journalist with over three decades of experience in media houses and educational institutions)

World Contraception Day on September 26 offers an opportunity to look closely at a part of family planning that receives very little attention: contraception for men. The key question here is why the range of methods available to men and women remains so different.
Women today have options including oral pills, injectables, implants, intrauterine devices and permanent sterilisation, though access and affordability to safe and reliable contraception in our country continues to remain a major challenge. For men, the practical choices are still largely limited to condoms for reversible contraception and vasectomy for permanent contraception. Male and female reproduction are governed by the same broad hormonal axis, yet the biology, anatomy and mechanics of preventing conception create very different problems. Understanding those differences helps explain why a male equivalent of the pill has remained elusive.

The setting for perhaps the country’s biggest exercise in public debate was quintessential rural India: fields of green paddy, a pond, a temple. On a normal day, as dusk falls in the village of Ajgara, in Uttar Pradesh, people gather beside the pond to chat about the price of crops, the weather, or the theft of a goat.
But for more than a month, metaphysics and ethical dilemmas replaced the usual topics. Is it permissible to use deceit to defeat an evil enemy? Is a lie justified to save a life? What is the nature of reality?
The debating tournament was the brainchild of Abhishek Pandey, district magistrate of Pratapgarh district in Uttar Pradesh. When he took up the post two years ago, he knew the area was rich in archaeological treasures connected to the ancient Indian epic, the Mahabharata.
Throughout the text, Yudhishthira, one of the central characters, debates the nature of human existence. In Ajgara he answers a string of philosophical questions to save the lives of his four brothers.
Pandey, 35, like most Indians, grew up on this story and was proud of the intellectual depth of the dialogues. When he attended Oxford University on a fellowship, he admired the debating society, which has a 200-year-long history. But India’s tradition of sophisticated public debate is much older, going back more than 3,000 years.
Pandey started to question why the tradition had not survived. “Indians have celebrated certain traditions for centuries,” Pandey says. “Why have we ceased to celebrate the legacy of debate and questioning?” Was it possible to revive this noble tradition, particularly when it was a vital component of a democracy?
He decided that the annual fair held in Ajgara in September would be a good time to stage the event. In the run-up to the fair, Pandey and his team arranged 1,500 debates across the district.
Age and education were no bar. The youngest participant was a 10-year-old schoolboy, the oldest an 80-year-old farmer. In debating for and against a motion, participants were judged on reasoning and moral clarity.
The overwhelming public response dumbfounded Pandey. Thousands of people participated in multiple rounds, and were whittled down to eight finalists – two women and six men.
While villagers milled around, enjoying the food, watching folk theatre, buying local crafts and taking a ride on a ferris wheel, a silence descended inside the debating tent.
The finale of the Great Ajgara Debate 2026 on 17 September lasted about six hours.
One topic was women’s rights. A finalist, Vivek Singh, argued that women might have equality on paper but society’s expectations of them impeded the exercise of these rights.
Another, Prajjwal Shukla, 24, argued that the real question was not what role society assigned to women but who had the authority to make those choices. Whether a woman chose a career, household responsibilities, or both, should be her choice and hers alone, he said.
“What amazed me the most was not the intellectual quality of the debates (which was great), but the atmosphere. Everyone listened respectfully, patiently, without interrupting. No one got personal. People sat for hours,” says Pandey.
Marx’s adage that history repeats itself, first as tragedy and then as farce, is a perfect description of how debate in India has descended from the sublime to the farcical.
In television studio debates everyone shouts at the same time. No one can finish a point. Personal abuse and gibes fly while the anchor whips them into ever greater frenzies.
Sadhana Dwivedi, one of the two women to progress into the last round of the Great Ajgara Debate, despises this new format.
“People need to learn to listen, to understand there may be value in another person’s point of view,” she says. “In a democracy, it is crucial for all opinions to be aired so that we can get to the truth.”
The turnout was a good demonstration of the thesis posited in economist Amartya Sen’s book The Argumentative Indian that India had a rich tradition of questioning authority and entertaining heterodoxy.
It is only in recent years that dissent has been suppressed, notably by the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party, which values conformity.
“It’s ironic, because the BJP wants to recreate a Hindu state but is not even acquainted with the traditions of ancient Hindu civilisation, such as that of debate and being open to different ideas,” says author and commentator Parsa Venkateshwar Rao Jnr.
At the end of the tournament, the eight finalists were garlanded and driven around in an open-top car to much cheering, feted as “intellectual heroes”. The winner was Shukla, who is preparing to sit exams to enter the civil service.
“I can’t believe I am the winner of a debate that took place at the exact same spot as in the Mahabharata all those centuries ago. I participated just because I wanted to hear other people’s thoughts,” he says.
Pandey is still processing the public enthusiasm. “My deputy asked me if we should get some police deployment because the turnout everywhere was so big, but I laughed and said no. That would be a sad affair.”
He hopes to spread the event across other Indian states and perhaps nationwide. “We have to inculcate a culture of debate. It’s the hallmark of a democracy.”
Meanwhile, he has planted his flag. The inscription on the stone slab he has installed at the site reads: “The Great Ajgara Debate. First Debate 3152 BC: Yudhishthira. Second Debate 2026: Prajjwal Shukla.”

It’s a quirk of the release calendar that when Vivo’s X Fold 6 launched in China this June, it was just another foldable. Now that it’s ready for its global release, the size and aspect ratio feel oddly old-fashioned.
Vivo’s X Fold 6 accidentally feels like a throwback

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with claims that it allegedly shows the Chief of the Army Staff, General Dhiraj Seth, dancing with Supreet Sapra, described as the wife of an Army major. The video features a purported CNN headline stating, “Indian Army Chief Dhiraj Seth Spotted Dancing with Army Major’s wife Supreet Sapra,” giving the impression that CNN published the video. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth dancing with Supreet Sapra, the wife of an Army major.
Fact: The video has been digitally manipulated to make it appear as though Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth is dancing with Supreet Sapra. CNN has not published any report or headline matching the one shown in the viral video. The original video, shared in March 2026, features a different man and woman dancing at a gathering. Supreet Sapra has also clarified that she is not an Army major’s wife and that the woman shown in the viral video is AI-generated. The Indian Army’s fact-check wing has also confirmed that the video is digitally manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but found no credible reports carrying the viral footage on CNN’s official website or any report or headline matching the one circulating with the video.
Upon closely reviewing the viral video, we noticed several inconsistencies. Though the man and woman appear to be dancing while holding glasses, the liquid inside them does not move or splash naturally as they dance. In one frame, the man’s ear and cheek area also appear smudged, while the faces of people in the background appear heavily blurred. The man’s face remains almost completely frozen with a wide smile throughout the video, further raising signs of AI manipulation.
We then ran the video through multiple AI detection tools, including DetectVideo AI and Meta AI’s verification platform. Both assessed the clip as likely AI-generated and detected AI signatures in the video.
The viral video contains an inset photograph showing a woman with a different man wearing a defence uniform. To learn more about the photograph, we conducted a reverse image search, which led us to an Instagram post (archived) by @sufimeranaam, dated 22 February 2026, featuring the same image. Newschecker contacted the account user regarding the viral video. She identified herself as Supreet Sapra and said, “I am Supreet Sapra, but I am not a major’s wife. My husband retired four years ago. The woman in the video is AI-generated, so apart from the name, everything is misinformation.”
Further investigation led us to an Instagram post (archived) by Rhythm Gupta, shared on 11 March 2026, with the caption, “Always dancing weirdly.” The video features a man and a woman dancing at a gathering. Their dance movements, the way they hold their glasses, and the song playing in the background are the same as those in the viral video. Although the background differs in colour and certain visual details, the overall setting and arrangement of elements are similar, and the movements of people around the dancing pair also closely resemble. This indicates that the viral video was likely manipulated using the earlier footage to make it appear as though the Army Staff chief was dancing with an Army major’s wife. Comparison of screengrabs from the viral clip and the Instagram video can be seen below.
The Indian Army’s fact-checking wing also clarified in an X post (archived) on 29 September 2026 that the viral video is digitally manipulated and fake.
To sum up, this viral video of Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth dancing with Supreet Sapra, the wife of an Army major, is AI-manipulated.

South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
- Published
South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself.
"Is he talking about us?", Roelf Meyer remembers thinking, when he first heard President Trump say it.
His response to the US president's claim is blunt.
The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so.
Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule known as apartheid in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April, after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa plummeted.
In an interview with the BBC, Meyer said the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and he never got a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
Since last year, nearly 13,000 refugees were admitted to the United States and all but three were South African.
Among them was Lielie, the name she uses publicly, who moved with her family to Texas from South Africa, where they had lived on her stepfather's farm, growing macadamia nuts and bananas.
Despite walls around the house, an electric fence, and eight bull terriers, she said she felt "fear the whole time" and that on three occasions she saw people entering her property.
"Nothing was stolen, we weren't harmed, but there are friends of my husband, people that lived around us, they were brutally attacked," she said.
She said since moving to the US under the Trump administration's refugee pathway her life had changed, she felt safer walking around, and "my kids can actually play outside".
The Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.
In a statement to the BBC, a White House spokeswoman said: "President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed and driven off their property across South Africa.
"While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart."
SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, has been trying to move to the US under the new scheme.
Du Venage is a council member of the Freedom Front Plus, a right-wing Afrikaner party, and argues that there is a "political drive towards killing white people, and killing the farmers on the farms".
"There's absolutely an agenda to wipe us out here," he says.

An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks".
Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners.
"I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind."
Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy" to speak about the subject.
The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party.
He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner".
"But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says.
Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue.
Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country.
While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution".
Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home".
He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing.
The programme has its critics among Afrikaners in South Africa too.
"Why single out the white Afrikaner to say this group qualifies to flee to the US? This country suffers gender-based violence. Why not single out women?" Rudi Swanepoel, a pastor from Johannesburg told the BBC.
Swanepoel thinks it is not persecution but a "loss of privilege" that is causing some Afrikaners to feel aggrieved.
"To use the metaphor of a cake, 30, 40 years ago the white people of South Africa controlled the cake," he says. "Since democracy came, the obvious reality was we had to now start sharing that cake and those privileges."
Alongside "rural safety", the Trump administration has raised other concerns about South Africa, including targets for companies to increase non-white employment and a law allowing the state, in exceptional circumstances, to expropriate land without compensation. These are aimed at redressing historic racial inequality.
Meyer wants Trump's executive order against South Africa, which underpins the refugee pathway, revoked.
He said South Africa had never prevented people from leaving and had addressed all the US concerns, stressing that the land expropriation law is awaiting a court judgement.
"South Africa has challenges with the prevention of crime and with the combatting of crime," he said.
But he added: "It's a problem all around. It's not rural. It's not farm attacks only. If you look at the total picture, the huge levels of crime in the black townships of South Africa are the biggest concern, proportionally, far more than anything else."
He said he would encourage the US to help South Africa with resources on combatting crime, including by providing equipment to speed up reaction times.
Meyer also has a message for Afrikaners protesting against "farm attacks" by laying white crosses in Washington.
"It doesn't help us to raise a voice outside, if we are not committed to doing something inside the country," he says.

Overnight, Meta deleted all her accounts. AI customer service won’t let her reach a human
It's part of a trend that experts say won't end until regulation is introduced
When she woke up in the middle of the night last Thursday, Jasmine Ault went to check her phone like she usually would.
But she didn’t expect to see a notification telling her that her Instagram and Facebook account had been permanently disabled by Meta.
It was only the start of an odyssey of frustration and anxiety spanning multiple days as Ault struggled to get to the bottom of how 20 years of personal data and professional contacts had been taken from her overnight — all while being stonewalled by AI customer service with no option to reach a human being, even after paying extra.
“It feels like I've lost everything in a metaphorical fire with my digital albums and my digital memories,” Ault, who lives in Toronto, told CBC News. “And who's going to protect those if I can only speak to AI?”
Ault is only the latest victim in a pattern growing increasingly common over the past two years. Numerous Canadians have reported their Meta accounts being abruptly wiped, leaving them stuck interfacing with AI chatbots unable to grasp the complexities of their situation.
One Canadian lost 18 years of data on Facebook after posting photos from a family trip, and had a second account banned when she tried to return. Others lost accounts vital to advertising their businesses. Many believe their accounts were incorrectly flagged by Meta’s AI moderation, and while some have had accounts restored after reaching out to media, others have never had them restored.
Meta has not responded to a request for comment from CBC News.
It comes at a time when companies are increasingly adopting AI in customer service, despite data showing customers aren’t on board.
Lack of empathy frustrating to customers
A global survey released earlier this year of more than 34,000 customers, service representatives and executives found that half of customers surveyed reported a lack of empathy as their biggest frustration with AI customer service.
And while 87 per cent of customers ranked phone calls as a preferred customer service channel, the survey found only seven per cent of executives plan to prioritize them. The research, commissioned by software company ServiceNow in partnership with research firm ThoughtLab, included 1,350 customers and 195 executives in Canada.
- AI agents lag far behind human workers. Why are tech companies laying off the humans?
- As more teens turn to AI for emotional support, experts say it's no substitute for human connection
Ela Veresiu, associate professor of marketing at the Schulich School of Business at York University, explained that companies are buying into AI en masse despite the backlash because of the promise of efficiency and lower costs.
“It is a lot cheaper to have an AI that responds to customer service queries than to hire people that can potentially respond, or be available to respond, 24/7,” she told CBC News.
But while an AI chatbot is able to direct customers to existing information, such as a business’s hours of operation, they can’t handle complex “why” questions, she said, and it can create huge problems.
If a company has competitors, customers frustrated with poor AI rollout can take their business elsewhere, potentially leading businesses to change strategies. But for singularly massive social media companies like Meta, which offer unique services, there’s no business incentive to change their policies.
“Customers may grumble and be dissatisfied by the overreliance of AI and customer service, but ultimately, they have no choice in the marketplace,” Veresiu explained.
‘It’s people’s lifelines’
Ault started her Facebook account in 2006, the first year it was public. After she received the news that her Instagram, Facebook and even a linked Instagram for her dog had all been deactivated, Ault says she stayed up for the next 26 hours straight, desperately trying to appeal the decision.
Screenshots she shared with CBC News stated that her accounts were disabled because her Facebook “doesn’t follow our rules,” but Ault said she was never told what rules her Facebook allegedly broke.
Ault believes her Facebook had been recently hacked, and that this may have caused her accounts to be flagged. But within minutes of pressing the appeal button, she was told her case was closed and she would not be permitted to appeal again, without giving her the opportunity to plead her case.
She created a backup Instagram account and paid for Meta Verification under the impression that it would allow her to reach a human support agent. Meta’s Verification program has various paid tiers with perks such as enhanced support. Standard, the option Ault went for, costs $14.99 US (roughly $21 Cdn).
But the enhanced support she received was simply another AI chatbot, which swiftly told her the ticket was being closed, and that she had reached her limit of support interactions.
- Hamilton woman says cooking business erased 'from existence' after Instagram account shut down by Meta
- 'It's sheer panic': Ottawa restaurateur says Meta wrongly banned her business accounts
- Meta suspended his business's social accounts — it took him a month to reach a human
CBC News has reached out to Meta, but the company has not responded to questions about Ault’s account and whether access to a human customer service agent — once a staple of all customer service interactions — is now only accessible at a high monthly cost. Of Meta’s verification tiers, only Premium and Max, which have a monthly fee of $150 US and $500 US respectively, mention the ability to “request a call from an agent.”
“It, to me, feels like Meta is trying to cut corners by not paying a human, when they're worth billions and billions of dollars,” Ault said. “And it feels almost sick to me that they just think, like, 'We can just shut these people's accounts down, they can't get through to us and talk to us,' and it's people's lifelines. It's people's memories. It's people's everything."
She added that since she used social media to provide marketing to clients for her side business, she’s now losing out on those financial opportunities and connections.
Jon Festinger, a lecturer at the Peter A. Allard School of Law at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, said Canadians may have legal recourse to challenge account deletion in court by arguing damages that demand a remedy, particularly if they used their social media for business purposes.
“It should be relatively easy to prove the damages, at least the reputational damage, and perhaps more,” he said.
Canadian courts have made some steps toward dealing with AI chatbots — Air Canada was found liable for its chatbot’s hallucinated advice to a customer in 2024, for instance — but there are still gaps in Canadian consumer law when it comes to customer rights and AI, he said.
Regulation needed now, experts say
That’s where experts believe regulation should come in.
"Any technical solution makes mistakes," Shion Guha, an assistant professor at the University of Toronto and director of the Human-Centered Data Science Lab, told CBC News. "What it's really about is that people lack a way to get the mistake fixed."
Companies must be required to provide a clear pathway to a human agent and a fair appeals process, especially if automated systems are being used to moderate social media, he said.

- Is AI evolving too fast? A look at the debate on slowing it down
“Literally in every other facet of our life, if we are appealing ... a potentially unfair decision, we reach a human being,” he added, giving the example of speeding tickets and tax appeals.
“People expect that that will transpose to private social media platforms, and it doesn't because … they're not required to, because there's no regulatory framework in place for that.”
An existing model is the EU’s Digital Services Act, which was implemented in 2024 to update rules for online services, including guaranteeing transparency and a full appeal process when content is removed.
New legislation around AI chatbots in Canada was introduced in June, but it focuses on increasing safety requirements to protect children online, not consumer rights.
CBC News has not yet received a response from AI Minister Evan Solomon’s office to questions on whether upcoming legislation will ensure Canadians have the right to access a human customer service agent during appeals processes.
In the meantime, Canadians like Ault have their digital footprints hanging in the balance, hoping that the thousands of photos, conversations and memories lost to their disabled accounts might one day be restored.

Mumbai, October 1, 2026: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is set to stage a protest in Mumbai on October 2, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and raising a series of other demands concerning the Election Commission of India (ECI). CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke will lead the demonstration.
The protest comes after reports of alleged differences within the Election Commission prompted criticism from the Opposition and calls for Kumar’s resignation.
The CJP has alleged that the poll body has not been functioning in the country’s interest under Kumar. The Election Commission, however, has rejected suggestions of an internal breakdown and maintained that its decisions had the approval of all three commissioners.
Three Demands At The Heart Of Protest
Dipke, along with CJP members Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, outlined three demands at a press conference on September 25. Apart from Kumar’s resignation, the party has sought the initiation of criminal proceedings against him.
The CJP has also demanded that the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) be frozen and the January 2025 voter list restored. Its third demand is the repeal of the 2023 law and reforms to the Election Commission.
The demands show that the planned protest goes beyond seeking the removal of one official. By raising questions over the voter list revision and seeking changes to the Election Commission, the CJP is attempting to broaden the agitation into a larger debate over the functioning of the poll body. At the same time, the Election Commission’s rejection of claims of internal discord puts the two sides’ positions sharply at odds.
No Permission, But CJP Plans To March On
Mumbai Police has denied the CJP permission to hold the October 2 protest at Shivaji Park. The party, however, has said it will go ahead with the demonstration.
Police said they were “not empowered to grant permission” for gatherings at Shivaji Park in accordance with a 2013 Bombay High Court order. They also cited rules governing gatherings as well as traffic and noise concerns.
Dipke alleged that the denial was an attempt to suppress citizens’ voices. In a post on X, he warned that the CJP would launch a “Jail Bharo Andolan” if it was denied the right to protest.
“Mumbai Police has also denied permission for our protest on 2nd October. Such tactics to suppress citizens’ voices are unacceptable. If we are denied the right to protest, CJP will launch a Jail Bharo Andolan in Mumbai on Gandhi Jayanti,” Dipke said.
Protest Plans Extend Beyond Mumbai
A CJP spokesperson said the first protest would be held at Gate No. 6 near Shivaji Park. Similar demonstrations are planned in Bengaluru, Goa, Kolkata, Patna and Ranchi.
“By the end of October, the protest movement will reach the national level,” the spokesperson said at the press conference.

Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit
- Published
US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age".
The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry.
The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity.
Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House.
1. AI 'self-regulation' pact
Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting.
The president said the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.
Under the agreement, which Trump posted online, external, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.
The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues.
They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."
The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said, referring to the agreement. "And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president."
Trump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board.
Zuckerberg said the accord gives the "American people and customers the confidence that the technology works" as intended, calling the meeting a "historic conversation".
Amodei called it was a way "to win safely", referring to the president's comment earlier this month that "whoever wins AI, wins".
But not all experts are impressed with the accord.
Nanyang Technological University AI governance researcher Jose Miguelito Enriquez said the pact shows "emerging consensus" but does not address whether AI developers should be held accountable for incidents.
It is "deeply unimpressive" and comes despite calls from some world leaders and industry figures for tighter regulations over the technology, said law professor Kimberlee Weatherall from the University of Sydney.
The agreement appears to allow firms to "define what counts as safety" and does not state what consequences there are to any breaches, Weatherall said.
"The accord should be ignored, for the distraction it is," she added.
- Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings 
  - Published16 September
- Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? 
  - Published17 September
Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks, even as major AI firms have called for tighter oversight over the technology.
On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns.
The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation.
Jeannie Paterson from the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne said self-regulation could mean that companies set "only minimal safeguards".
The agreement inspires "very little confidence" as recent incidents of AI going rogue suggest companies have been undisciplined in their approach, she added.
2. Doubling down on data centres
Trump also reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centres - the crucial computing infrastructure that powers AI.
The rollout of data centres has drawn pushback around the country over concerns about electricity usage and their potential impact on from communities.
Data centre construction has also emerged as a potential political obstacle for Trump's Republican party ahead of the US midterm elections in November.
A survey conducted by Marist Poll in partnership with NPR and PBS News, external earlier this month found that 65% of registered voters opposed data centres being built in their areas.
Responding to those concerns, Trump said tech companies would work to make people "happy" about the construction of data centres.
"These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities," Trump told reporters.
Trump previously said on social media that the only reason communities should oppose data centres is if they "want to end up being backwards and poor".
Huang from Nvidia, which produces computer chips essential for running AI, said after the meeting that data centres should be called "super intelligence factories".
These facilities are "reindustrialising the United States", creating jobs across the economy, he added.
3. It's now 'Super Intelligence'
Also on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of term artificial intelligence.
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.
"As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence," the order said.
During an address to the United Nations General Assembly last week, Trump said the word "artificial" made the technology "sound fake".
Some tech leaders, including Zuckerberg and Musk, and other people close to the president have already started to use the term.
With tech leaders adopting the term, the US "may well be able to set the nomenclature," Paterson said.
But some experts said after Trump's UN speech that they thought the term was unlikely to gain widespread traction because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems.

When the government officials arrived in Tarluvada last year, they came with abundant promises.
Google, one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech companies, would soon be bringing a “golden opportunity” to this tiny village in south India: a $15bn AI datacentre.
The project, being built in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, is set to be Google’s largest “hyperscale” AI datacentre outside the US and would, officials said, make the village of Tarluvada into a world-famous tech hub. Jobs, usually scarce in this impoverished community, would become bountiful, real estate prices would soar and compensation for any land would be generous.
Few in the village – which sits on a dusty unpaved road and is surrounded by farms and forest – had even heard of AI or knew what a datacentre was. Yet it did not take long for local jubilation over Google’s arrival to turn to suspicion.
Just as protests have erupted globally over AI datacentres – from California and Texas to Scotland and Australia – communities in Andhra Pradesh, too have been gathering in opposition to the project, fearing that the people will end up bearing a crippling environmental and economic cost.
“We have learned that America does not want the problems of datacentres and so now Google is bringing them here,” said Tarluvada’s village head, BRB Naidu, who admitted he was torn about whether the datacentre would bring prosperity or ruin to their community. “Many in the village are very worried. But the government has refused to answer our questions.”
Pointing up to the nearby hillside – where bulldozers recently stripped the land bare of trees to ready it for Google’s mega AI campus – Naidu adds: “The work just continues every day.”
The state government, which is allied with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s party, have been accused of trying to obfuscate the true scale of the vast AI hub being built in Andhra Pradesh, to push the project through at lightening speed and avoid more stringent environmental scrutiny. Google has partnered with the Adani Group, one of India’s largest and most politically powerful conglomerates with a reputation for getting approvals through quickly, to build the project.
Publicly it was announced as a 1GW project – already a larger energy requirement than most AI datacentres. In its response to the Guardian, Google referred to it only as an unspecific “gigawatt scale AI hub”, that was “comparable to other projects”.
But state environmental clearances reveal that permission has been granted for it to be more than double that size – 2.51GW; the power equivalent of two large nuclear reactors at full output. Over a year, it amounts to upwards of 30% of the current energy consumption of the whole of Andhra Pradesh, a state home to more than 55 million people.
Activists fear that meeting the datacentre’s vast energy demands will lead to seismic environmental consequences for the region, including driving up fossil fuel emissions. While Google has pledged to help generate “new, clean energy” to power its AI hub, currently 75% of the country’s electricity grid is run on coal.
The state government argues AI datacentres will be essential to India’s growth and long-term digital competitiveness. According to the government of India’s Economic Survey 2025–26, India generated nearly 20% of the world’s data but hosts only about 3% of global datacentres.
But locals and activists say that building one of the world’s largest AI datacentres in a region of India already struggling with issues over extreme heat, water, land, forests, power shortages and environmental regulation comes at a heavy cost.
Google’s project will in fact encompass three separate datacentres around the state capital of Vizakhapatnam. One other site nearby to Taluvada is a few metres from reserve forest, a drinking water reservoir and a wildlife sanctuary home to endangered species such as leopards.
Despite the AI datacentre’s expansive footprint, the state government issued environmental clearances to Google in just nine days, with no public consultation.
Three petitions challenging the state’s quick approval of the project have now been filed to India’s National Green Tribunal (NGT), the country’s top environmental court. The petitions allege that government’s assessment of the risks to the environment and water supplies were “grossly inadequate, scientifically unrealistic, and misleading”. A public litigation has also been filed in the Andhra Pradesh high court.
“This datacentre will be unprecedented in scale but there was no public hearing and no substantial evaluation of the ecological damage or the economic cost for local communities,” said VS Krishna, an activist with Human Rights Forum, the organisation which filed the NGT cases.
Krishna alleged that their campaign to protest against the datacentre had been met with a deliberate silencing, including videos and social media pages being taken down. The government did not respond to this allegation.
“We just have to look at the protests happening across the world to understand how environmentally catastrophic this will be,” Krishna added.
In Tarluvada, temperatures regularly soar to about 45C during the summer and there are concerns the datacentres – documented emitters of heat – could make this even worse. The mass deforestation required for the project – more than 100 acres, could drive up temperatures even more. In response to the Guardian, Google said the project would have “no expected impact” on the local community.
The strain on water supplies in this already water-stressed area has also been a cause of concern. In similarly water-stressed cities in the US, datacentres have been accused of exacerbating drought while polluting the water supply. Google said this project would use air-cooling instead of water, and would therefore have no impact on local drinking water supplies.
Venkat Surynarayana, 40, a farmer in Tarluvada, said that when officials had initially come to measure land for the datacentre “they never mentioned anything about risks of pollution or water or heat, they didn’t even tell us what the project was.
“We are sick with worry since we learned about the problems a datacentre can bring. This area can not afford to be any hotter. What if this makes our land dry and worthless? What will happen to my crops and my livelihood?”
Surynarayana claimed attempts to get answers from the local administration had been met with police threats and protesters such as himself had been routinely detained. “When we raised our voices, they ignore us and then they shut us down,” he said. “But if this is not stopped, it could be the end of Tarluvada.”
For the state government of Andhra Pradesh, the deal struck with Google to build this vast datacentre on its turf is a source of enormous pride, part of a wider policy to make the state into India’s most advanced and affluent tech hub. “Artificial intelligence is becoming foundational infrastructure for the global economy,” said Sribharat Mathukumilli, a local MP with the ruling state government, who rejected the environmental concerns.
The subsidies and incentives they offered to Google, from decades-long tax breaks and discounted land to access to cheap electricity and water, are estimated to amount to 220bn rupees ($2.2bn) over 20 years.
“Our objective is not simply to host a datacentre, but to create an AI and digital ecosystem,” said Mathukumilli. Late last year, the state granted permission for another 1GW AI datacentre, to be built by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries.
Google insisted the design choices of its AI datacentre have been tailored to local conditions and that it had “engaged deeply” with local communities, claiming it would generate thousands of jobs around Vizakhapatnam.
But swathes of villagers in Tarluvada allege they were forced to give up land for the project against their will, and say they have not been given all they were promised in return.
“No one will tell us the truth about this project,” said T Applaraju, 40, who was one of the 520 local families in Tarluvada who recently had land taken back that the government had allocated to him 20 years ago. He claims he was given no notice that his land was to be taken until April this year, when security guards working for the Adani Group erected fences and blocked locals from entering the plots they had farmed for years.
“They took land that we thought belonged to us, it’s a big shock,” he said. “Why are Google building this here and not in America?”
The state government claims no lands were forcibly taken and that it gave “generous compensation” to those who were eligible. The Adani group says that all necessary legal approvals were given. But many of the 47 farmers from the impoverished Dalit community who were compensated for their land are also unhappy.
One farmer, P Venkat Rao, alleged he was pressured by the government into giving up his only acre of land against his will. He received $40,000 in compensation, but said the government’s promise to give them a replacement piece of land and one job per family had not materialised. Without land to farm, Rao described the compensation as “worthless”.
“I am a farmer, without my land I am nothing,” he added. “They have taken my livelihood and broken their promises.”

George Russell is hopeful Mercedes' long-awaited car upgrade at the Bahrain Grand Prix will further help his performances as he bids to build on his return to winning ways from Azerbaijan last week.
Russell dominated the Baku event to not only secure his first win in seven races but also claim the maiden 'Grand Slam' of his Formula 1 career, meaning he led every lap from pole position and set the fastest lap.
The Briton had been happier with his performances in Mercedes' W17 since the August summer break, yet he had still finished behind title-leading team-mate Kimi Antonelli in each of the previous three races, with Antonelli extending his championship advantage to 81 points after victory in Madrid.

But after reducing that deficit by 15 points last Saturday on a weekend that Antonelli finished only fifth after crashing in qualifying, Russell is feeling optimistic as he goes in search of the first back-to-back wins of his F1 career on the sport's return to Malaysia's Sepang International Circuit - a track neither of the title contenders have driven on before.
"As I've really said this whole season, firstly I never really felt in a position to fight for the victories because I didn't feel that the performances were strong enough," replied Russell when asked if another win could sow some doubts in Antonelli's mind.

"It's definitely been a conscious adjustment of my driving," he explained.
"I think I went through a few races when I was having to think how to make those adjustment, whereas now it's all a bit more intuitive and natural.
"What I set out to achieve in terms of getting the car in a slightly better window, I'm now achieving without having to think about it as much, so I can just focus on driving fast."
Russell reiterated that all the pressure was on Antonelli in the chase for the Drivers' Championship over the closing two months of the season.
"For sure there's a lot of pressure in his position," added Russell.
"For any driver fighting for your world championship there's a lot of pressure. At this point of the season it is his to lose so, from my side, I'm just going to go out there and enjoy every race."
'My grandmother went back home!' - Antonelli hopes to learn from Baku lessons
Despite finishing only fifth at the last race, Antonelli remains in firm control of the world championship with his 66-point lead still the joint-second highest he has held this season.
But the 20-year-old Italian said that the events of last week had taught him some valuable lessons.
"Last weekend was probably the worst weekend from me, from my side, of the season," said Antonelli.
"But still very good learning from the weekend. I needed a clean result after a very disrupted weekend.
"But after the race I wasn't happy with the result but I learned many things and the most important learning is I need to always be 100 per cent and I really do my best to achieve the best result.
"If I don't try to do everything right in my power than nothing is going to come my way."
And having joked that he had driven like his grandmother, Antonelli quipped on Thursday: "My grandmother went back home! I booked her a flight and she's back in Italy!"
On Russell, Antonelli added: "He did an incredible weekend in Baku and he's got the momentum.
George has been doing great, especially last weekend, so it's going to be a tough challenge but I'm looking forward to it."
What are Mercedes expecting from Malaysia car upgrade?
Russell and Antonelli's prospects of winning on Sunday are set to be boosted by the introduction of an upgrade package for the W17, Mercedes' first significant update since the Canadian Grand Prix in late May.
"It's a good step," said Russell. "We think it's a good step purely because it's been so long since we last brought some upgrades.
"It's quite abnormal to have an upgrade back in May and then only again in October.
"So, as an individual upgrade step it's large, but in a normal season it's just the normal trajectory you would expect from a May to October upgrade package.

Mercedes have won the last three races to extend their lead over Ferrari at the top of the Constructors' Championship to 160 points. "I think we have a very efficient car on the circuits that are lower drag, so in Azerbaijan, Monza we were very competitive. Red Bull were also on the podium in Monza as well as in Azerbaijan," added Russell.
"I expect Malaysia to be slightly more closer to the circuits of Madrid, Budapest, Zandvoort, where we saw likes of Ferrari and McLaren competing strongly, so that's going to be an interesting one."
Antonelli is also keen to see how the aerodynamic changes will help the team on a track where medium-high-speed cornering is a crucial part of the lap.
"I think this weekend is the right one to bring it," he said.
"Our car is very efficient. It's not draggy, especially on tracks like Monza, Baku, where we were very quick because it's new tarmac, short corners.
"Whilst I think in these type of tracks without the upgrade we would struggle. For example, Zandvoort McLaren was very quick and Zandvoort has very open tarmac. So I think this race was the right one to bring the upgrades and see if we can improve on these kind of tracks with long corners and very old tarmac."

Jaissle learned a lot about life after tumour aged five
- Published
Matthias Jaissle points to his neck.
"I had a tumour when I was five years old," the Newcastle United head coach says. "Here in my neck so I couldn't move it anymore.
"That was a period where I already learned a lot about life, how important it is to be healthy, and how grateful you can be to be healthy and to follow your dream.
"It was not clear that I could play football as a kid anymore."
He did not elaborate further, but such perspective would be needed.
Jaissle, like so many, visualised one day becoming a professional footballer, but he was among the rare few to actually go on to do so.
The former Hoffenheim defender even felt he was on the verge of a senior call up to the German national team at one stage, only to suffer a serious knee injury.
He was just 20 at the time.
Jaissle refused to give up, and "kept the dream for a lot longer than the doctors did", but the setback ultimately curtailed his career and he retired a few years later in 2014.
It left him in a dark place, as he previously detailed in an interview with BBC Sport, but the "wounds" he experienced in life have shaped him.
"That makes you the person you are, whatever aspect it is, with the belief you can overcome every obstacle," he says.
"Every setback also has a positive side. If you overcome these challenges then you become stronger, more resilient."
'I felt joy back in life'
This outlook gave Jaissle a head start in his second career, but he did not necessarily plan on being a coach. Not at first.
Ralf Rangnick, his former manager at Hoffenheim, invited him on to a training programme at RB Leipzig, where his mentor was working at the time, to sample life behind the scenes at the club.
Jaissle was due to be redeployed in a new department every six weeks and started his placement as an assistant youth team coach to ex team-mate Sebastien Hoeness, who now manages Stuttgart.
He was pencilled in to spend time with the club's sporting director and figures from their administrative, commercial and marketing departments.
But he never ended up doing so.
"I didn't move on," Jaissle says. "After two weeks, wow, I felt joy back in life."
It set Jaissle on the path to Newcastle. He climbed the coaching ladder and won trophies at Austrian side Red Bull Salzburg and Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli.
Players and staff alike were quickly struck by his intensity and work rate.
"Since the first meeting, it was clear this was our guy," a senior Newcastle source says.
'I really love the fans and the people here'
It was still a baptism of fire for the 38-year-old, who had never previously managed in the Premier League, after predecessor Eddie Howe stepped down.
Jaissle insists friend Thomas Tuchel "didn't need to warn" him about what was coming in the top flight, but he had just three weeks to prepare for the visit of Liverpool on the opening weekend and the squad was in flux.
Captain Bruno Guimaraes was about to follow Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali out of the exit door and complete a £75m move to Arsenal at the time.
Although Newcastle would end up making eight signings, they were all aged 24 and under as the club went from having one of the most experienced sides in the Premier League to the youngest almost overnight.
It was a huge amount of change in a short space of time.
There have also been a spate of injuries to key players, but Jaissle has only lost one of his opening seven matches in all competitions, a chastening 4-1 defeat at Leeds United.
"I think there were elements in games where we saw a lot of the things we were looking for," he says. "There were also phases in games where we were not happy and satisfied, so there's still a lot of potential that we can improve."
Jaissle accepts it has been "tougher than expected" to "get stuff into the players' heads" given pre-season was "so short and packed with friendly matches we couldn't change", adding "but considering all these things, we're doing good".
He remains convinced that his aggressive style of play and so-called vertical football will "work anywhere", even if this team is clearly still a work in progress at such an early stage of his reign.
Newcastle have made the most errors leading to shots (12) in the Premier League this season while, at the other end of the field, Jaissle's clinical side have only averaged little more than three efforts on target per match in the top flight.
It feels like there will be ups and downs throughout, given the age of the side, but Jaissle has been struck by the backing of supporters and has quickly settled into life on Tyneside.
He moved out of a hotel into a new home earlier this week and has ventured into the city to sample a handful of restaurants - but only to celebrate wins.
Following the 2-1 victory against Hull City at St James' Park last time out, he even paid for a supporter's birthday meal.
"I really love the fans and the people here," he adds.
