The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.
As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.
The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.
The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently, with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.
Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.
This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.
Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population.
But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
Reuters reported on Saturday that India’s summit would result in a generic joint declaration that would show unity by condemning unilateral war, but was unlikely to name any single country.
Jiang Shixue, vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”.
“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post.
Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group.
China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility.
India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world.
Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency.
“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote.
“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

A father is fighting for life after he fell 80ft while rappelling down an Arizona canyon with his toddler.
The man was rock climbing on a trip to Virgin River Gorge with his family, that included five young children and three women.
The father and the one year-old child were reportedly on the same rope near the Ghost Valley Trailhead when they fell. While the toddler suffered minor injuries his father was found in critical condition when emergency services arrived on the scene.
The child’s mother suffered injuries to her hand as she tried to pull on the rope holding them, Beaver Dam/Littlefield Fire Department Captain Larry Lydon told ABC4.
“On Saturday Beaver Dam Fire Rescue was notified of a fall near the Ghost Valley Trailhead, along the county road,” a statement from the department said. “Initial call notes reported that an adult male and a one-year-old child had sustained an approximately 80-foot fall while rappelling, with the condition of both patients initially unknown.
“Upon reaching the patients, responders determined there was one critical adult patient and one pediatric patient who was not injured.Crews and assisting agencies worked for approximately three hours to complete the extrication from the remote location.”
The fire department has released images from the rescue effort, showing a helicopter and an ambulance on the scene.
The Mohave County Sheriff’s Office Search and Rescue team and Washington County Sheriff’s Office - Utah also provided support, with the latter sending its technical rope team.
The unnamed fathe was rushed to a nearby hospital. Asked for comment about the father’s condition by People, a spokesperson for the local sheriff’s department said that they had not yet received an update.
On social media, the fire department warned thrillseekers to be careful while rappelling.
“Please use extreme caution when recreating in remote areas, and always consider the risks associated with rappelling and other outdoor activities,” the department said in a statement.
Rappelling, also known as abseiling, involves adventurers slowly descending down a rock face while secured by a rope. Arizona is a hub for rappelling due to its rocky terrain, providing a huge wealth of locations well suited for the activity.
The Virgin River Canyon Recreation Area sits between Mesquite and St. George. According to the Bureau of Land Management, the gorge drops around 70 feet per mile - making it around 10 times steeper than the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon.

What happened in failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
- Published
US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in hospital and being given "life-saving measures" after Tennessee authorities failed in their attempt to execute her by lethal injection.
The case of Pike, whose attempted execution had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, has raised a number of questions.
These include what went went wrong, what happens next, and - for opponents of the death penalty - fresh concerns around the suffering of an inmate when an execution does not go to plan.
What happened?
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, an attack that was perpetrated alongside her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp.
She was scheduled to be put to death on Wednesday evening, local time. The injections were allowed by the US Supreme Court at the eleventh hour after the legal battle.
Pike was given two syringes of the drug pentobarbital, though her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring.
- US death row inmate survives execution attempt after two lethal injections 
  - Published3 hours ago
The Tennessee Department of Correction defended the method it used, and said "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening".
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.
Authorities have yet to provide their explanation of why the dosage given to Pike proved to be non-fatal, although medical experts have provided theories of their own.
Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine who told the BBC he had been retained by Pike's legal team as a medical expert, said she probably never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause apnoea and cardiovascular failure.
What happens next?
The state correction department added that Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility.
One of her lawyers said she was "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital.
Her health status is unclear as of Thursday morning.
In his emailed comments to the BBC, Zivot said: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury."
A third-party review has been ordered by the state governor, Bill Lee, who also says the year's last remaining execution will not go ahead as planned.
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who had pushed for Pike's execution to take place, told NBC News the events had been "a mess".
Opponents of the death penalty have similarly been quick to react.
Maya Foa, the chief executive of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "We cannot know exactly what went wrong, because so much happened behind a curtain – lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life."
Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. There is a historical precedent of authorities making a second attempt to execute those on death row.
Meanwhile Shipp, Pike's boyfriend and co-defendant, remains in prison, having been spared the death penalty under state law. He was 17 at the time that Slemmer was killed.
What is the drug pentobarbital?
Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.
Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review - which took place under the presidency of Joe Biden - raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
His government banned its use in federal executions but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
- Why the death penalty is on the rise in US 
  - Published13 August
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded". Drugs may degrade for a number of reasons, including if it has aged beyond its use-by date and its potency has decreased.
The department issued a broader defence of its method, writing in a statement: "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective."
Has this happened before?
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal injection. He was given a one-year reprieve by Governor Bill Lee.
More widely across the US, the issue of botched executions continues to cause alarm.
In 2022, more than a third of executions in the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) - an organisation that provides statistics and research on the death penalty but does not take a stance on it morally.
The DPI says lethal injection has the highest rate of botched executions.
An incident in Oklahoma in 2014 gained particular notoriety. The execution of Clayton Lockett was postponed after 20 minutes because the lethal injection of three drugs failed to work properly when one of his veins ruptured, and he went on to writhe and shake uncontrollably.
In the US, 27 of the 50 states have the death penalty under state law. The federal government can also carry out executions after President Donald Trump, a supporter of capital punishment, ended a moratorium last year, However, it is yet to actually carry out any executions since then.

Singapore launches matchmaking service for government workers
- Published
Singapore has rolled out a matchmaking service for its government workers, an initiative that comes as the country wrestles with a record-low fertility rate.
FirstDate, which launched this week for those aged 21 to 35, boasts "a different approach to dating", where it uses a Nobel-winning algorithm to match participants to one date at a time. "Swipe fatigue ends here," its website reads.
Participants sign in using the national digital identity system and answer a survey about their interests, habits and values.
FirstDate's launch drew mixed responses among Singaporeans, with some describing it as "dystopian" and others saying they would be keen to give it a shot.
On its website, FirstDate highlights the Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage algorithm which powers the programme.
The mathematical framework pairs two equally sized groups of people based on their preferences.
The late mathematician Lloyd Shapley was awarded the 2012 Nobel memorial prize in economic sciences for discovering the algorithm, which has been used in public school admissions, medical residency matching, and dating apps, among other things.
"At the end of the day, I think the experience of meeting someone through an application doesn't change much across the [different types of] applications," Elizabeth, a 29-year-old who works in Singapore's defence ministry and is keen on trying FirstDate out told the BBC.
"But it is nice to know that the likelihood of being scammed is much lower. We're all public servants looking for a partner, right?"
But some social media users say the initiative, which is currently in its pilot phase, discriminates against those not working in government.
Others criticised the age limit. "They are only doing this to raise the total fertility rate. They don't actually [care] about whether we find a partner otherwise.
"Since there are higher risks involved in having kids at 35 and older, the government just writes [the older singles] off," wrote another Reddit user.
It is not clear if the pilot programme will be available to the wider public in future. The BBC has reached out to GovTech, the statutory board behind the pilot, for comment.
The pilot launch comes as Singapore's birth rate has slumped to historic lows. For the first time in the past 60 years, fewer than 30,000 babies were born in 2025.
The number of deaths meanwhile have been rising steadily in the greying nation, hitting about 26,500 in 2025.
In August, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a series of new measures to better support families and to encourage couples to have children, including almost S$70,000 ($54,000; £41,000) in financial support for every child by the time they turn 17.
FirstDate is not the first time the citystate is trying to play Cupid to its citizens.
In 1984, it set up the Social Development Unit (SDU) tasked with organising social events to encourage graduate singles to mingle.
Its exclusive target audience of university graduates was criticised as being elitist, but authorities justified the approach saying non-graduates did not seem to have difficulty finding partners. The SDU was eventually phased out.
The next year, the government set up another agency to promote marriages among non-graduates.
The idea of a government-run dating service is not unique to Singapore. In September 2024, Tokyo's metropolitan government launched an AI-powered dating app in an effort to combat the country's declining birth rate.
The app, which is open to single residents in the city, resulted in 265 couples getting married, according to government data released in July this year.
Additional reporting by Osmond Chia in Singapore

On Tuesday, executives for Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI, and Nvidia all signed “The White House Accord on Super Intelligence,” which was announced following a luncheon held by President Donald Trump.
The effort was an act of “tremendous self-regulation,” as Trump put it, but the agreement is not the sweeping AI regulation that people inside the companies themselves have been asking for. And while failing to honor these public commitments could count as illegally lying to consumers, even that wouldn’t be enough to trigger massive reforms.
The statement says that companies “should implement” several things: First, they should ensure they have “robust internal controls” to monitor their models’ capabilities and ability to not go rogue or hack things in unintended ways. Second, they should “empower” an internal team to do that work (and remediate when things go wrong). Third, it encourages them to partner with an external monitor who is “empowered” to do independent assessments to make sure that all of that work is happening. And finally, they should make sure their board of directors has set up a committee to receive reports about all of these efforts.
The voluntary commitments are some indication that the frontier labs are making an effort to figure out how to make products that are safe for the general public. However, if there were any hopes for a blanket blessing from the US government, those were quickly dashed after news broke that the Federal Trade Commission intends to investigate several AI companies over potential consumer protection issues.
The statement is the culmination of weeks of debate over AI regulation. It also follows frontier AI labs seeking an antitrust exemption so they can coordinate on safety work without regulatory scrutiny. (Notably, antitrust experts and practitioners say such an exemption is unneeded because AI ending humanity—which researchers have warned will come about if nothing is done—is arguably anti-competitive because humans are an essential part of any given marketplace.)
There’s been a lot of build-up to this particular statement, but this is not the first time that these companies have signed a voluntary agreement about their AI safety practices with a government. In early 2025, the United Kingdom and the Republic of Korea announced a set of “Frontier AI Safety Commitments,” which included promises about doing internal and external red-teaming of AI models for “severe and novel threats” and also “to work toward information sharing” on AI safety issues.
Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment. The White House also did not immediately respond.
Neil Chilson, a former chief technologist for the FTC, posted on X of the accords that “this is the kind of pledge that the FTC could potentially enforce, if a company materially failed to follow through on any of these promises.”
But those hoping for a sweeping settlement and a dramatic reining-in of rogue “super intelligence” based on the accords alone might find themselves disappointed.
(Disclosure: This story’s author previously worked in the Office of Technology at the FTC and resigned in November 2025.)
Not following through on a public promise could be considered a deceptive business practice and a violation of the FTC Act. When the FTC alleges that a company deceived its customers, the remedy it usually prescribes is making the company promise not to lie again.
For example, the FTC recently announced it had settled with three companies after it alleged they were touting a service that could help businesses target ads based on audio recordings collected from smartphones, smart TVs, and other devices. The companies, the agency said, lied to businesses about their ability to creep on consumers. The fix? The companies are no longer allowed to misrepresent their advertising services and the collection and use of consumers’ voice data, among other things. The case does not address whether it’s OK to collect voice data from your phone, and the settlement doesn’t set out any guardrails if one of the three companies wanted to actually do that in the future (other than not lying about it.)
OpenAI has been remarkably open about the number of times its agents have broken into other people’s systems and how it needs to improve its safety practices. But, as experts have pointed out to WIRED, the US government can open investigations into companies even if they eventually decide there’s no enforcement action to bring. (The FTC, for example, reportedly sent a civil investigative demand to OpenAI in 2023, but it’s unclear what came of that.)
Following Tuesday’s AI luncheon with Trump, the New York Post reported that the FTC was planning a “sweeping probe” into Anthropic, OpenAI, other unnamed frontier labs, and a nonprofit called METR that does third-party evaluations. METR and the labs didn’t respond to a request for comment.
The Post says that the agency still hasn’t issued any civil investigative demands to its intended targets—usually one of the first steps in any sort of investigation. An FTC spokesperson confirmed that there is some sort of investigation, but they declined to provide any additional details, including what consumer protection issues were of concern.
FTC chairman Andrew Ferguson, who was included on the “super intelligence” luncheon’s seating chart, has previously explained that enforcers don’t always have a fully baked case from the get-go. “You're constantly looking for smoke to see if there's fire,” he told a crowd of antitrust enthusiasts last year.
Even if the FTC investigation moves forward and the agency does identify violations, some are skeptical that it will result in any action against the AI firms.
“It should be encouraging to Americans worried about AI that the FTC is investigating these companies,” says Douglas Farrar, who was the head of public affairs for the FTC during Lina Khan’s tenure as chair. “But let’s remember that Ferguson may chair the FTC, but Donald Trump runs it, and I doubt after yesterday's love fest with his AI CEO buddies that Trump will allow any legal action with teeth against these companies.”

The security alert issued by MI5 regarding a Chinese state-owned conglomerate accused of conducting espionage in the UK reveals the extent to which British intelligence remains concerned about Beijing’s influence, and risks casting a shadow over UK-China cooperation at a time when the bilateral relationship is enjoying a revival.
The UK’s domestic security service on Wednesday warned researchers and academics to cease work with the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), an organisation MI5 described as a “significant threat”.
The CAGT, which is also known as the China General Technology Research Institute, is accused of paying UK academics working in sensitive fields such as artificial intelligence and cybersecurity for “research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage”. The MSS is China’s Ministry of State Security, its intelligence agency.
China’s approach to intelligence gathering involves hoovering up vast amounts of data, often from unsuspecting individuals who believe they are participating in normal research or consultancy work.
This year the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned businesses about Beijing-backed attempts to hack into everyday devices such as wifi routers.
Last year, MI5 issued another China-related security alert, warning parliamentarians about approaches from two LinkedIn profiles thought to be linked to Chinese intelligence.
Wednesday’s alert said academic institutions or researchers should be aware of the 2023 National Security Act, which makes it an offence to engage in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence agency. The warning is likely to send a chill through the UK’s cash-strapped higher education institutions, which have for years turned to China for funding and collaboration opportunities.
The UK is one of the leading countries to partner with China’s higher education sector. In May, China’s education ministry announced 219 new transnational education partnerships, with more than a fifth of the approvals being with British universities. That puts the UK at the top of the list of partner countries, ahead of Russia, France and Italy.
Chinese students are also the largest group of non-EU international students in the UK, generating about £600m a year for the higher education sector.
There has been growing concern in the UK that partnerships with China pose a risk to national security. The 2023 Intelligence and Security Committee report on China said UK academic institutions “provide a rich feeding ground for China to achieve both political influence and economic advantage” and flagged the risk of China “directing or stealing UK academic research”.
In this case, MI5 said that more than 100 academics linked to the UK had contributed to projects funded by the MSS via the front company. The areas of interest were AI, cybersecurity and steganography, the embedding of hidden data in pictures online.
Sam Goodman, the senior policy director at the China Strategic Risks Institute, said UK academics were “between a rock and a hard place” when trying to navigate areas of advanced interest that could be of interest to Chinese intelligence. “There is a lack of a coherent steer from government on something like AI. It isn’t particularly clear on AI at this juncture what levels of collaboration we can have with the Chinese,” Goodman said.
Analysts say the UK should do more to highlight which areas are of potentially dual-use interest to Chinese intelligence and provide more guidance to universities and academics.
“It’s all very well issuing these warnings,” says Charles Parton, a senior fellow at the Royal United Services Institute. “Actually far more important, surely, is a consideration of which technologies can be cooperated with China, and which can’t.” He said naming specific Chinese companies as a risk would not help UK researchers to do due diligence on every potential partnership. “The Chinese are not stupid. If they want to hide the origin of someone, they’ll do it,” Parton said.
Meia Nouwens, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said more clarity was needed on the UK side to help guide researchers working in sensitive fields.
Nouwens said: “A problem has been that in the past there hasn’t been a great deal of discussion of what areas of research constitute a national security risk. Without understanding the limits are of what the UK seeks to protect, it is impossible to have a conversation about managing risk.”
The MI5 alert specifically accused the CAGT of being a front for China’s intelligence. But any research institution in China is ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist party. “Research institutes that are conducting research on areas of strategic interest for China such as technology will have oversight from the party-state,” Nouwens notes.
That does not mean any collaboration with Chinese educational institutions is inherently dangerous, but it does mean UK academics working in sensitive fields will feel increasingly uneasy about working with a country that has financially underpinned the UK’s higher education sector for decades.

The hardest conversation in cancer care rarely begins with the words, “There is nothing more we can do.” It usually begins much earlier. “Should we tell him?” “Can we try one more treatment?” “Will she lose hope if she knows?”
These questions are asked quietly: in hospital corridors, outside intensive care units, or after doctors have left the room. They are spoken in whispers because families are not simply making medical decisions; they are trying to protect someone they love.
As a palliative medicine physician working alongside oncology teams, I have learned that when treatment is no longer working as expected, families often find themselves facing conversations they never imagined having. The challenge is not only accepting that the disease has changed; it is learning how to talk about what comes next.
The conversations we prepare least for
Modern oncology has transformed countless lives. New drugs, targeted therapies, immunotherapy and better supportive care have helped many people live longer than ever before. Yet an important gap remains.
We prepare families remarkably well for chemotherapy schedules, blood tests and scan reports. We prepare them far less for conversations about uncertainty. What happens if the treatment stops helping? How much should the patient know? When should children be told? How do we decide what matters most now?
These questions do not signal that hope has disappeared. They signal that hope is changing.
A young man I recently cared for had advanced blood cancer and was admitted to the ICU with severe pain. Over the next few days, his greatest distress was not only physical. Watching critically ill patients around him, he became convinced that he would be next. When he finally asked, “Am I going to die?” he was not asking for a statistical answer. He was asking whether someone would help him understand what was happening.
Another family kept asking whether there was “one last option.” As our conversation unfolded, it became clear that they were not asking for another medicine. They wanted enough time to gather siblings from different cities, celebrate one more birthday together, and prepare for conversations they had been postponing. Often, the real question is different from the one being asked aloud.
Weaving honesty and hope
Many families worry that honest conversations will extinguish hope. In reality, compassionate communication does not require choosing between honesty and kindness. Patients frequently sense when their condition is changing, even when nobody says it directly. Silence can sometimes create greater fear than truth because people begin imagining conversations they are not allowed to have.
Good communication means understanding how much information a patient wishes to receive, respecting cultural and family dynamics, and revisiting discussions as situations evolve. It is rarely a single conversation. More often, it is a series of conversations built on trust.
Hope also evolves. Early in illness, hope may mean cure. Later, it may mean attending a daughter’s wedding, spending time at home instead of the hospital, sleeping through the night without pain, or simply being able to share one meaningful conversation with a loved one.
What palliative care adds
One of the biggest misconceptions is that palliative care begins only after treatment ends.
In reality, it works alongside cancer treatment by helping patients manage pain, breathlessness, nausea, anxiety, fatigue and caregiver distress while supporting difficult decision-making. Some of the most meaningful palliative care conversations happen while patients are still receiving active treatment. Instead of asking only, “What is the next treatment?”, we also ask: “What matters most to you?”; “What are you hoping for?” and “What are you worried about?”
These questions often reveal priorities that laboratory values never can.
Here are some conversations families should not delay having with loved ones who have cancer. When facing advanced cancer, especially, these discussions are easier before a crisis occurs: Ask what the patient wants to know about their illness. Discuss goals that matter to them beyond treatment. Talk about symptom control early rather than waiting for unbearable pain. Identify who should make decisions if the patient cannot. Ask for a palliative care consultation early-alongside oncology-not only during the final days.
These conversations are not about giving up. They are about giving families the chance to make decisions with clarity instead of panic.
Care that continues
There is one moment I return to often. A family once told me, after losing someone they loved, “We don’t remember every medicine that was given. We remember that she wasn’t in pain, that we were able to sit together, and that we got to say goodbye.”
Years later, families rarely remember every chemotherapy cycle. They remember whether someone explained what was happening; whether suffering was relieved; whether they felt alone. Perhaps that is the real purpose of these conversations. Not to predict the future; not to remove grief: but to ensure that even when treatment changes, care never does.
(Dr. V. Divya Sai is a palliative medicine specialist at MNJ Institute of Oncology & Regional Cancer Centre, Hyderabad. vdivyasai22@gmail.com)

The first illegal ebikes seized under new laws have been crushed in New South Wales, as a major Sydney hospital has warned of a spike in trauma injuries driven by those riding under the influence.
The NSW government crushed 23 ebikes at a wrecking yard in western Sydney on Thursday, turning them into scrap metal. NSW police are assessing applications for the return of an additional 13 bikes seized during a joint operation with Transport for NSW in the northern beaches in September.
The NSW transport minister, John Graham, told reporters onsite on Thursday “this isn’t a scene from Mad Max. This is where illegal ebikes go to die.”
Graham said tough new laws were necessary “because of some of the bad behaviour we’ve seen … on our state’s streets, on the golf courses in Sydney suburbs, even on the Sydney Harbour Bridge”.
On the same day, St Vincent’s hospital released figures that showed a 22% spike in legal and illegal ebike injuries, with 42% of those injuries triggering a trauma response and the majority being injured while riding under the influence of alcohol or drugs, riding too fast or without a helmet.
It found 361 patients presented to the hospital for ebike injuries between January and July, compared with 296 presentations during the same period last year.
Dr Ed Lewis, acting head of rehabilitation medicine, told reporters injuries included fractures, internal bleeding, as well as the “perforation of certain organs”. He said they often included brain injuries from severe head trauma, “as well as milder knocks, like a concussion, which can still have long-term repercussions for patients”.
Lewis told Guardian Australia that those contemplating riding an ebike home while intoxicated “need to have a plan B or a backup solution”.
“The message that we want to say to people is: enjoy using ebikes, but respect what they are. Respect that they are fast. Wear a helmet and just don’t ride impaired.”
Graham said the government was concerned by the number of injuries, but it was “important to keep it in context”.
“The number of ebike injuries is still low compared to cars … but is rising,” he said. “If you’re not wearing a helmet, you are dicing with danger.”
He stepped aside to allow a giant metal claw pick up a tangle of ebikes, cracking frames in half and popping tyres. They were loaded into a conveyor belt before being crushed and shredded. Graham said batteries had been removed for safe disposal and recycling beforehand.
Under powers which came into effect in August, police and transport officers can seize bikes not restricted to 25km/h, whose maximum speed while not pedalling does not exceed 6km/h, and maximum continuous power of 500 watts, due to reduce to 250 watts in March 2029.
The government says the bikes crushed include one capable of speeds of more than 90km/h seized from a 14-year-old, a food delivery bike, and bikes with speed restriction settings that had been tampered with.
The 36 ebikes seized so far represent a fraction of the estimated 760,000 in the state. The changes were prompted by a surge in injuries and high-profile incidents, including one in which about 40 ebikes swarmed the Sydney Harbour Bridge in February. An expert review on implementing an age limit of between 12 and 16 was due to report back to the government in June.
The NSW premier, Chris Minns, appearing on the debut of Kyle Sandilands Live in August, said the government was “examining an … age limit of 12”, but hadn’t finalised the details.
On Thursday, Graham would not say if the premier had revealed the planned age limit. “I want to discuss this with my colleagues and also with the public,” he said.

Saracens boss Venter skips more media duties
- Published
Saracens head coach Joe Shaw has refused to say when, or if, director of rugby Brendan Venter will speak to the media again, despite the club facing fines for him not doing so.
Venter was not at Wednesday's pre-match press conference for their forthcoming game with Sale after not attending Prem Rugby's pre-season launch day, or doing any media duties before, during or after the opening-weekend victory at Leicester.
The Daily Telegraph reported on Tuesday that Venter had "resigned" as director of rugby and taken up a new role as "head of rugby culture and wine consultant", but this has not been confirmed by the club nor Prem Rugby.
When asked if Venter would resume media duties, as part of his responsibilities as a director of rugby, Shaw said: "I'm just going to talk about the rugby.
"I'll leave the club to talk about where we stand on all those kind of things."
BBC Sport has contacted Saracens for comment.
It is understood Sarries have already been fined £5,000 after Venter was not present at the Prem's pre-season launch day.
It is also thought a change of job title would not preclude Venter from his contractual responsibilities.
Saracens announced in January that Venter would be returning as director of rugby and have yet to publicly confirm any change to his day-to-day responsibilities.
He succeeded Mark McCall, who stepped down at the end of last season after 15 years in the job.
New injury blow for Hartley
Shaw confirmed that centre Olly Hartley broke his arm in Sunday's 40-38 win at Leicester.
Hartley, who required full knee reconstruction after a serious injury sustained in a match against Gloucester in April 2024, came off 13 minutes into the match at Welford Road.
Sarries were already 14-0 up but the next 13 minutes after Hartley's injury saw the hosts reduce the deficit to 14-12.
"When you play and train with somebody, like they have been with Olly for so long, and then it's the first game of the season and someone gets properly hurt, breaks their arm, you're human beings, it affects you," Shaw said.
"We managed to to shuffle things around really calmly, with good leadership from the people on the pitch, and it was really pleasing to get through that adversity."

This story originally appeared on Mother Jones and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
We’ve been hearing a great deal recently about the specter of AI-driven human extinction. Maybe our misplaced trust in AI intelligence will set off World War III. Or AI agents will unleash widespread cyberattacks and take over the internet. Given too much autonomy, the machines will run amok. They may seek to deceive their creators—wait, that’s already happened. Suppose they conclude, like Agent Smith in The Matrix, that “human beings … are a plague, and we are the cure.” Or perhaps the chatbots help bad humans unleash a literal plague—a biological weapon.
That last one isn’t merely theoretical. A “misuse” report Anthropic made public earlier this month detailed five cases in which foreign scientists tried to evade Claude’s guardrails on “gain of function” inquiries. That’s a euphemism for when scientists tinker with a pathogen’s genes to enhance it in some way, making it more infectious, deadlier, or better able to spread among mammals, for example.
Anthropic denied those users the answers they sought and cut off their accounts, even while noting that their motives may not have been sinister. Such information also can be used to help scientist develop pandemic countermeasures like vaccines and drugs. And there’s the rub. Like so many technologies, AI included, genetic engineering can be used for both good and evil. Hence another euphemism: “dual use.”
I studied to be a molecular biologist, and have been covering the gain of function debate since long before AI was on everyone’s radar. In my experience, researchers who work on high-risk pathogens tend to default to the view that it’s better to publish than not, and that we’re better off doing the work to understand which genetic traits make organisms a threat to humankind—never mind the potentially catastrophic consequences of an accidental release, or a deliberate one.
Is humanity really better off doing the work? I have my doubts. And I have more of them after reading the latest book from Annie Jacobsen, whom I last interviewed about her best-selling book Nuclear War: A Scenario. Her new book, Biological War: A Scenario, came out in late July and follows the same template. And because I know you were about to ask, yes, I’m sure she is great fun at cocktail parties.
One thing about Jacobsen, who has decades of high-level national security reporting under her belt, is her unrivaled access to current and former military and government officials and scientists—people who spend their days thinking about threats to humanity and gaming out how the government might respond if such-and-such horrific thing were to happen.
Beyond the notion of human extinction, perhaps the most terrifying aspect of both of her books relates to the limitations in our government’s preparation and response. America’s general plan for nuclear war was, and no doubt remains, complete madness. As for biological war, spoiler alert, it turns out we really can’t defend against it. (You’re welcome.) I’ve edited our conversation for length and clarity.
MICHAEL MECHANIC: So, Annie, now that you’ve done both the nuclear scenario and the biological scenario, which is more likely to keep you up at night?
ANNIE JACOBSEN: The Defense Department document that I reprinted in the book, on the weapons of mass destruction threat spectrum, lists nuclear weapons at the far end of the curve because they are the most destructive. But I was really surprised to see how biological weapons are a close second. And I believe the reason they’re the greatest overall threat very much ties into the discussion the entire world is having today, which is that the threshold for entry is extremely low, and therefore it is more likely to happen.
To have a nuclear weapon, you have to have weapons-grade fissile material, and then you have to think about containing those weapons within the arsenal. You have to have an ICBM, a B-2 bomber, a nuclear-armed submarine.
You’ve got to be a state!
Yes. A terrorist with a dirty bomb, that’s just a completely different threat. The component that makes biological war so incredibly dangerous and the greatest overall threat is that there are nine nuclear-armed states tasked with this containment component, but then you look at the rest of the world and who has access to [potential pandemic agents] …
Most everyone.
Yes. And that becomes terrifying.
If you were a bioweapons designer, what would you look for in a pathogen?
My mind does not think that way because I am a mother and I’m a member of society. But If I were a pandemic planner, what would scare me the most is the concept of an airborne agent and the public’s naivete to that very concept. I would think about how important it is to educate the public about the reality of what is an extraordinary threat and what isn’t.
Your scenario involves the accidental release of a weaponized pathogen from a high security lab in Russia. Based on the experts you spoke with, is an accidental release more or less likely than someone deploying a bioweapon?
Accidental release is positioned as a much greater threat for a couple of reasons. One, I learned there are very serious counterproliferation efforts at the CIA and other intelligence agencies to disrupt bioweapons programs. Whether you want to sleep better at night knowing the CIA is out there countering these things is up to you, but there are examples of biological weapons programs in the hands of terrorists being shut down.
What I came to understand is that the only people crazy enough to deploy or release a biological weapon into the community, knowing full well that the blowback would be extraordinary and would create a pandemic around the world, would be someone who had a death wish. Many terrorists fit that that category, so that is deeply unsettling. But that’s a smaller group.
And then you think about all the people—scientists, nation states, academic institutions—that are manipulating pathogens for greater virulence, for greater transmissibility in these BSL-3 and BSL-4 labs [Biosafety Level 4 is the highest security designation]. I mean, there are 3,600 of those labs around the world. There are not 3,600 terrorist organizations that I am aware of. So the chance for an accident is statistically far greater. That’s why I begin my scenario with a lab leak, and also because it’s happened before.
One can imagine a researcher sticking themself with a syringe at a BSL-4 lab and freaking out, humans being humans, and kind of going into denial and heading home.
One hundred percent—and as has happened. Then you have other examples, like [Nikolai] Ustinov, whom I wrote about in a little history lesson in the book, sticking himself with a deadly Marburg virus, from which there is no cure, and doing the good Soviet scientist thing, which is tell on himself, and then be left in a isolation ward behind sort of submarine-lock type doors to die a horrific death by hemorrhagic fever. Accidents happen.
You and I have both written on the risks of gain-of-function research, like reconstituting pandemic flu strains that can spread among ferrets—god help us if that ever got out. You write in the book that it was after 9/11, when someone was mailing around anthrax, when the riskiest research accelerated.
Yes, and I think it’s interesting. With anthrax, you’re a “dead-end host,” meaning if you breathe it in, it will kill you but it’s not transmissible. The anthrax wasn’t ever going to become a pandemic. It was meant to make people experience terror. But it’s very different when you’re talking about an airborne pathogen.
And so, flash forward to where we are now, with [advanced] genetic engineering, with gain of function research, with AI-enabled bio, and you have a situation whereby everything is on the table in terms of pandemic potential. You can tweak things. Scientists in a lab can work to create a pathogen that’s able to evade existing immunity, like the mouse pox experiment, or make something airborne, like the H5N1 ferret flu experiments. We are in a completely different world now.
I was taken aback when I called up that flu researcher, how arrogant he was: Of course you have to publish the sequence of this incredibly deadly thing. He didn’t think twice about it. There’s a hubris with some of these guys.
A hubris, or an elitism, where you talk down to the laymen because they are not scientists. As if they can’t make decisions about national security or public health because they are not scientists. I find that incredibly alarming. One of the things that’s been most impactful about my scenario books, both nuclear and bio, is that I have had subject-matter experts around the world, people who write treaties, the cardinals at the Vatican, diplomats at the United Nations, say to me: “Thank you for making this very simple to understand.”
Simplicity is powerful! I’m glad you mentioned AI, as we’re being deluged lately with existential concerns, including the Anthropic report about people using Claude to potentially try and facilitate bioweapons work. Your book doesn’t address AI at all. Did your sources have serious concerns about this technology further lowering the bar to creating deadly pathogens?
Not even a question! I chose to not include AI-enabled bio in the book because I wanted to show readers how easy it is [even without AI] for a scientist in a lab just to tweak Mother Nature’s pathogens and have a pandemic that is a near extinction-level event. But in the acknowledgements, I write about the very frightening concept of mirror life, which David Relman, the biosecurity expert and presidential advisor, explained to me, where you can extinguish all humans on the planet. I wrote Biological War: A Scenario, not Biological War: The Worst Scenario, which is pretty crazy to think about.
What’s been interesting is the subject matter experts I’ve spoken to since the book published. I was recently invited to the BSL-4 lab in Fort Detrick [in Frederick, Maryland] by Dr. Nicholas Bergman, the lab director, to do a Q&A with the staff. He explained that when the book published, the phone started ringing off the hook. Everyone [who works there] was being asked, Is this really true? Could this happen? And people’s next question was, Why don’t we know about this?
Dr. Bergman said to me, “Annie, you said the quiet part out loud.” And so, I think the fact that AI-enabled bio-threats have exploded into our consciousness is a good thing, because it is making people pay attention to the quiet part.
The threat has always been there, but you are not going to have people who work at these labs raising the flag. That’s not their job, as it was explained to me. Their job is to work on the countermeasures. Many of their questions to me were about AI-enabled bio—they were looking to me for the zeitgeist. This conversation is now happening literally in the grocery store, and also at the highest levels of subject matter expertise.
Your book talks about how President Richard Nixon unilaterally scrapped the US bioweapons program way back when. Did your experts believe we no longer have a covert program?
Biological weapons are illegal and the US position is very clear. The State Department in the current administration and previous administration both made declarative statements that it is their position that Russia and North Korea have illegal biological weapons programs, and that China and Iran have programs of concern—which I take as a euphemism.
Given the likelihood of a bioweapon coming back on its creator, it really does seem like any deliberate release would have to be a non-state actor who maybe doesn’t care so much whether they live or die.
To map out these scenarios and understand how they roll, I looked at Pentagon biological war gaming scenarios and also at pandemic planners’ unclassified scenarios. Former public health officials and cabinet-level people gather and do these exercises. For one that I referenced in the book, called Glade X, they used an ecoterrorist group that had genetically modified a Nipah virus to make it more transmissible. In this scenario, the ecoterrorists’ ideological position was that there are too many people ruining Earth, so let’s depopulate.
Sounds like the agent from The Matrix: “Humans are a virus.”
Pandemic planners come up with these very dramatic narratives to play out and understand how these situations would unfold, and that’s where most of my major plot points, if you will, come from.
You also borrowed some details from Covid, including the outbreak aboard the Diamond Princess cruise ship, except your pathogen is way deadlier.
Yes. And when I was researching Glade X, I was stunned to learn that the government is deeply concerned with a mass exodus—in that scenario it was people from Venezuela making their way to Puerto Rico in boats. And what would happen if the US Navy had to open fire on infected persons in vessels just storming into the Caribbean. It seems apocryphal until you’re reading that these pandemic planning scenarios are being thought through by the government.
One key aspect of your book is the fragility of our social order in a plague scenario. So much hinges on how people react, and how authorities react.
I was interviewing [retired Air Force] Colonel Tom Ehrhard, who ran Pentagon war game scenarios. These are nuclear and biological catastrophic-level scenarios conducted for the Office of the Secretary of Defense [via] a legendary organization called the Office of Net Assessment. Ehrhard told me, “There is no real defense against a large-scale biological attack, only things you can do to mitigate extermination.”
That is a shocking thing to hear from someone who gamed out these scenarios for the Pentagon based on an understanding of how the government functions and how the people will respond.
As a fan of Devo, I was intrigued to learn that “devolution” is part of our government’s planning. Would you talk about that?
I don’t get the reference.
The band Devo! They were big in the 1980s. Still around, I think.
Was that a reference to devolution?
Yes, but their thing was the devolution of American culture.
I did not know that. Devolution is an actual plan I learned about from [President Barack] Obama’s former FEMA director Craig Fugate. It happens in the event of a catastrophic biological event like the one I describe, and anarchy breaks out—which is expected based on the population’s fear of infection and the realization that there are not enough medical countermeasures to go around, if at all.
Anarchy leads to insurrection. The president declares the Insurrection Act, and at that point, as things really spiral out of control, the “continuity of government readiness” condition is lifted to Condition 1, which is the most extreme.
With COGCON 1 comes the triggering of the devolution plan. It involves a predetermined set of individuals, separate from those elected or appointed or in government, all of whom know who they are and have signed a contract committing to their responsibilities. They immediately leave the DC region for a series of classified bunkers located across the country. We only know that they’re called hot sites, cold sites, and warm sites. And those individuals go there and essentially wait out the catastrophe so that they can reconstitute the government.
It seems like something ripped from the pages of a dystopian novel.
It really does. The plan is classified. The name was leaked to the press about a decade ago, so FEMA officials decided to declassify the name, and that’s why Fugate could talk about it a little bit, and I was able to bring information to the table that lets your imagination kick in.
You chose a particularly nasty, weaponized, strain of the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis for your scenario. Why that particular pathogen?
I’m particularly interested in plague because we have all this history, and I could draw from accounts written contemporaneously by survivors. It was illuminating to see the utter devastation of humanity, the moral costs. I reference a lot of that in the book to give readers a sense of what actually happened: a pandemic that killed 150 million people, up to a half of Europe.
We think of plague as a disease of the past because of antibiotics. It’s astonishing that here we are, in the age of technology so advanced that we’re now worried about machines becoming smarter than humans, and we’re reverting to a situation where, because of science and technology, the medical countermeasure of antibiotics can be zeroed out. That’s why I chose plague: because it seems to be this dark metaphor for the two different uses of science and technology, one for good and one for bad.
Just like AI.
Was it your piece on the flu where someone said, “Well, we’re not just going to stop making knives because knives can kill people?”
Yes, that was the arrogant flu scientist. He also mentioned airplanes. It wasn’t too long after 9/11.
Yes! We’re not going to stop making airplanes! I’ve spent my career thinking about intent, and that’s the human component in all of this. I was astonished to learn that the Soviets had this incredibly dark, nefarious, very advanced plague program—a super plague weapon they were building—and this was 30 or 40 years ago, where genetic engineering was in its infancy. I interviewed the CIA and the British intelligence minders of these Soviet defector scientists who came here and told these [intelligence officials] what they were doing, so we got to hear things like, their intention was to kill all the people and leave the infrastructure intact. You can’t make that up.
You’d have to inoculate your entire population—and maybe that wouldn’t work by the time the pathogen circulated back around to you.
The Soviet Union was very much a castle on the hill. The wall hadn’t come down yet when they were building the plague super-weapon. And the Russians didn’t exactly fly to Paris for the weekend, so maybe there was this idea of, “We’ll inoculate everybody with a plague vaccine and the West can all die off and we’ll march in later and take over.”
You also point out that plague was perhaps the first bioweapon—when a 14th-century army led by a descendant of Genghis Khan threw plague-ridden corpses over the walls of the Republic of Genoa.
Yeah, it has had a long history, and it’s something pandemic planners and Pentagon war gamers consider a very serious threat. Pneumonic plague is airborne, with a 100 percent kill rate.
There aren’t many things with that kill rate.
Just rabies virus and plague. So, working to erase the existing medical countermeasure of antibiotics from a disease with a 100 percent case fatality rate [as the Soviets did]—that is dark.
You even made your plague a chimera—two pathogens in one!
Only because the Soviet scientists did it in the 1980s.
You think such demonic things still exist in Russia?
I can’t imagine that they wouldn’t. The way the State Department describes it, the illegal Soviet-era program was absorbed into the new Russian program. Which is deeply disturbing.
So, what’s next on your agenda? More terrifying scenarios?
[Laughs.] I write in my acknowledgements that the point is not panic. The point is pressure. On book tour, I’ve had so many people [who’d heard my book was terrifying] say, “I read it and I actually feel less terrified.”
You begin to realize there are existential fears that are based on hypothetical worry, and then there are real threats that you should be aware of. I would hope that my books would add to that part of the conversation.

Restaurant named after Xi Jinping attacked by Chinese nationals in South Korea
- Published
A restaurant in South Korea named after Chinese leader Xi Jinping has been vandalised by a group of Chinese nationals who fled home right after the attack, police say.
Surveillance footage from the restaurant in Seongnam, a city south of Seoul, shows four masked men storming the premises in the early hours of 24 September, smashing furniture and spraying lacquer.
The restaurant's owner told local media he picked the name Xi Jinping because he "wanted it to be the best Chinese restaurant [in South Korea]". He added that "There was no political intent".
The restaurant has been running for eight years but only began getting demands for a name change over the past year, The Chosun Daily reported.
The owner said that in August last year, when news broke that Xi would be attending the Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation Summit in South Korea, he received dozens of phone calls relating to these demands. Some people even offered money, he said.
"People claiming to run businesses in China proposed large sums if we changed the name," he told The Chosun Daily. "They were persistent."
In April this year, someone filed a complaint with South Korea's Ministry of Intellectual Property regarding a dish on the restaurant's menu called Xi Jinping Special Rice, but the ministry eventually closed the case, finding no issues.
The owner said last week's attack was the largest one he's experienced over the past year, telling local media the property damage amounted to about 15 million won ($11,100; £8,400).
Xi Jinping restaurant closed for five days following the attack and reopened on Tuesday. The owner says his team is now considering a new name for the eatery.
Police on Tuesday said the four suspects were Chinese men between the ages of 20 and 40. After the attack they are believed to have fled to Shanghai and Yantai, a city in China's Shandong province.
Police say they are planning to request red notices from Interpol for the four men. These are not arrest warrants, but rather requests to police around the world to detain someone pending extradition.
Xi Jinping restaurant serves a wide range of Chinese dishes, although its menu also includes some South Korean offerings, according to screenshots shared online. Google reviewers have given it an average score of four out of five stars.

From Beckham to Bale - ranking the best British exports this century
- Published
Gazza's baggy Roman shellsuit, John Charles plundering black-and-white goals in Turin, King Kev's floodlit perm dazzling Volksparkstadion terraces, Glenn Hoddle's minuscule Monegasque shorts.
They were all trailblazers and trendsetters, their tales relayed through continental dispatches and espresso-fuelled Saturday morning showreels.
Yet what was once an exotic European escapade for Britain's star footballers is now a well-trodden pilgrimage, as an increasing number of players eye opportunities further afield.
Eight of England's most recent World Cup squad are currently playing abroad - from Munich to Madrid, and Milan to the Middle East - while Scotland have even more overseas, predominantly in Serie A.
So while we acknowledge and applaud the groundwork put in by those early jetsetters, this week we're looking at the best British exports since the turn of the century.
I've ranked my top 10 below - you can have you say in the comments, too.
10. Kieran Trippier - Atletico Madrid
Kieran Trippier was seemingly deemed surplus to requirements at Tottenham after the north London outfit's Champions League final defeat by Liverpool in 2019, but the defender managed to renew his career under Diego Simeone in Spain.
The right-back became Atletico Madrid's first English player in almost a century, and then helped Los Rojiblancos win only their second La Liga title since the turn of the millennium, breaking the Barcelona and Real Madrid stranglehold.
It was the first trophy of his career, and Trippier returned to the Premier League after his Spanish sabbatical renewed, refreshed and ready to enjoy a successful spell at Newcastle.
9. Fikayo Tomori - AC Milan
John Charles, three-times winner; Jimmy Greaves, with Milan in 1961-62; and Gerry Hitchens, with Inter the following season, were the only British players to clinch a Scudetto before Juventus' Aaron Ramsey ended a wait that stretched back more than half a century in 2020.
Ramsey's Turin expedition, though, was inconsistent and expensive, and while Ashley Young then helped Inter win a first title in 11 years, his San Siro stay lasted only 18 months.
So the Scudetto winner we're plumping for here is Milan stalwart Fikayo Tomori.
The England defender lifted the prize in 2021-22, earning a spot in the Serie A team of the season on the way. And, despite ups and downs under various bosses since, the 28-year-old is now into his seventh season with the European giants. A quietly impressive feat.
8. Jadon Sancho - Borussia Dortmund
Jadon Sancho's career may not have continued on the trajectory many expected when he departed Germany in a £73m move for Old Trafford, four years after initially leaving Manchester, but his time at Dortmund was an undoubted success.
It was brave, as a 17-year-old, to reject Manchester City and move to a new country, but the young winger was vindicated with rapid progress at Dortmund.
In his second season, Sancho scored 12 goals and added 18 assists in 34 Bundesliga games, the following term he netted 17 times.
In fact, by the time Sancho left Dortmund aged 21 he'd scored 50 goals and made 64 assists across 137 games in all competitions, winning a German Cup and finishing runner-up in both the European Golden Boy prize and the Kopa Trophy for the world's best young player.
More than that, he helped establish a pathway for young British prospects to grow and develop abroad that many have followed since.
7. David Beckham - Real Madrid, LA Galaxy, AC Milan & PSG
It was tempting to include Bradley Wright-Philips, a man who followed a half-season stint at League One Brentford with a move to New York Red Bulls, winning a pair of Golden Boots, three Supporters' Shields and netting more than 100 goals during his time in the Big Apple.
But if we're talking Major League Soccer impact then there's only one winner. David Beckham swapped the Galactico comforts of Real Madrid, where he spent four seasons and collected a sole La Liga crown, for a Hollywood welcome at LA Galaxy.
Beckham's presence was at times questioned, especially when spending loan spells in Milan, but the England captain and global superstar brought a huge amount of eyeballs and allure to the American game. He left with silverware, too, twice winning both the MLS Cup and Supporters' Shield.
There was room for a five-month stay in Paris before the midfielder hung up his iconic Preds, winning Ligue 1 and waving an emotional goodbye in 2013.
6. Scott McTominay - Napoli
Maybe it's the tomatoes. Scott McTominay wouldn't touch one back in Manchester, but since moving to southern Italy he boasts the glow of a man loving both the local Neapolitan cuisine and his football.
The Lancaster-born Scot has undergone a slick transformation. Few would have expected him to veer from United squad player to cult hero mentioned in the same breath as Napoli's greatest adopted son, Diego Maradona.
But McTominay, with a little help from compatriot Billy Gilmour, has thrived in the football-obsessed maze that is Naples, firing the club to only a fourth Scudetto in history with 12 goals from midfield during his debut Serie A season.
It landed him the league's MVP award.
Finishing runners-up last term, McTominay has already etched his name in Napoli folklore, with more goals - and tomatoes - likely to follow.
5. Owen Hargreaves - Bayern Munich
Owen Hargreaves is something of an anomaly. You could argue he shouldn't count as an export given he was born and raised in Canada, before moving to Bayern Munich aged 16.
Indeed, he's the only player to represent England without having previously lived there. But winning 42 Three Lions caps legitimises his inclusion.
Born in Calgary, having also represented Wales at youth level, Hargreaves cleaned up on the silverware front during his seven seasons in Munich - winning four Bundesliga titles and several German Cups.
Yet his most impressive achievement came in Europe.
Then a 20-year-old, yet to be capped by England, he played 120 minutes in central midfield alongside captain Stefan Effenberg as Bayern beat Valencia on penalties at San Siro in 2001.
Several British players previously lost European Cup finals for foreign clubs - Kevin Keegan with Hamburg, Laurie Cunningham at Real Madrid, Steve Archibald with Barcelona and Chris Waddle at Marseille.
But Hargreaves became only the third to win it - and only two have done so since. Dortmund's Paul Lambert in 1997 was the first, we'll get to the others in a moment.
4. Jude Bellingham - Borussia Dortmund & Real Madrid
Well done for those of you who guessed. Yes, Jude Bellingham has joined the list of British players to win the Champions League for a foreign club.
Bellingham, a teen sensation at Birmingham, followed Sancho's playbook by first moving to Dortmund, where he blossomed into one of the most sought-after midfielders in Europe.
Bellingham became Dortmund's youngest ever goalscorer and also the youngest English player to start a Champions League match. Three productive seasons in Germany was enough evidence for Real Madrid to agree a deal worth more than £100m for him.
He hit the ground running, scoring 23 goals in all competitions as Madrid won both La Liga and the Champions League, and finished third in that year's Ballon d'Or.
3. Harry Kane - Bayern Munich
It was a tight call between Bellingham and Harry Kane. The midfielder boasts the accolade of becoming European champion, after all, but Kane's individual form at Bayern Munich is simply staggering and nudges him into third spot.
To date, Kane has scored 101 Bundesliga goals in 98 games - that figure stands as 152 goals in 154 games overall for Bayern Munich.
The Three Lions captain has shattered all kinds of records in Bavaria. He won the European Golden Shoe in his debut season, the first Englishman since Kevin Phillips to do so, and is the fastest player in Bundesliga history to hit a century of goals.
Oh, and Kane finally won the team silverware he craved for so long, too. He now has two Bundesliga titles and a German Cup to his name, though the Champions League - and potentially a Ballon d'Or - remain the ultimate target.
2. Steven McManaman - Real Madrid
Was Steven McManaman underappreciated? He perhaps didn't earn the number of England caps his talent deserved. In fact, the last of those 37 Three Lions outings came before he won a second Champions League with Real Madrid, despite pleas from club team-mates such as Zinedine Zidane that he should be given a recall.
The marauding winger's move to Madrid in the summer of 1999 was unique - he was the first English player since Laurie Cunningham in 1982 to feature for Los Merengues and the first to move to the Bernabeu directly from the Premier League.
It came at a time when Spanish football was harder to consume for UK audiences, before the peak Revista de la Liga era, making McManaman, renowned for his dribbling and creativity, something of an enigma.
But the Bootle-born midfielder enjoyed an impressive four-season stint in Spain, scoring a volley against Valencia in the Champions League final win of 2000 and coming off the bench to collect another winner's medal two years later, adding to two La Liga successes.
1. Gareth Bale - Real Madrid & LAFC
There is, however, one clear leader when it comes to the best British exports since the turn of the century - and potentially of all time.
Gareth Bale, the Welsh marvel, who has more Champions League winner's medals than the rest of this list combined. Five of them, in fact, across a nine-year spell that saw Real Madrid dominate Europe's showpiece competition.
Bale's commitment to Los Blancos' cause was sometimes questioned - he did make it clear Wales, and golf, were his priorities - but his return was still impressive.
The flying forward scored 106 goals in 258 games, with three of those coming in Champions League finals, including an outrageous overhead kick in 2018.
His short stint before retirement in Los Angeles was less memorable, but still yielded a Supporters' Shield and MLS Cup triumph, where he scored a last-gasp leveller before LAFC won on penalties.
