A video showing smoke emerging from a skyscraper is being shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it shows Iranian missile attacks on Israel. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows the damage caused by Iranian missiles launched at Israel in 2026.
Fact: This video shows a fire that broke out at Marina Pinnacle, a 67-storey skyscraper also known as Tiger Tower, in Dubai in June 2025. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to a video posted on X featuring similar visuals by nexta tv in June 2025. The post was captioned, “Dubai skyscraper engulfed in massive fire — nearly 4,000 people evacuated from the building. Fortunately, there were no casualties. Rescue teams responded quickly and assured that the residents of the complex are now safe.”
Taking this as a clue, we conducted a relevant keyword search and found media reports featuring the viral visuals (here, here, and here). According to these reports, a 67-storey skyscraper known as Marina Pinnacle, also called Tiger Tower, had caught fire. The Dubai Civil Defence took six hours to completely extinguish the blaze. The Dubai Media Office reported that there were no casualties.
We also reviewed the location of Marina Pinnacle in Dubai on Google Street View and found that the buildings and other visual details match those seen in the viral video.
To sum up, an old video of the Dubai Skyscraper Fire is being falsely shared as a video of an Iranian missile strike on Israel.

Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?
- Published
Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army.
Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict.
There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted.
This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago.
Why has fighting broken out now?
It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray.
The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions.
This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting.
This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation.
The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray.
Who are the TPLF?
For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government.
It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades.
At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population.
When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence.
Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century.
The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine.
An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022.
Why has the peace deal faltered?
There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray.
The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army.
Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991.
When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa.
The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum.
For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms.
The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy.
But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy.
This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions.
Who is backing the TPLF?
A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies.
Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army.
Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power.
So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside.
TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated.
Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests.
What is the government's position?
As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country.
It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies.
During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out.
Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports.
Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force.
What do we know about the bombing in Tigray?
Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces.
The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify.
Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war.
This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces.
The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks.
What is being done to stop the fighting?
The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks.
It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently.
The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict.
The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume.
The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated.
Could the fighting spread?
Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia.
The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia.
The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily.
There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government.
The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters.
The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis.

Frontier-level AI models right on your desk. Unprecedented AI and gaming performance on Mac. Very small for this amount of power. Tons of ports. Supports up to four 5K monitors.
TIRED
Can get very hot. Still can't compete with Nvidia in GPU. There are cheaper AI boxes out there.
The Mac Studio has a new calling in life. For awhile, it seemed like overkill for just about anyone, regardless of profession.
But these days, computers with over 64 GB of RAM and tons of GPU performance have an entire playground of on-device AI tools to exclusively explore. With a Mac Studio, you can have a full-on agentic AI framework, generate high-end video all on-device, or run the latest foundation-level large language models (LLMs). The Mac Studio is relatively unique among the available options—at least, for now.
But beware: If you're tired of hearing about AI, turn away now.
Power Box
Apple has always catered to a high-performance crowd, and with the surge of interest in local AI, its systems are uniquely set up to excel in that area. But first, the box itself. It's about as tall as a coffee mug, but it's a 7-inch-square footprint. I bet most people have never seen a Mac Studio in person, and if you get the chance, you might be surprised by how large it actually is.
The Mac Studio remains the only Mac to keep USB-A ports around. That alone's worth the souped-up $11,000 model, right? (That's a joke). Here, you get two, along with four, Thunderbolt 5 ports, Ethernet, HDMI, and a headphone jack. You can connect up to four 5K external displays at 120 Hz using the Thunderbolt and HDMI ports, if that's your jam. Interestingly, as compared to the Mac Mini, the Studio swaps the front-facing headphone jack with a full SD card slot. Photographers and videographers will appreciate that.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
I do wish the Mac Studio came in more than one color, such as Space Black. Still, the Mac Studio comes in two distinct versions. The M5 Max model starts at $2,499, which comes with 36 GB of memory and 512 GB of storage. This is the reasonable configuration, designed for content creators, game developers, and media professionals. One way to think about it: It delivers the same performance as the MacBook Pro with M5 Max, but for substantially less money. There's a $1,250 difference in price even when similarly configured. The other benefit is that Apple offers more expandability in storage and memory options on the Mac Studio than on a MacBook Pro.
But that's not the model I tested. The configuration I was sent for review is that aforementioned $11,000 model, with the M5 Ultra processor and unified memory maxed out to 256 GB. That's definitely the most expensive computer I've ever had on my desk, but it's not even the priciest Mac Studio configuration you can get. The M5 Ultra is the most singularly powerful chip Apple has ever made (yet), and its first quad-die chip. It's absolutely massive. Over its high-speed interconnect, it essentially stitches together two M5 Max chips, for a total of 36 CPU cores. Think of this as the equivalent of Apple's $3,299 Studio Display XDR in terms of use case. It's extremely targeted.
Regardless of the configuration, the Mac Studio's true power comes from its obscene number of GPU cores and unified memory. You can configure it with anywhere from 36 GB to 256 GB of memory (a 512 GB model is coming in October), and up to 80 GPU cores. Let's be real—only AI enthusiasts and AI developers need more than 64 GB of memory. If that's you, there's reason to be excited about this version of the Mac Studio. While you've always been able to configure it with up to 256 GB of unified memory, the M5 Ultra adds unprecedented GPU performance to the mix. It has twice as many GPU cores as the M5 Max, the same amount as the previous M3 Ultra.
Don't think of the M5 Ultra as providing the same uplift as upgrading from the M5 Pro to the M5 Max, which is a more modest upgrade that focuses primarily on GPU performance. But two generations of GPU improvements in the Ultra chips have made each core more powerful, in both gaming and AI. Notably, each GPU core now includes a Neural Accelerator, a feature of the entire “M5” family of chips that further enhances AI workload performance.
All the AI
The astounding part about the Ultra is that, in some cases, it really doubles performance over the Max. While single-core benchmarks don't show much difference, the doubled CPU cores allow the M5 Ultra Mac Studio to outperform the M5 Max (as tested in a 16-inch MacBook Pro with an 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU, plus 48 GB of memory) by 51 percent—as tested in Cinebench 2026. I'm still a bit shocked by that. The GPU performance doesn't scale quite as perfectly, but it was 32 percent faster than the M5 Max. Gaming tests put these two scores together and really show how vastly superior the M5 Ultra is. The industry-standard 3DMark Steel Nomad benchmark put the M5 Ultra at a 41 percent higher score than the M5 Max.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
But it's in actual games where the Mac Studio really impresses. It can run Cyberpunk 2077 at 160 frames per second on the M5 Ultra, which is 61 percent faster than on the M5 Max. The happy-medium preset I landed on was running it at 2560 x 1400 resolution on Ultra. The game looks incredible, especially on an HDR screen. (I just so happened to be testing it with a Studio Display XDR). It can even run the game natively in 4K at 53 fps at this same preset, though I found myself most comfortable in 1440p on Ultra. Having options on how you want to tweak a game is always ideal, and for the first time, the M5 Ultra is fast enough to do just that. It's no RTX 5090-powered gaming PC, but this is as close as a Mac has ever been.
No one is buying a Mac Studio for gaming, of course. And while it's a useful test of performance, I really wanted to see how the system could handle on-device AI workflows. This Mac Studio configuration offers huge amounts of memory, but the bandwidth is another major benefit the M5 Ultra Mac Studio has over the M3 Ultra (Apple skipped the M4 Ultra). It's 1.2 TB per second compared to 89 GB per second, which is crucial for running models on-device.
I set up a simple agentic AI task in LM Bionic to summarize a dozen local files, running on a fairly small 9-billion-parameter Qwen 3.5 model; it completed the task in 2 minutes, compared to almost 10 minutes on the M5 Max MacBook Pro. But here's where I got sufficiently impressed. I loaded up a much larger, 122-billion-parameter version of Qwen 3.5, and I was blown away by the speed. It felt very much like using a frontier-class LLM right on my computer, completely offline and without accessing the cloud. And, of course, being local means it has access to your machine. So I set up the same simple agentic task using this much more expansive model, and it still finished in under 2 minutes (with much more accurate and useful results, too).
Over in Draw Things, I ran some on-device image and video generation to really see what an 80-core GPU can do. Using the MiniMax H3 model, it took over 11 minutes to generate a 15-second video completely on-device. There's a long way to go before this feels like a viable alternative to cloud-based options or needing a high-powered discrete GPU like an RTX 5090 or 5080 for this kind of task. Obviously, paying this much to run AI locally is a niche endeavor. But as models get more efficient and quality improves, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio's capabilities should improve over time. We're still in the early days.
During these AI tests, in particular, I noticed how warm the Mac Studio gets when it's fully under load. You definitely don't want to touch it or set anything on top of it. You also want to leave some room behind it, since it blows a lot of hot air out of the vents. The fans can spin up quite loudly too—though, like all modern Macs, it takes a couple of minutes for the fans to really get going. The front-facing ports stay cool, though, thanks to the vents in the thermal system sitting right underneath the Mac Studio.
Only the Beginning
The Mac Studio is certainly unique. Because mini Windows PCs typically use laptop chips, they don't typically support more than 64 GB of RAM. That's where this top-end M5 Ultra Mac Studio really feels unbeatable (and even earns its sky-high price from that perspective). Add the upcoming option for 512 GB of memory (and the ability to connect four Mac Studios and use them as a single computer), and you have something extremely niche—but wholly unrivaled.
The base M5 Max Mac Studio does have stronger competition, though. For $2,399, you can get a Geekom A9 Mega Mini PC with 64 GB of RAM, 1 TB of storage, and AMD's new Ryzen AI Max+ 388. That's more memory and more storage for less money. Importantly, that AMD chip uses unified memory the same way Apple Silicon does, which is crucial for running local AI workloads. We'll hopefully be getting the Geekom A9 in for testing to see how it stacks up in real-world tests.
More competitors are coming soon, too. Nvidia's RTX Spark “superchips” are the main upcoming rival, offering up to 128 GB of unified memory in both laptops and mini PCs. They still can't do 256 GB of memory like the Mac Studio, but these will hopefully turn up the heat on the Windows and Linux side.
Luke Larsen is a product writer and reviewer at WIRED, covering laptops, PCs, Macs, monitors, and the wider PC peripheral ecosystem. Srinagar, Sep 23: Police on Wednesday attached a residential property in Jammu and Kashmir's Baramulla district under UAPA in a terror-related case.
The residential property was attached under Section 25 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, in connection with an FIR registered in the north Kashmir district, a police spokesman said.
The attached property comprises a double-storeyed residential house at Namblan village in Sheeri belonging to accused Aijaz Ahmad Ganie, he said.
During the course of the investigation, the property was found, prima facie, to have been used for providing shelter and logistical support to terrorists and facilitating terrorist activities, thereby attracting the relevant provisions of the UAPA concerning proceeds of terrorism, the spokesman said.
The attachment was carried out after obtaining requisite approval from the Director General of Police, he said.
A public notice was also displayed at the property, prohibiting its sale, transfer, lease, mortgage or creation of any third-party interest, the spokesman added.
He said the action forms part of Baramulla Police's sustained efforts to disrupt and dismantle the logistical and support infrastructure of terror networks and to proceed, in accordance with law, against persons and properties found involved in facilitating terrorist activities.

Family of Renee Good files wrongful death lawsuit over ICE shooting
Mother and poet, 37, shot dead by federal immigration agent in Minneapolis in January, sparking wave of public protest

The family of Renee Good, the mother shot and killed by an ICE agent in Minnesota this year, has filed two federal lawsuits alleging wrongful death.
Good, 37, was fatally shot on January 7 on Portland Avenue, Minneapolis, after a confrontation with ICE agent Jonathan Ross, who opened fire on her as she sat behind the wheel of her SUV, apparently attempting to leave the scene of their argument.
“Renee’s death was not an accident,” the law firm representing Good’s family, Romanucci and Blandin, said in a statement. “It was the predictable result of a coordinated campaign by senior officials in this administration to target Minnesotans of Somali or Hispanic origin and silence anyone who dared to raise their voice in protest.”
Attacking the federal immigration crackdown in which the agent concerned was deployed, they said: “Operation Metro Surge was built on exaggerated fraud accusations that the White House embraced as a pretext for thousands of masked, unidentified federal agents to rove neighborhoods and stop people based on how they looked.
“Administration officials told agents to force confrontations with observers like Renee and led agents to believe they would face no consequences for using force.”
The two lawsuits were filed by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and the deceased’s brother Brent Ganger.
The first, filed against “the United States of America,” alleges the wrongful death of Renee Nicole Macklin Good under Minnesota law predicated on claims of battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused her death.
The second alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights. It names among the defendants: Ross, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller; former Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem; former Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino, Corey Lewandowski and “John Doe federal agents 1-10.”
Good’s death was met with a huge public outcry, which only grew louder when another citizen, Alex Pretti, was also killed by federal agents in the same city later that month.

Christa Pike's failed lethal injection attempt: What is pentobarbital and why did Biden ban it?
Christa Pike, 50, remained alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection

Christa Gail Pike survived on Wednesday after being given two doses of the lethal drug pentobarbital, according to her lawyers.
Pike, 50, was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and was taken by an ambulance from the prison, her attorneys said. She was being treated at a hospital, but they said they hadn't been told about her condition.
She had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. Wednesday for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
A death penalty expert said it was an unprecedented failure, and Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee halted the remaining executions for the rest of the year.
Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said in court filings late Wednesday. The Biden administration had previously removed pentobarbital from the federal protocol for single-drug lethal injections over concerns about the potential for unnecessary pain and suffering.
Gov. Bill Lee said in a statement that he has ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred" and that the remaining scheduled execution will not take place this year.
"Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State's most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective," he said.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that they "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General's Office."
The state's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered "if the inmate is not deceased" after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.
Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced is "singular and unparalleled."
Seven other people have survived medical problems due to an execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.
Media witnesses observing from a separate room said officials raised curtains to the execution chamber at 7:27 p.m., showing Pike strapped to a gurney.
Christa Pike’s ‘last words’
"I'm going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life and that is in love," she said in her "last" words. She described herself as at peace.
But Pike remained awake and at one point raised her head and asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way. It was unclear what she was referring to.
By 8:26 p.m., execution witnesses reported that the second dose of pentobarbital had been administered. Pike continued to snore behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8:53 p.m. At that time, an announcement told media witnesses to leave the area.
Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday to the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in "unnecessary agony" and it was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit Court and a district court.
It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to carry out an execution: In May, state officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried and failed for over an hour to place an IV to administer pentobarbital.
What is pentobarbital?
Pentobarbital, a barbiturate that slows activity of the brain and nervous system, is often used by doctors to treat seizures and convulsions. In an execution, pentobarbital can be used in combination with other drugs or by itself. So far this year, 14 inmates have been executed by single-drug doses of pentobarbital — seven in Texas, six in Missouri and one in Georgia.
In America, pentobarbital is known by its brand name, Nembutal.
Despite the limited availability of pentobarbital, it has been used in many cases of euthanasia or assisted suicide across the world.
It belongs to the class of drugs known as barbiturates. Invented in the late 19th century, they depress various aspects of brain function. Barbiturates have been used for many purposes, including to treat sleep disorders, epilepsy and traumatic brain injury.
In high doses, these drugs can cause suppression of breathing and death. Because of the risks associated with overdoses, they have been withdrawn from routine medical use over the last 20 years.
History of pentobarbital
States use a variety of drugs and drug combinations in lethal injections. Two of the most common are midazolam and pentobarbital.
Attorney General Merrick Garland in the final days of the Biden administration withdrew the pentobarbital lethal injection policy after a government review of scientific and medical research found there remains “significant uncertainty” about whether its use causes unnecessary pain and suffering.”
The Justice Department this year reauthorized the use of single-drug lethal injections with pentobarbital that were used to carry out 13 executions during the first Trump administration — more than under any president in modern history.
A Trump administration report claimed the Biden administration ‘got the standard and the science wrong’.. The Biden administration’s findings, among other things, “failed to address the overwhelming evidence” that an inmate injected with pentobarbital quickly “loses consciousness—rendering him unable to experience pain,” the report said.
“The prior administration failed in its duty to protect the American people by refusing to pursue and carry out the ultimate punishment against the most dangerous criminals, including terrorists, child murderers, and cop killers,” Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement at the time. “Under President Trump’s leadership, the Department of Justice is once again enforcing the law and standing with victims.”
Since capital punishment was reinstated in the 1970s, more than 1,600 prisoners have been executed in the United States, the vast majority by state authorities.

Loved ones of a missing Australian trekker who was last seen nearly two weeks ago on a remote South American hiking trail are urging local authorities to help with the search.
A wide-scale sweep by a private rescue crew has so far failed to find any trace of 30-year-old Jordan Yap, who last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru’s Huayhuash mountain range, 400km north-east of Lima.
He was last seen near the beginning of his trek across the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, which is regarded as a challenging, high-altitude trek through the remote Andes mountains.
Regarded as a very experienced hiker by friends and family, the Melbourne man failed to make contact on Wednesday, his estimated return date.
He also failed to check back into the Krusty hostel in Huaraz, where his luggage remains stored, and missed a scheduled flight from Lima to Cusco on Thursday.
“It’s really uncharacteristic of him to not have communicated at any point in his journey if he had the chance to,” longtime friend Kevin Nguyen said.
“It is a very popular trek, where you might have 200 to 300 hikers and guides per week during the busy season, so it is very uncharacteristic that no one’s seen him since day one or day two.”
The avid trekker misplaced a satellite beacon he was travelling with days before he set off on the 120km hike, raising further concerns.
Local mountain rescue organisation Socorro Andino Peruano has been hired by Yap’s family to help with the search.
His loved ones are holding out hope the rescue group, which recently rescued a Canadian trekker from the same trail, will be able to find him safe.
“Time is of the essence … because ultimately, as much as we were saying he’s been missing since the 23rd, he’s had no contact with anyone since the 14th,” Nguyen said.
Rescue crews completed their biggest day of search operations so far on Saturday (Sunday morning AEST), scouring various trails on the circuit to no avail.
“I know Jordan likes to orienteer and navigate and he’s quite an adventurer himself, so I wouldn’t be surprised if he tried an alternative route,” Nguyen said.
Yap had been planning the trek for more than a year and had recently bought a GPS watch to allow for offline maps to guide him on the hike.
“He was telling everyone about how he was ready to go on a big hike like this, [he was] really excited,” Nguyen said.
He was last known to be wearing a white jacket, green sunshade sweater and grey pants.
The experienced trekker was believed to be carrying a 40-litre hiking bag, Durston dome tent and hiking poles.
Family and friends are urging the Australian government to work with Peruvian officials and local authorities to mobilise further resources in and around the rugged region.
The Australian embassy in Peru is helping his family.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has been contacted for comment.

The All India Mobile Retailers Association (AIMRA) and the All India Consumer Products Distributors Federation (AICPDF) have called off their “No UPI Day” protest, which was earlier scheduled for October 2. The move came after representatives of 20 trade associations met finance minister (FM) Nirmala Sitharaman to raise concerns related to the likely impact of the UPI merchant discount rate (MDR) on small and medium businesses. The delegation was led by Praveen Khandelwal, who is a BJP member of Parliament (MP) from Chandni Chowk and secretary general of the Confederation of All India Traders (CAIT). “More than 20 organisations, including AIMRA and AICPDF, expressed their concerns. The finance minister assured that all issues would be considered with utmost seriousness. Accordingly, the call for the proposed ‘No UPI Day’ on October 2 has been withdrawn,” said Khandelwal while briefing the media after meeting the FM. According to Economic Times, the two industry bodies sought deferment of the proposed MDR ahead of the upcoming festive season and heightened business activity. They also reportedly called for keeping merchant-to-merchant transactions outside the ambit of the proposed regime. As per the report, the trade associations also called for increasing the ₹1 Lakh monthly receipt limit for merchant exemptions to ₹5 Lakh. Meanwhile, Khandelwal also said, “Dialogue between the government and traders' organizations on all essential issues, including cybersecurity, will continue moving forward”. The development comes days after AIMRA and AICPDF called for a nationwide protest against the proposed UPI MDR on October 2. At the time, the latter had said that its network of around 4.5 Lakh distributors and 1.3 Cr retailers will participate in the protest. At the heart of the row is the MDR debate, which gained momentum earlier this month after the finance ministry allowed a 0.4% MDR on specified P2M UPI transactions above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and above. It is set to come into effect from October 15. The move marked a major shift from the zero-MDR regime, which was implemented almost seven years to spur UPI payments. However, banks, payment aggregators and third party application providers (TPAP) have lauded as the framework unlocks a new revenue stream for companies operating in the UPI ecosystem. However, the proposed charges have triggered a wider debate over their impact on merchants, businesses and consumers. Retailer groups have warned that the MDR could discourage UPI acceptance, particularly as festive-season transactions often exceed ₹2,000. Fuel dealer associations have also sought government intervention over higher payment processing costs. Meanwhile, brokers and investment platforms such as Zerodha and INDmoney have raised concerns about charges on transactions that may not generate corresponding trading revenue. Shortly after the proposal was introduced, a petition was filed in the Supreme Court (SC), challenging the framework. The plea argued that merchants could indirectly pass on the cost to consumers through higher prices. However, the SC later temporarily refused to stay the new MDR framework, but has sought responses from the Centre, the RBI and the NPCI on the petition.

Srinagar, Sep 22: The Jammu and Kashmir National Conference Additional General Secretary and Rajya Sabha Member Choudhary Mohammad Ramzan Tuesday said that the discontinuation of the December 5 holiday commemorating the birth anniversary of Sher-e-Kashmir Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah and attempts to obstruct the elected government’s efforts to restore the holiday, raise serious questions about respect for the democratic mandate and public sentiment.
He said the manner in which BJP legislators reacted to the proposal in the Assembly to restore the holiday on Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah’s birth anniversary reflected their narrow-mindedness, communal outlook and hostility towards the National Conference.
Choudhary Ramzan, as per a party statement, said Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah’s stature and legacy do not depend on any official holiday. His historic struggle against subjugation, deprivation, poverty and economic backwardness in Jammu and Kashmir and his efforts to politically awaken and empower the people, remain deeply associated with the history of the region. The measures undertaken under his leadership concerning popular rights, land reforms and social justice constitute an important chapter of modern Jammu and Kashmir’s history.
He said the changes made to official holidays associated with July 13, Martyrs’ Day, and Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah’s birth anniversary are viewed by the National Conference in the context of its historical legacy and the memory of those who sacrificed their lives for the political rights of the people. He stressed that the martyrs of July 13, 1931, hold an important place in Jammu and Kashmir’s political history and that their sacrifices cannot simply be erased from public memory.
Choudhary Ramzan said the National Conference has, from the outset, expressed its concerns over the fundamental changes made to Jammu and Kashmir’s constitutional and administrative framework after August 5, 2019. He said the abrogation of Jammu and Kashmir’s special constitutional status and its reorganisation into two Union Territories raised profound questions among the people regarding their political, constitutional and democratic rights.
He said the people of Jammu and Kashmir have elected their representative government through the democratic process and the elected government should be provided adequate constitutional and administrative space to implement its decisions and fulfil public expectations. If an elected government decides to restore a holiday associated with the birth anniversary of a historic personality, he said, the matter should not be subjected to unnecessary administrative hurdles.
He further said that decisions concerning the constitutional and democratic rights of the people of Jammu and Kashmir, which have been altered or restricted over the past several years, should be addressed through democratic processes, constitutional institutions and in accordance with the aspirations of the people.

The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said, after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly.

WASHINGTON — The Department of Health and Human Services announced a set of new initiatives aimed at speeding up clinical trials by incorporating more artificial intelligence and computational models and moving away from sharply delineated trial phases.
The centerpiece five-year program, dubbed SURPASS — “Simulation-augmented, Real-time Platform Adaptive Seamless Trials” — will kick off later this fall by accepting “ground-breaking ideas from cross-disciplinary teams in statistics, AI, and clinical trial design, operations, and regulation,” reads a website about the program.
HHS is launching the program through the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health. The initial announcement did not note how much funding was designated for the new initiatives, nor did it provide details on whether participants would be offered more flexibility or resources.

Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far
- Published
Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months.
The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police.
Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer.
The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
Here's what we know.
Busisiwe Mahlangu
Case 1
Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties.
Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed.
Itumeleng Kekana
Case 2
Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026.
The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park.
No arrests have been made so far.
Nomfesane Mjobo
Case 3
Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park.
Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises.
No arrests have been made.
Unknown woman
Case 4
Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear.
No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made.
Gracious Nkomo
Case 5
Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area.
Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death.
Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo
Case 6
Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park.
Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case.
Unidentified woman
Case 7
Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed.
No arrests have been made.
Dineo Motapane
Case 8
The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive.
Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni.
She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case.
Jabulile Ntimba
Case 9
The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni.
According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence.
The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice.
Ntombifuthi Nxumalo
Case 10
The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.
This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death.
A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge.
Unidentified woman
Case 11
The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni.
The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area.
The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared.
No arrests have been made.
Boitumelo Gift Mashita
Case 12
Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken.
Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand.
Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies.
While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September.
The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg.
It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni.
President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience".
South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day.
Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests.

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners.
“Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.
As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together, in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”
The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi university, by three men who posed as police officers.
Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood, after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.
Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year old were also reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by the bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.
Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.
Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say that nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic underreporting.
This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and they could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.
Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi university, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.
While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country requires a deep societal shift where men no longer feel they have ownership over women’s bodies.
“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,’ she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”
Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.
“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”
Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women; as one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.
Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old a graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender-equality initiative, said she has experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.
She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”
The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before – but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.
“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago, but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe.’”
Many of the Delhi university students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.
“Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades,” said Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for her masters in English at Delhi University. “It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”
Many on the marches said that it was no coincidence the protests took place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, which saw hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians take to the streets over education reform.
“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

Jammu, Sep 23: The 17-year-old son of BJP Hiranagar MLA Vijay Kumar was traced to Delhi early Wednesday, a day after he was reported missing from his hometown in Kathua district of Jammu and Kashmir, officials said.
Aditya Kumar, a Class 11 student, left for Delhi on Tuesday evening to meet his sister without informing his family, prompting them to file a missing person report at the local police station, the officials said.
After hectic efforts, police teams traced Kumar while he was travelling on a Delhi-bound bus.
Acting on leads gathered during the night-long search, the police located the bus and established contact with the teenager, who is now being brought back to Jammu, the officials said.
His father had also left for Delhi on getting information about his son's whereabouts

- Take-Two has signed a new publishing deal with Xbox and Microsoft ahead of GTA 6's November 19, 2026, release.
- According to the deal, Take-Two can develop, publish, market, advertise, and sell Xbox products for all Xbox devices.
- Microsoft retains approval rights over marketing materials, while Take-Two earns revenue from Xbox digital sales.
After weeks of Sony boasting about how GTA 6 plays best on PS5, Take-Two has now signed a new publishing deal with Xbox and Microsoft less than two months before the game’s release on November 19, 2026. Most Xbox players would think that the GTA 6 publisher is doing a hard pivot towards their platform, but that’s not the case.
According to Take-Two’s SEC filing, the GTA 6 publisher and Xbox’s parent company, Microsoft, have entered a new “long-term XBOX Publisher License Agreement with an effective date of September 17, 2026. The Agreement grants the company to develop, publish, have manufactured, market, advertise, distribute, and sell Xbox compatible products for all XBOX devices.”
In the deal, Microsoft retains approval rights over game concepts, final versions, and certain marketing materials. So, this has less to do with GTA 6, and more so about a deal renewal that both companies already had. Microsoft will also pay Take-Two through wholesale pricing and/or revenue sharing on its digital products.
Take-Two could have renewed the deal to cover Project Helix, which is rumored to launch in 2027, after mentioning “all Xbox devices.” The previous publisher agreement was specific to Xbox consoles such as Xbox One and Xbox Series X|S, so the new one should encompass all the upcoming ones too, including Project Helix.
So, what does this mean for Rockstar’s upcoming title? Nothing, really. It means that Microsoft can continue to market GTA 6 on its Xbox consoles ahead of its November 19 launch. Given that GTA 6 is already “breaking records” on Xbox, the renewed publishing deal simply ensures that Take-Two and Microsoft can continue their existing commercial relationship as the game heads toward release.
Some people also seem to think that this is a sign of a potential Xbox sale in the future. However, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has already confirmed that Microsoft isn’t selling Xbox. That said, do you think this new publishing deal between Take-Two and Xbox will have an impact on GTA 6? Let us know.

India’s startup ecosystem entered a more selective funding environment in Q3 2026, with investors deploying capital more cautiously amid macroeconomic pressures, elevated valuations and a sharper focus on high-conviction bets. According to Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’, homegrown new-age tech ventures raised $2.2 Bn between July and September, up 5% from the $2.1 Bn raised in the year-ago quarter. However, the number of deals fell 13% from 240 in Q3 2025 to 210 in the just-concluded quarter. The median ticket size remained flat year-on-year (YoY) at $3 Mn. The funding momentum was largely driven by four mega deals (rounds of at least $100 Mn) versus just one such transaction in Q3 2025. The quarter also saw two startups, Emergent and Astrotalk, enter the coveted unicorn club against zilch in the year-ago period. It must be noted that Q3 2025 was the weakest third quarter for the Indian startup ecosystem since 2023, when startups managed to raise just $1.7 Bn across 205 deals. At $2.2 Bn, funding in Q3 2026 was well below $3.4 Bn in Q3 2024 and the eight-quarter historical average of approximately $2.7 Bn. The number of active unique investors also fell 24% YoY to 511 in Q3 2026 from 676 in Q3 2025. In terms of venture capital (VC) activity, 3one4 Capital recorded the highest deal volume with 19 transactions, followed by Rainmatter, Zerodha’s corporate investment arm, with 16 deals and IvyCap Ventures with 15. That said, macroeconomic pressures, including higher inflation, softer household spending, high fuel prices, and weak equity market performance, continued to impact capital deployment across the ecosystem this year. Nevertheless, cumulative startup funding since 2014 has crossed $176 Bn across more than 12,600 deals. Now, let’s take a look at some of the trends that dominated startup funding activity last quarter. Growth Stage Startups Lead Q3 Funding Trend A defining structural shift during the quarter was the distribution of venture capital between growth and late stage startups. Growth stage funding (Series A and Series B) emerged as the primary driver of quarterly funding growth. Capital deployed at this stage rose 38% YoY to $1.1 Bn across 90 deals. This is despite a meagre 4% YoY uptick in median ticket size for investments at this stage to $8.3 Mn. Late stage funding (Series C and above) declined 10% YoY to $994 Mn across 27 deals. Even though the quarter recorded more mega deals, the median late stage ticket size fell 18% to $18 Mn, pointing to more cautious deployment at the top end of the funding cycle. Early stage funding also weakened, falling 18% YoY to $164 Mn across 93 deals, a 15% decline in deal volume. However, the median ticket size increased 20% YoY to $1.2 Mn, suggesting that investors were writing larger cheques for a smaller set of early stage companies. Aina, Dextr AI, DeHaat Honest Farms and BCT Ventures each raised seed rounds exceeding $3 Mn during the quarter, highlighting continued investor appetite for startups with strong early traction or a differentiated proposition. AI Dominates Sectoral Charts Big ticket deals made a comeback in Q3 2026. Four mega deals materialised during the quarter compared with just one in the year-ago period. Here’s a sneak peek: Emergent ($130 Mn): The AI startup raised $130 Mn from Creaegis, Khosla Ventures, SoftBank, Lightspeed and Y Combinator, entering the unicorn club River ($120 Mn): The electric vehicle (EV) maker secured $120 Mn from Elev8 Venture Partners, Claypond Capital, Anicut Capital, Alteria Capital, InnoVen Capital and Stride Ventures Navi ($100 Mn): The IPO-bound fintech startup raised $100 Mn from Prosus in its first institutional funding round Pixxel ($100 Mn): The spacetech company raised $100 Mn from Temasek, 360 ONE Asset, IMM Investment, Radical Ventures and growX ventures The distribution of these rounds across AI, mobility, fintech and spacetech suggests that high ticket investor conviction is broadening beyond consumer internet businesses. On the sectoral front, AI attracted the most capital in Q3 2026, raising $438 Mn across 35 deals. Funding surged 265% YoY, while deal volume rose 35% YoY. Emergent’s $130 Mn round and Ema’s $77 Mn Series B were two of the largest AI funding rounds during the quarter. However, concerns over high entry valuations are tempering investor enthusiasm for AI startups. According to Inc42’s survey of 85+ institutional investors, 63% said Indian AI valuations had risen beyond comfortable levels. While 32% expected a meaningful correction over the next 18 months, 31% described valuations as mildly elevated but supported by actual revenue. Only 12% considered current valuations fully justified, while 25% said it was too early to assess. Notably, capital deployment across the AI segment in Q3 2026 was largely concentrated around startups building in the application layer of AI. So, it was no surprise that 39% of the surveyed investors favour vertical AI applications over base infrastructure. While 23% of investors see greater opportunities in AI hardware startups, only 14% believe sovereign AI models offer meaningful investment opportunities. Beyond AI, cleantech attracted $433 Mn across 23 deals, more than three times the year-ago figure. EV startups accounted for 57% of cleantech deals, led by River, Yulu and Ultraviolette. Deeptech startups raised $290 Mn, up 176% YoY, even though deal volume remained flat at 28. Spacetech companies accounted for 21% of overall deeptech funding. Conversely, traditional capital magnets (fintech and ecommerce) saw a more muted response from investors this quarter. Although the highest number of funding deals (44) materialised in the ecommerce segment, total funding in the sector tanked 31% YoY to $245 Mn. Meanwhile, fintech funding fell 11% YoY to $249 Mn across 13 deals. Bengaluru Leads The Startup Squad Bengaluru widened its lead as India's primary startup hub in Q3 2026. Startups based in the city raised $1.4 Bn+ across 80 deals during the quarter, up 157% YoY. The city also accounted for 64% of the total startup funding. Delhi NCR ranked second with $301 Mn (down 27% YoY) across 53 deals, followed by Mumbai with $223 Mn (down 64% YoY) across 34 deals. Bengaluru’s funding total was driven by large rounds raised by Emergent, River, Pixxel, Navi, Yulu, Ultraviolette, and Ultrahuman. Bengaluru also accounted for 65% ($189 Mn) of the $290 Mn raised by Indian deeptech startups, buoyed by big-ticket rounds of Pixxel, Airbound and QNuLabs. Bengaluru has long maintained a dominance in venture capital activity in the world's third largest startup ecosystem and, per investors, will continue to be the favoured spot for their capital deployment. Given the underlying deeptech shift within the ecosystem, more than half of the investors surveyed by Inc42 identified Bengaluru as the startup hub best positioned to lead India’s deeptech ecosystem by 2030. Meanwhile, 25% backed Chennai and Hyderabad followed at 20%. A Quarter Of Investor Exits The quarter remained especially favourable for early investors, as consolidation and IPO activity remained rampant. The Indian startup ecosystem recorded 22 M&A deals during the quarter under review, up 69% YoY from 13 in Q3 2025. Prominent completed transactions included upGrad’s Unacademy acquisition for $200 Mn, Imarticus Learning’s BELLS buyout for $84 Mn, and Housing.com’s acquisition of Aurum PropTech for $48 Mn. With this, total quarterly startup M&As remained above 20 for three consecutive quarters in 2026, with 24 in Q1 and 28 in Q2. Meanwhile, the likes of ESDS Software Solution, Klassroom, Shiprocket and Rentomojo made their public market debuts during the quarter. All in all, six (nearly 50%) new-age tech stocks listed on the Indian bourses in Q3, giving investors many lucrative exits. Here are some of the notable investor exits of this season: KKR-managed Vertical Holdings, which commanded a 73.78% stake in LEAP India, sold its stake worth ₹1,998.6 Cr via the IPO. Accel India, RentoMojo’s largest institutional shareholder, sold 78.47 Lakh shares for ₹317 Cr, registering a gross return multiple of 8.6X. Shiprocket’s early investor 500 Global generated 77.6X returns, while Tribe Capital sold shares worth ₹120 Cr at a return multiple of 7.6X. The Beginning Of A New Startup Exit Cycle? Of the 85+ investors surveyed by Inc42, 72% said they held late stage portfolio companies with some degree of IPO readiness. Of this group, 57% described their companies as “moderately ready” but waiting for a more favourable market window, while 15% said that their portfolio companies were actively preparing to file their respective draft red herring prospectuses (DRHPs). Despite the expanding IPO pipeline, only 32% of investors expect domestic IPOs to generate the largest share of their portfolio liquidity over the next 24 months. Secondary buyouts emerged as the preferred route, with 38% of investors expecting them to deliver the highest liquidity volume. Meanwhile, listed new-age technology companies delivered mixed but broadly positive returns. Between July 1 and September 25, Inc42’s New Age Tech Index gained 3.38%, outperforming the Nifty 50 by nearly seven percentage points. As of September 25, 2026, Inc42’s New Age Tech Index included 65 of the 72 new-age tech stocks listed on India’s mainboards that had traded for more than a month during the quarter. Excluding Nasdaq-listed MakeMyTrip and Freshworks, the combined market capitalisation of the remaining India-listed new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s coverage touched $177 Bn, or ₹16.47 Lakh Cr, during the quarter. India’s startup ecosystem ended Q3 2026 on a cautiously resilient note. While funding grew 5% YoY, fewer deals and a decline in active investors pointed to a more selective market. Capital increasingly favoured growth stage ventures, AI, deeptech and cleantech, while fintech and ecommerce saw muted investor interest. At the same time, rising M&A activity and a growing IPO pipeline signalled improving exit opportunities. However, secondary buyouts remain the preferred liquidity route among investors, suggesting that public markets alone may not drive the next phase of exits. Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.
Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.
The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.
Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:
‘Climate risk maps’ in China
In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.
Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.
In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.
Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.
The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.
Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater
El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.
The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.
In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.
But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.
Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.
The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.
Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia
In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.
During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.
“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.
The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.
“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”
With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.
To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.
“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”
South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system
South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground.
The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.
Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.
Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons
Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.
El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.
Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.
Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.
The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.
This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.

I've been a chef for over 15 years, and even though professional kitchens aren't for everyone, there are several lessons and tricks I learned in culinary school that can come in handy for anyone.
Here are some of the most helpful tips to take your at-home cooking game to the next level.
Use a damp napkin or towel to keep your cutting board in place.
If you're tired of your cutting board moving around while you use it, place a damp paper or dish towel underneath it.
Whether your board is wood or plastic, this trick will help keep it in place and create a more stable work surface.
Keep your knives sharp.
A sharp knife is a safe and effective tool, but dull ones can slip off food and cause all sorts of unintended injuries.
You can buy tools to sharpen your knives at home if you don't want to visit a professional. Just do a bit of research to see what type of sharpener works best for your particular knife.
Prep as much as you can in advance.
The more you prep, the more you can sit back and relax when it's time to actually cook. Chop up your ingredients, measure out your spices, and set yourself up for success and save time later.
For example, most restaurants strain scrambled eggs the day before, then pour out individual portions to cook.
You can do something similar if you're having people over for brunch — crack your eggs in a container with a tight-fitting lid, mix them up, and keep them in a very cold fridge until you're ready to cook them.
Plus, ingredients like scallions and greens can be washed, sliced, and wrapped in paper towels or kept in an ice bath until ready to use.
Don't wait to bring your pasta water to a boil.
When making pasta, get that large pot of water salted, filled up, and on the stove first thing. A lot of prepping can be done while the water boils.
Salt each component of your dish.
Make sure to salt each individual component of your dish, not just the finished product. If the parts taste great, the whole will too.
Use water to easily thin sauces or soups.
Most restaurants actually thin dishes with water. If they can do it, so can you.
If your sauce is too dry or soup is too thick, you don't need to run to the store for more stock or broth — simply turn on the tap.
Just make sure to add a little bit at a time, since you can always pour in more, but you can't take it away.
Be mindful about which oils and fats you choose to cook with.
If a recipe is telling you to use a specific oil or butter, you may want to listen. Not all fats are created equal.
Butter and olive oil burn at high temperatures, so use avocado or grapeseed oil for sautéing.
If you want to use butter, you can clarify it — or remove the milk solids by melting and pouring off the liquid — to keep the flavor high and the risk of burning low.
When making something like risotto, add cold butter at the end.
Butter is the secret to a rich risotto as the ingredient tones down acidity, adds creaminess, and generally makes things taste really good.
Following the beurre monté technique, add a pat of cold butter to a saucepan with a bit of simmering water and swish it around until the mixture is thick and emulsified.
Then, to make the most of the fat, add it to your risotto at the end. This can upgrade things like veggies or pasta, too.
Many meals can be elevated with a touch of acidity.
If your sauce is boring or a bit flat, acid may be just the thing to fix it.
Whether it's lemon juice or vinegar, just a splash of acid can make all the difference in brightening a dish.
Don't overmix your batters.
For the fluffiest pancakes and the lightest desserts, mix all your ingredients only until they're just combined (unless a recipe states otherwise).
Don't worry about leftover lumps. They'll generally absorb and hydrate into the batter as it cooks, making those light-as-air baked goods a reality.
You probably don't want to cook everything on the same rack in your oven.
You shouldn't cook everything in your oven the same way or at the same height.
Roast veggies at high heat on the bottom rack for maximum browning, and finish dishes up top under the broiler for a crispy, melted look.
For baking, you should cook most things in the middle so the heat is evenly distributed from top to bottom.
Let meat and fish rest at room temperature before cooking.
Pull meat and fish out of the fridge about 30 minutes before cooking to temper them, which can help them cook more evenly.
Also, rest your meat on a paper towel to absorb surface moisture and help achieve an evenly browned finished product.
